A 58-year-old woman is seen in clinic for review. She is halfway through 6 cycles of chemotherapy and complains of tiredness, muscle weakness and lethargy. Routine blood tests are taken with the following results.


Hb	112 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	211* 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	4.62 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Na+	137 mmol/L	(135 - 145)
K+	4.2 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Urea	2.8 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	56 µmol/L	(55 - 120)
CRP	9 mg/L	(< 5)
Calcium	2.19 mmol/L	(2.1-2.6)
Phosphate	1.23 mmol/L	(0.8-1.4)
Magnesium	0.24 mmol/L	(0.7-1.0)

Which of the following cytotoxic agents is most likely to be responsible?
options_json: ["Docetaxel", "Vincristine", "Cisplatin", "Cyclophosphamide", "Cytarabine"]
explanation_text:
Cisplatin is associated with hypomagnesaemia

The correct answer is cisplatin. Platinum-based compounds are commonly used to treat ovarian cancer and can cause a number of side effects including peripheral neuropathy, ototoxicity and hypomagnesaemia, as seen here.

Taxanes such as docetaxel are often used in combination with platinum-based compounds to treat ovarian cancer. Common side effects include neutropenia but they do not cause hypomagnesaemia.

Vincristine is more commonly used to treat haematological malignancies and breast cancer. Common side effects include peripheral neuropathy and paralytic ileus.

Cyclophosphamide can be used to treat ovarian cancer, but is not associated with hypomagnesaemia. It more commonly causes haemorrhagic cystitis, myelosuppression and transitional cell carcinoma.

Cytarabine is used to treat haematological malignancies and can cause myelosuppression and ataxia.

question_text:
An 18-year-old man presents with recurrent but relatively infrequent severe episodes of chest and abdominal pain on a background of fatigue and anaemia. Haemoglobinopathy screening identifies sickle cell disease. His parents are not affected.

What genotype is associated with a milder form of this disease and the likely genotype of this patient?
options_json: ["HbAA", "HbAC", "HbAS", "HbSC", "HbSS"]
explanation_text:
Hb SC is a milder form of sickle disease

HbSC

disease is the second most common type of sickle cell disease. It occurs when you inherit the Hb S gene from one parent and the Hb C gene from the other. Individuals with HbSC have similar but milder symptoms to individuals with HbSS.

Normal adult haemoglobin, Haemoglobin A, is the most common haemoglobin found in adults and is composed of two α and two β-globin chains. If a person inherits a haemoglobin A gene from each parent

(HbAA)

, that person will have normal haemoglobin.

Haemoglobin C is an abnormal type of haemoglobin and is a type of haemoglobinopathy. The disease is caused by a problem in the β-globin gene and is one of the most common structural haemoglobin variants. People with haemoglobin C trait

(HbAC)

are phenotypically normal, with no clinically evident limitations or symptoms.

People who inherit one sickle cell gene (HbS) and one normal gene (HbA) have sickle cell trait

(HbAS)

. As sickle cell disease is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern, people with sickle cell trait usually have no medical problems related to sickle cell trait.

HbSS

is the most common and most severe type of sickle cell disease. It occurs when you inherit the haemoglobin S gene mutation from both parents. In this type, the body only produces haemoglobin S.

question_text:
A 28-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with abdominal pain and constipation. She drinks 4 bottles of wine per week.

On examination, there is mild abdominal tenderness, but the abdomen is soft and there is no guarding or rigidity. A sensory peripheral neuropathy is noted, affecting the lower limbs.

Blood tests:


Hb	88 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	189 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
MCV	72 fL	(80-96)
WBC	4.6 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Na+	138 mmol/L	(135 - 145)
K+	4.2 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Urea	5.3 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	88 µmol/L	(55 - 120)
CRP	4 mg/L	(< 5)
Film comment	Basophilic stippling	

What is the likely diagnosis?
options_json: ["Acute intermittent porphyria", "Alcohol excess", "Familial Mediterranean fever (FMF)", "Lead poisoning", "Polyarteritis nodosa"]
explanation_text:
Abdominal pain, constipation, neuropsychiatric features, basophilic stippling → lead poisoning

Lead poisoning

is correct. The patient has abdominal pain, constipation and peripheral neuropathy in association with microcytic anaemia and a blood film demonstrating basophilic stippling. The unifying diagnosis is lead poisoning.

Acute intermittent porphyria

is incorrect. This is a plausible differential as it can also cause gastrointestinal and neurological symptoms and signs. However, basophilic stippling is typical of lead poisoning.

Alcohol excess

is incorrect. Excess alcohol use may result in abdominal pain and peripheral neuropathy. It is also a cause of sideroblastic anaemia, which may cause microcytic anaemia. Basophilic stippling is not typical but rather a dimorphic blood film in this case.

Familial Mediterranean fever (FMF)

is incorrect. This can cause abdominal pain in the form of peritonitis and theoretically could cause peripheral neuropathy with secondary amyloidosis. However, the abdominal findings here do not suggest peritonitis given the abdomen is soft and there is no guarding or rigidity. Additionally, it is not associated with microcytic anaemia or basophilic stippling.

Polyarteritis nodosa

is incorrect. This can cause abdominal pain and peripheral neuropathy. However, vasculitis is typically associated with systemic inflammation e.g. raised CRP, which is absent here.

question_text:
A 26-year-old female is diagnosed with an unprovoked DVT and a thrombophilia screen is performed.

What abnormality is most likely to be found?
options_json: ["Factor V Leiden", "Lupus anticoagulant", "Protein C deficiency", "Protein S deficiency", "Waldenstrom's macroglobulinaemia"]
explanation_text:
Factor V Leiden is the commonest inherited thrombophilia

Factor V Leiden is the commonest inherited thrombophilia in European populations (approximately 5% prevalence of a heterozygous mutation).

Protein C and S deficiency are possible answers but both are less common than Factor V Leiden. Lupus anticoagulant is another possible answer and features in antiphospholipid syndrome but this is again less common.

Waldenstrom's macroglobulinaemia typically presents in elderly males with symptoms of hyperviscosity.

question_text:
A 31-year-old male with a past medical history of known sickle cell disease presents to the emergency department with pain in his right leg.

He described the pain as a throbbing, severe pain which he believes has been precipitated by the recent cold weather. He has had three similar episodes in the last five years.

The pain is not initially controlled with two boluses of 5mg of subcutaneous morphine. He reports no chest pain is not short of breath.

His observations are taken: heart rate 95 bpm, blood pressure 134/78 mmHg, temperature 36.3 ºC, saturations 96% on air, respiratory rate 15/min.

What further information is required to arrive at a diagnosis of acute vaso-occlusive crisis?
options_json: ["Chest X-ray", "Full blood count", "No further investigations are required", "Peripheral blood film", "X-ray of the right femur"]
explanation_text:
In sickle-cell, acute painful vaso-occlusive crises should be diagnosed clinically

Whilst other investigations may be required for making sure other complications of a sickle cell vaso-occlusive crisis are taking place, the initial diagnosis of a vaso-occlusive crisis should be diagnosed clinically. Hence, no further investigations are required in the diagnosis of vaso-occlusive crises.

A chest X-ray is not required to diagnose a vaso-occlusive crisis. Chest X-rays are indicated where a patient has respiratory symptoms, fever or chest pain. The presence of pulmonary infiltrates may be an indication of acute chest syndrome. A chest X-ray may be requested as part of routine investigations in the emergency department but it is not required for the initial diagnosis.

A full blood count may demonstrate a degree of longstanding anaemia or possibly a sudden drop in haemoglobin from an acute haemolytic crisis. This is a rare complication of vaso-occlusive crises and is not required for the initial diagnosis. The patient is haemodynamically stable and does not appear to be exhibiting features of an acute haemolytic crisis. A full blood count is likely to be requested as part of the routine investigations for a patient with sickle cell before admission.

A peripheral blood film may show the presence of nucleated red blood cells, sickle-shaped cells and Howell-Jolly bodies. It may be indicated in the monitoring of patients with sickle cell to rule out other causes of anaemia but cannot be used to determine whether a patient is in a vaso-occlusive crisis.

An X-ray of the femur can be used to demonstrate areas of bone infarction. Infarctions can be seen on X-ray as irregular bony margins, or moth-eaten destruction with overlying periosteal new bone formation. Nevertheless, most bone infarctions are diagnosed clinically by symptoms and X-rays are not required for the diagnosis.

question_text:
A 25-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with profuse bleeding from his gums and fluctuating levels of consciousness. On examination, he has a blood pressure of 97/45 mmHg and a widespread petechial rash over his trunk.


Platelets	45 * 10 9/L	(150 - 400)
Prothrombin time (PT)	22 secs	(10-14 secs)
Activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT)	41 secs	(25-35 secs)

Following stabilisation, he is transferred to a ward where an oncologist reviews him and arranges cytogenetic testing, which reveals a t(15;17) translocation.

What is the most appropriate initial management for this man?
options_json: ["All-trans retinoic acid (ATRA)", "Anthracycline-based chemotherapy regimen", "CHOP chemotherapy regime", "Haematopoietic stem cell transplant", "Methotrexate"]
explanation_text:
APML is treated with all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) to force immature granulocytes into maturation to resolve a blast crisis prior to more definitive chemotherapy

Acute promyelocytic myeloid leukaemia (APML) typically presents with disseminated intravascular coagulopathy (DIC), as demonstrated in this patient. Clinical manifestations include both haemorrhagic symptoms (evidenced by gingival bleeding and a petechial rash) and thrombotic events (suggested by fluctuating levels of consciousness, which may indicate cerebral micro-emboli). The patient's haematological profile is consistent with DIC, characterised by thrombocytopenia and prolonged prothrombin time (PT) and activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT). Additionally, APML is commonly associated with the t(15;17) chromosomal translocation, which can be identified through cytogenetic analysis. The initial management of patients diagnosed with APML involves the administration of

all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA)

, followed by definitive chemotherapy.

While an

anthracycline-based chemotherapy regimen

is a therapeutic option for APML, it is not the most appropriate initial treatment. According to the clinical scenario provided, ATRA should be administered first, with subsequent chemotherapy to follow.

A

CHOP chemotherapy regimen

, consisting of cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine and prednisolone, is primarily indicated for non-Hodgkin's lymphoma rather than APML. Therefore, its use in this context would be inappropriate.

Considering a

haematopoietic stem cell transplant

, this intervention may be reserved for severe or treatment-resistant cases of APML but is not considered standard initial therapy before ATRA administration. Thus, it is not the correct choice in this instance.

The use of

methotrexate

may have a role in the maintenance phase of APML treatment to prevent relapse; however, it does not constitute an initial therapeutic approach and hence is not correct here.

question_text:
A 58-year-old woman presents with a mass in the left breast and general weight loss. She has no significant past medical history. She is urgently referred for further investigations, which demonstrate oestrogen receptor-positive invasive ductal carcinoma. Following a discussion at the local breast oncology meeting, she is commenced on anastrozole.

What is the mechanism of action of this drug?
options_json: ["Aromatase inhibitor (AI)", "Gonadotropin releasing hormone (GnRH) agonist", "Human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) modulator", "Selective oestrogen receptor modulator (SERM)", "Topoisomerase-II-mediated DNA repair disruptor"]
explanation_text:
Anastrozole and letrozole are aromatase inhibitors that reduces peripheral oestrogen synthesis

A number of drugs are used depending on which receptors and markers are positive in the disease. In the case of oestrogen receptor positivity, an anti-oestrogen drug should be used. This patient is 58 and can be assumed to be postmenopausal. As such, anastrozole and letrozole are typically used. These drugs are

aromatase inhibitors

(AIs) - aromatisation accounts for the majority of oestrogen production in post-menopausal women.

Goserelin is an example of a

GnRH agonist

, not an AI. This is typically used in pre-menopausal women, not post-menopausal, to suppress ovarian function as an alternative to tamoxifen.

Trastuzumab is an example of a

HER2 modulator

. These may be considered for patients with HER2-positive early-stage breast cancer. Anastrozole does not fall into this category of drugs.

In pre-menopausal women with oestrogen receptor-positive breast cancer,

SERMs

are typically used in preference to AIs. The most common example of this family of drugs is tamoxifen.

Doxorubicin is a disruptor of

topoisomerase-II-mediated DNA repair

. This is a chemotherapy agent sometimes used in the treatment of breast cancer, not a hormonal agent.

question_text: Which one of the following translocations is associated with acute promyelocytic leukaemia?
explanation_text:
Acute promyelocytic leukaemia - t(15;17)

The correct answer is

t(15;17)

. This translocation is typically associated with acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APL), a subtype of acute myeloid leukaemia. In this chromosomal abnormality, there is a reciprocal translocation between the long arms of chromosomes 15 and 17. This results in a fusion gene, PML-RARA, which produces an abnormal retinoic acid receptor protein that blocks the maturation of myeloid cells and leads to an accumulation of promyelocytes.

t(9;17)

is not associated with any specific type of leukaemia. It's worth noting that chromosomal translocations in leukaemia often involve genes that regulate cell growth and differentiation. However, t(9;17) does not involve such genes and hence it's not linked to any known malignancies.

t(9;22)

, on the other hand, is associated with chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML), not APL. This translocation results in the Philadelphia chromosome and generates BCR-ABL1 fusion gene which has tyrosine kinase activity leading to uncontrolled cell proliferation.

t(15;22)

is linked to Ewing sarcoma, a rare type of cancer that occurs in bones or soft tissue around the bones. This translocation results in a fusion gene EWSR1-ERG which promotes cell proliferation and inhibits cellular differentiation.

Finally,

t(17;22)

is associated with dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans, a rare skin cancer. The result of this translocation is COL1A1-PDGFB fusion gene which leads to overproduction of platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF), causing cells to multiply excessively.

question_text:
A 43-year-old man, currently an inpatient on a surgical ward for acute pancreatitis, develops episodic epistaxis. Blood tests are taken which demonstrate the following:


Platelets	52 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
Prothrombin time (PT)	23 secs	(10-14 secs)
Activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT)	46 secs	(25-35 secs)
Fibrinogen	0.8 g/L	(2 - 4)
D-Dimer	1203 ng/mL	(< 400)

Given the likely diagnosis, what would be expected on blood film?
options_json: ["Elliptocytes", "Heinz bodies", "Howell-Jolly bodies", "Schistocytes", "Spherocytes"]
explanation_text:
DIC is associated with schistocytes due to microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia

The diagnosis here is disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), a procoagulant state due to the activation of coagulant pathways. It can be triggered by a number of factors - in this instance, an acutely unwell patient. The blood tests show a depletion of platelets and coagulation factors, characteristic of DIC. The condition is associated with

schistocytes

due to microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia.

Elliptocytes

would not typically be expected due to DIC. These are erythrocytes that appear rod- or pencil-shaped. These are seen in iron deficiency, thalassaemia and a number of other conditions.

Heinz bodies

are inclusions within red blood cells due to a number of conditions, including alpha-thalassaemia and glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency. They would not be expected in DIC.

Howell-Jolly bodies

are inclusions within red blood cells, characteristic of decreased splenic function, such as post-splenectomy. They would not be expected in DIC either.

Spherocytes

are erythrocytes that are sphere-shaped rather than biconcave. These would not be expected in DIC, and are seen in hereditary spherocytosis.

question_text:
A 23-year-old woman is reviewed in the Allergy clinic. She had presented to the Emergency Department two weeks ago with a wheeze and swollen lips, which was unresponsive to multiple doses of adrenaline. She reports that both she and her mother have had a number of allergic reactions in the past, but have never been able to identify a trigger.

Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following is the most appropriate test to request from this clinic?
options_json: ["C1 complement levels", "C1 inhibitor levels", "C2 complement levels", "C4 complement levels", "Mast cell tryptase"]
explanation_text:
Hereditary angioedema - C4 is the best screening test inbetween attacks

This patient has a likely diagnosis of hereditary angioedema. Features pointing towards this are repeated episodes of spontaneous angioedema without an obvious allergenic trigger; failure of resolution of the angioedema with adrenaline; and a family history of a similar problem. The most reliable laboratory test to screen for hereditary angioedema between acute attacks is C4 levels, which are characteristically low.

C1 complement levels, particularly C1q levels, tend to be normal in hereditary angioedema, and hence this is not used as a diagnostic test for the condition.

Low levels of C1 inhibitor are the best diagnostic test to send during an acute attack, but this test would have lost its sensitivity two weeks after an acute episode.

C2 complement levels are often also low between acute attacks of hereditary angioedema, but C4 levels are a more reliable, and hence more widely used screening tool.

Mast cell tryptase is useful in confirming suspected anaphylactic reactions, but cannot confirm a diagnosis of angioedema due to C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency. When mast cell tryptase is used, it tends to be used within the first 24h of suspected anaphylaxis, and is not a useful test two weeks after suspected episodes.

question_text:
A 22-year-old man attends the allergy clinic. Over the last 12 months, he has had recurrent attacks of swelling of his lips and tongue. These are often proceeded by a painful macular rash.

At the clinic, what investigation is most appropriate to identify the diagnosis?
options_json: ["ANA", "C1-INH", "C2", "C4", "Tryptase"]
explanation_text:
Hereditary angioedema - C4 is the best screening test inbetween attacks

C4

is correct. The clinical features are highly suggestive of hereditary angioedema.  Low C2 and C4 levels are seen both during and even between attacks in this condition. However, serum C4 is the most reliable and widely used screening tool.

ANA

is incorrect. Although autoimmune conditions (such as systemic lupus erythematosus) can cause angioedema, there are no other clinical features in this case to suggest an autoimmune pathology.

C1-INH

is incorrect.  Low levels of C1-INH occur during an attack, however, return to normal levels following recovery.

C2

is incorrect. Although low C2 levels are associated with hereditary angioedema, serum C4 is the most reliable and widely used screening tool.

Tryptase

is incorrect. Although anaphylaxis remains within the differential diagnosis, the presence of a painful macular rash makes this an exceedingly unlikely diagnosis.

question_text:
A 67-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a 4-week history of progressive dyspnoea, weight loss, and haemoptysis. Chest X-ray shows a right hilar mass with mediastinal widening. CT scan confirms a 5 cm right hilar mass with extensive mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Serum biochemistry reveals hyponatraemia. A bronchoscopic biopsy is performed.

Which tumour marker would most likely be elevated in this patient?
options_json: ["Alpha-fetoprotein", "Bombesin", "CA 19-9", "Carcinoembryonic antigen", "Prostate specific antigen"]
explanation_text:
Bombesin is a tumour marker in small cell lung carcinomas

Bombesin

is the correct answer. The clinical presentation strongly suggests small cell lung carcinoma (SCLC). The patient has a hilar mass with mediastinal lymphadenopathy, which is typical of SCLC. Additionally, the presence of hyponatraemia is a common paraneoplastic manifestation of SCLC due to inappropriate ADH secretion (SIADH). Bombesin is a neuropeptide that functions as a tumour marker in SCLC. It is produced by neuroendocrine cells and has been found to be elevated in patients with SCLC. Bombesin stimulates the growth of SCLC cells and may contribute to the aggressive nature of this malignancy. It can be used as a diagnostic marker and potentially as a therapeutic target, though it's not routinely measured in clinical practice compared to other markers like neuron-specific enolase for SCLC.

Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP)

is incorrect. AFP is primarily associated with hepatocellular carcinoma and germ cell tumours, particularly non-seminomatous testicular cancer and some teratomas. It is not typically elevated in lung cancers, including SCLC. The clinical scenario does not suggest liver involvement or a testicular primary with metastasis to the lung.

CA 19-9

is incorrect. This tumour marker is primarily associated with pancreatic adenocarcinoma, although it can also be elevated in biliary tract malignancies, gastric cancer, and colorectal cancer. It is not a characteristic marker for lung cancers, including SCLC. The clinical presentation with a hilar mass and mediastinal lymphadenopathy is not consistent with pancreatic cancer.

Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA)

is incorrect. While CEA can be elevated in various malignancies including some lung cancers, it is more commonly associated with colorectal cancer. It is not specifically elevated in SCLC compared to other lung cancer types. Non-small cell lung cancer, particularly adenocarcinoma, is more likely to show CEA elevation than SCLC.

Prostate specific antigen (PSA)

is incorrect. PSA is specific to prostate tissue and is elevated in prostate cancer and some benign prostatic conditions. There is no indication in the scenario that this patient has prostate pathology, and PSA is not associated with lung malignancies. The clinical presentation with respiratory symptoms and a hilar mass is inconsistent with prostate cancer as the primary diagnosis.

question_text:
A 10-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with acute onset pain in his hands for the past 2 hours. He has a history of recurrent infections. Physical examination shows tender diffuse swelling of his hands bilaterally.

His blood tests show:

Hb	80 g/L	Male: (119-150)
Female: (119-150)
Platelets	200 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	5 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)	86 fL	(80-100)

Peripheral smear examination shows numerous sickled red blood cells (RBC) and Howell-jolly bodies. Haemoglobin electrophoresis confirms sickle cell disease.

Which of the following is a beneficial prophylactic drug for him?
options_json: ["Hydroxyurea", "Morphine", "Paracetamol", "Methotrexate", "Erythropoietin"]
explanation_text:
Hydroxyurea increases the HbF levels and is used in the prophylactic management of sickle cell anemia to prevent painful episodes

Management of sickle cell disease comprises of two different aspects. Acute episodes are treated with sufficient hydration using intravenous fluids and effective analgesia which may include morphine.

Chronic management attempts to prevent the occurrence of acute episodes and prevent or treat the complications that may arise from this condition. Hydroxyurea has been shown to reduce the frequency of painful crisis and reduce the need for blood transfusions. It acts by increasing the level of fetal haemoglobin (HbF) in the blood which has a higher affinity for oxygen than haemoglobin A. As HbF binds strongly to oxygen, it prevents desaturation of the red blood cells which is a precipitant of sickling. Another aspect to be considered is that HbF causes a left shift of the oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve which prevents sickling.

Paracetamol is an analgesic that acts by inhibiting cyclooxygenase enzyme. It can be used in cases of mild pain and thus not useful in preventing attacks and unlikely very helpful alone for management of acute episodes which often present with severe pain. Methotrexate is a chemotherapeutic agent that competitively inhibits dihydrofolate reductase so reduces the synthesis of tetrahydrofolate. It is used in the treatment of several cancers but has no role in the management of sickle cell disease.

Erythropoietin is a naturally occurring hormone synthesised in the renal interstitium in response to hypoxia. It acts on the bone marrow to increase the production of red blood cells. It can also be used as a medication in certain conditions to raise the red blood cell count such as renal failure.

question_text:
A 65-year-old man presents to the emergency department with frank haematuria. He has a history of diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis with lung fibrosis. He has recently been treated with cyclophosphamide.

Observations:


Heart rate 88 beats per minute
Blood pressure 101/65 mmHg
Temperature 37ºC

On examination, there is mild suprapubic tenderness.

Urinalysis


leucocytes	++
Protein	-ve
Blood	+++
Nitrites	-ve
Glucose	-ve

Blood tests:


Hb	131 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	189 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	4.2 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Na+	138 mmol/L	(135 - 145)
K+	4.2 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Urea	5.2 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	88 µmol/L	(55 - 120)
CRP	8 mg/L	(< 5)

Given the likely diagnosis, what medication would have been most appropriate to administer to prevent this complication?
options_json: ["Azathioprine", "Idarucizumab", "Mesna", "Septrin", "Tranexamic acid"]
explanation_text:
Cyclophosphamide - haemorrhagic cystitis - prevent with mesna

Mesna is the correct answer. The patient presents with frank haematuria and abdominal tenderness after recent treatment with cyclophosphamide. This is likely to represent haemorrhagic cystitis, which is a known complication of this treatment.  Mesna detoxifies acrolein, a urotoxic metabolite of cyclophosphamide that accumulates in the bladder. It is typically co-administered with cyclophosphamide to prevent this complication.

Azathioprine is incorrect. This may be used as a disease-modifying agent in scleroderma related lung disease but would not prevent haemorrhagic cystitis.

Idarucizumab is incorrect. This is a reversal agent for the anticoagulant agent dabigatran. Haematuria is a possible complication of anticoagulation treatment. However, the patient is not on anticoagulation in this scenario and it has no role in preventing haemorrhagic cystitis.

Septrin is incorrect. Antibiotic prophylaxis with septrin during cyclophosphamide treatment is designed to prevent

Pneumocystis jirovecii

pneumonia rather than haemorrhagic cystitis.

Tranexamic acid is incorrect. This is not the usual treatment for prophylaxis against haemorrhagic cystitis with cyclophosphamide treatment. Additionally, there is the risk that it precipitates clot retention in haematuria and so is typically avoided.

question_text: A 34-year-old man who is known to have type 1 von Willebrand's disease asks for advice. He is due to have a tooth extracted at the dentist next week. Which one of the following is the most appropriate management to reduce the risk of bleeding?
options_json: ["Mefanamic acid", "Vitamin K", "Desmopressin", "Factor VIII concentrate", "Factor VII concentrate"]
explanation_text:
Desmopressin is used in the management of Von Willebrand's disease

The correct answer is

Desmopressin

. Desmopressin (DDAVP) is a synthetic analogue of vasopressin that stimulates the release of von Willebrand factor (vWF) and Factor VIII from endothelial cells. In type 1 von Willebrand's disease, where there is a quantitative deficiency of vWF, desmopressin is the first-line treatment for minor procedures such as dental extractions. It can be administered intranasally or intravenously and effectively raises vWF and Factor VIII levels for several hours, providing adequate haemostasis for minor procedures.

Mefanamic acid

is incorrect as it is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) that inhibits platelet function and would actually increase the risk of bleeding in this patient. NSAIDs should be avoided in patients with bleeding disorders, particularly around the time of procedures.

Vitamin K

is incorrect as it is involved in the synthesis of clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X. It would not help in von Willebrand's disease as this condition involves a deficiency of vWF, not vitamin K-dependent factors. Vitamin K is useful in warfarin reversal or vitamin K deficiency states.

Factor VIII concentrate

is incorrect as monotherapy for type 1 von Willebrand's disease. While Factor VIII levels are often secondarily reduced in von Willebrand's disease, replacing Factor VIII alone without addressing the vWF deficiency would not be the most appropriate first-line treatment for a minor procedure.

Factor VII concentrate

is incorrect as it is primarily used in the treatment of Factor VII deficiency or as activated Factor VII (NovoSeven) in severe bleeding or specific indications. It would not address the underlying vWF deficiency in von Willebrand's disease and would be an inappropriate and costly choice for a dental extraction in type 1 disease.

question_text:
A 26-year-old man has been referred to the immunology clinic after three hospital admissions in the last year with lip and tongue swelling and shortness of breath. On all of these occasions, he denies exposure to specific allergens and nothing could be identified that may have precipitated the attacks.

On all three occasions, he was given hydrocortisone, chlorphenamine, and adrenaline with no improvement in his symptoms.

Clinical examination was normal with no evidence of lip or tongue swelling. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations were normal.

Which test is likely to confirm the diagnosis?
options_json: ["Immunoglobulins", "Mast cell tryptase", "C1-INH (C1 esterase inhibitor)", "C2", "C4"]
explanation_text:
Hereditary angioedema - C4 is the best screening test inbetween attacks

The correct answer is C4. C4 is the most reliable screening test for hereditary angioedema.

Immunoglobulin levels are not used in the investigation or management of hereditary angioedema.

Mast cell tryptase is helpful in anaphylactic and allergic reactions, but of no benefit in hereditary angioedema.

C1-INH can be tested during an acute attack of hereditary angioedema and are often low. However, this is not a valid screening tool for hereditary angioedema and so shouldn't be performed between episodes.

C2 is low between attacks of hereditary angioedema, however, levels are not as reliable as C4 and therefore this is not the correct answer.

question_text:
An 18-year-old female presents to the emergency department with easy bruising, bleeding gums, and recurrent epistaxis. Additionally, she reports heavier than usual menstruation 2 weeks ago. She is otherwise well. On examination, there are areas of petechiae on the upper and lower limbs, evidence of dried blood in the nasal cavity, and small blood blisters on the tongue. There are no other abnormal findings. There is no evidence of active bleeding and she is haemodynamically stable.

Investigations:


Hb	110 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	34 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	8.0 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)

Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line therapy for this patient?
options_json: ["Cyclophosphamide", "Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG)", "Oral prednisolone", "Platelet transfusion", "Splenectomy"]
explanation_text:
First-line treatment for ITP is oral prednisolone

Oral prednisolone is the correct answer. The history provided above with significant thrombocytopaenia, normal white cell count and relatively normal haemoglobin in an otherwise well patient is consistent with a diagnosis of idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP). The first-line treatment for ITP is 1-2mg/kg oral prednisolone.

Cyclophosphamide is an incorrect answer. Cyclophosphamide is not a first-line therapy for ITP. It can be used as a second-line therapy in the management of severe refractory ITP, although targeted monoclonal antibodies, like rituximab, have become a more preferred option.

Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) is an incorrect answer. IVIG is used as a first-line therapy for patients with life-threatening haemorrhage or the potential for life-threatening haemorrhage. Typically this refers to patients with severe thrombocytopenia (<30x10

9

/L) and evidence of a haemostatic defect (e.g. mucous membrane haemorrhage) or active bleeding. This patient has no evidence of active bleeding, her platelets are >30x10

9

/L and she is haemodynamically stable.

Platelet transfusion is an incorrect answer. Platelet transfusion is reserved for life-threatening bleeding in ITP. This patient has no evidence of active bleeding. Platelet transfusion in this scenario would result in rapid immune destruction of the platelets.

Splenectomy is an incorrect answer. Splenectomy is not a first-line therapy for ITP. It is used as a second-line treatment for patients with steroid-refractory ITP.

question_text:
A 15-year-old girl is referred to haematology. She started having periods three years ago which have always been heavy and prolonged. Unfortunately the menorrhagia has responded poorly to trials of tranexamic acid and the combined oral contraceptive pill. Blood tests show the following:


Hb	10.3 g/dl
Plt	239 * 109/l
WBC	6.5 * 109/l
 
PT	12.9 secs

What is the most likely diagnosis?

question_text:
A 59-year-old woman has presented to the emergency department following a fall. Plain radiographs have confirmed a left hip fracture.

She has a history of breast cancer, type 2 diabetes, hypercholesterolaemia and recurrent urinary tract infections.

Which of the following drugs that she is taking is most likely to have contributed towards her hip fracture?
options_json: ["Fenofibrate", "Letrozole", "Methenamine hippurate", "Nitrofurantoin", "Sitagliptin"]
explanation_text:
Anastrozole and letrozole are aromatase inhibitors that reduces peripheral oestrogen synthesis

Letrozole is an aromatase inhibitor that reduces peripheral oestrogen synthesis by blocking the conversion of androgens into oestrogen.

It is used in the treatment of oestrogen-receptor-positive breast cancer in postmenopausal women. This helps to prevent oestrogen-mediated growth stimulation in cancer tissues. In postmenopausal women, oestrogens are mainly derived from the action of the aromatase enzyme; ovarian synthesis of oestrogen has ceased.

The inhibition of oestrogen production subsequently increases the risk of osteoporosis which can predispose to fractures. Hence it is advised to assess bone mineral density before letrozole treatment and at regular intervals.

Fenofibrate, methenamine hippurate, nitrofurantoin and sitagliptin have not been associated with increased fracture risk.

question_text:
A 68-year-old man who takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation is taken to the emergency department after being involved in a road traffic accident. His GCS is reduced and a CT head shows an intracranial haemorrhage. Bloods on admission show the following:


Hb	132 g/l
Platelets	222 * 109/l
WBC	11.2 * 109/l
INR	3.1

In addition to vitamin K, which one of the following blood products should be given?
options_json: ["Cryoprecipitate", "Platelet transfusion", "Prothrombin complex concentrate", "Packed red cells", "Fresh frozen plasma (FFP)"]
explanation_text:
Prothrombin complex concentrate is used for the emergency reversal of anticoagulation in patients with severe bleeding or a head injury

The correct answer in this scenario is

prothrombin complex concentrate

. Prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) is the preferred treatment option to rapidly reverse the anticoagulant effect of warfarin in patients with life-threatening bleeding, such as an intracranial haemorrhage. PCC contains factors II, VII, IX and X, which are essential for normal blood clotting. In addition to vitamin K, PCC will help to quickly normalize the patient's INR and reduce the risk of further bleeding.

The first incorrect option is

cryoprecipitate

. Cryoprecipitate is a concentrated source of fibrinogen and factor VIII. It is typically used in cases of massive bleeding where fibrinogen levels are low or when there is a deficiency of factor VIII, such as in patients with haemophilia A. However, it does not contain the necessary factors to reverse warfarin's anticoagulant effect.

The second incorrect option is

platelet transfusion

. Platelet transfusion may be considered in patients with thrombocytopenia or platelet dysfunction who are experiencing active bleeding. In this case, the patient's platelet count is within normal range (222 * 10

9

/l), so platelet transfusion would not be appropriate for reversing his elevated INR due to warfarin.

The third incorrect option is

packed red cells

. Packed red cells are used to increase oxygen-carrying capacity in patients with anaemia or acute blood loss. While this patient has been involved in a road traffic accident and has an intracranial haemorrhage, his Hb level remains within normal limits (132 g/l). Therefore, packed red cells would not address his elevated INR from warfarin therapy.

The final incorrect option is

fresh frozen plasma (FFP)

. FFP contains all coagulation factors and can be used to correct coagulopathy in patients with severe liver disease or disseminated intravascular coagulation. Although FFP can also help to reverse warfarin's anticoagulant effect, it is less concentrated than PCC and requires a larger volume infusion, which may increase the risk of fluid overload. Furthermore, PCC has a faster onset of action compared to FFP, making it more suitable for emergency reversal of warfarin anticoagulation in life-threatening bleeding situations like this one.

question_text:
An 18-year-old is due to start chemotherapy for a new diagnosis of testicular cancer. He is being counselled on a platinum-based cytotoxic medication which works by causing damage to purine bases on DNA.

It is explained to him that certain baseline tests may be done before treatment to help identify adverse reactions to the chemotherapy.

What is the most appropriate test to identify a potential adverse reaction to this medication?
options_json: ["Audiometric testing", "CT chest", "Gait analysis", "Transthoracic echocardiogram", "Upper GI endoscopy"]
explanation_text:
Cisplatin may cause ototoxicity

Audiometric testing

is correct. Ototoxicity is an uncommon but important adverse effect of cisplatin in both paediatric and adult patients. Cisplatin is a platinum-based anti-neoplastic medication used in the treatment of testicular cancer. It binds to the purine base guanine, interfering with DNA repair and inhibiting its replication. For some patients, especially children or those with prior hearing loss, audiometric testing may be done before and after administration. The degree of toxicity is dose-related.

CT chest

is incorrect. This would identify lung fibrosis which is more typically associated with methotrexate and bleomycin. Regardless, CT chest would not be a suitable baseline test to perform prior to starting methotrexate or bleomycin.

Gait analysis

is incorrect. This would detect ataxia which is more commonly associated with cytarabine which is normally used in the treatment of acute myeloid leukaemia. Cisplatin does not commonly cause ataxia.

Transthoracic echocardiogram

is incorrect. This would identify cardiomyopathies which are typically associated with doxorubicin. Doxorubicin typically causes a dilated cardiomyopathy and an echocardiogram may be performed prior to starting treatment.

Upper GI endoscopy

is incorrect. This would identify mucositis (inflammation and erosion of the mucosa of the GI tract). Mucositis is typically associated with fluorouracil (5FU) which is used for solid tumours and basal skin cancer, but not commonly testicular cancer.

question_text:
A 24-year-old man attends the emergency department with lip and tongue swelling which he developed whilst at a restaurant. He also complains of an itchy rash and abdominal pain. On examination, his observations are within normal limits. There is marked swelling of the throat and tongue and he has a hoarse voice and stridor. An urticarial rash is present on his limbs, torso and back.

Which of the following blood tests may play a role diagnostically?
options_json: ["Amylase", "C1 esterase inhibitor", "C4", "Lipase", "Tryptase"]
explanation_text:
Anaphylaxis - serum tryptase levels rise following an acute episode

The clinical features are suggestive of anaphylaxis which is a severe, life-threatening, generalised or systemic hypersensitivity reaction.

Sometimes diagnosing anaphylaxis is not always straightforward. In this setting, a serum

tryptase

can be helpful. Serum tryptase concentration is increased in anaphylaxis and anaphylactoid reactions.

NICE recommends that 'after a suspected anaphylactic reaction in adults or young people aged 16 years or older, take timed blood samples for mast cell tryptase testing as follows: a baseline sample as soon as possible after emergency treatment has started, and a second sample ideally within 1-2 hours (but no later than 4 hours) from the onset of symptoms'.

Amylase

and

lipase

are useful investigations to assess for pancreatitis. Although the patient has abdominal pain, this is most likely related to anaphylaxis rather than pancreatitis.

C1 esterase inhibitor

and

C4

are useful investigations for diagnosing hereditary angioedema. This is an uncommon disorder that results in recurrent attacks of severe swelling most commonly affecting the arms, legs, face, intestinal tract, and airway. An urticarial rash is not typical of this condition, favouring a diagnosis of anaphylaxis in this case.

question_text:
A 62-year-old woman is admitted under the gynaecology team with vaginal bleeding. She has a history of breast cancer and is taking letrozole 2.5mg.

What is the underlying mechanism of action of this medication?
options_json: ["Increases oestrogen breakdown", "Oestrogen receptor antagonist", "Reduces oestrogen release from the ovaries", "Reduces peripheral oestrogen synthesis", "Selective oestrogen receptor degrader (SERD)"]
explanation_text:
Anastrozole and letrozole are aromatase inhibitors that reduces peripheral oestrogen synthesis

Letrozole and anastrozole are aromatase inhibitors which are used as a treatment in post-menopausal women with hormone-dependent breast cancer. They work by reducing peripheral oestrogen synthesis from body fat and muscles. Common side effects include osteoporosis, hot flushes and vaginal bleeding.

Tamoxifen is another medication used in oestrogen-receptor-positive breast cancer, but it can be used in pre- and post-menopausal women and works as a selective oestrogen receptor antagonist.

Fulvestrant is less commonly used in oestrogen-receptor-positive breast cancer. Rather than decrease oestrogen synthesis, it works by blocking and damaging oestrogen receptors. It is known as a selective oestrogen receptor degrader (SERD).

Goserelin (zoladex) is a gonadorelin analogue which down-regulates the gonadotropin-releasing hormone receptors and therefore reduces the release of follicle-stimulating hormone and luteinising hormone which in turn reduces oestrogen release from the ovaries.

question_text: A 51-year-old female is referred to the haematology clinic with a haemoglobin of 19.2 g/dl. She is a non-smoker. Her oxygen saturations on room air are 98% and she is noted to have mass in the left upper quadrant. What is the most useful test to establish whether she has polycythaemia vera?
options_json: ["Bone marrow aspiration", "Blood film", "Red cell mass", "Transferrin saturation", "JAK2 mutation screen"]
explanation_text:
Polycythaemia rubra vera - JAK2 mutation

The correct answer is JAK2 mutation screen. According to British Society for Haematology guidelines, testing for JAK2 V617F mutation is the initial investigation of choice in suspected polycythaemia vera (PV).

JAK2 mutation screen

is positive in approximately 95% of PV cases, making it highly sensitive and specific. The presence of JAK2 V617F or exon 12 mutations is now a major diagnostic criterion for PV in the WHO classification.

Bone marrow aspiration

is not the most useful initial test as it is invasive and should only be performed after JAK2 mutation testing. While bone marrow examination can show characteristic features of PV such as panmyelosis and reduced iron stores, it is typically reserved for cases where the diagnosis remains unclear after initial investigations or when transformation is suspected.

Blood film

, while useful in the overall assessment, is not specific enough to establish the diagnosis of PV. It may show features such as increased red cells and sometimes basophilia, but these findings are non-specific and can be seen in other conditions including secondary polycythaemia.

Red cell mass

measurement was historically important in diagnosing PV but is now rarely performed. It has been largely superseded by haemoglobin concentration and haematocrit measurements, combined with JAK2 mutation testing, as these are more readily available and provide sufficient diagnostic information.

Transferrin saturation

is not particularly useful in establishing the diagnosis of PV. While iron studies may be altered in PV (typically showing low iron and ferritin due to increased red cell production), these changes are non-specific and can occur in many other conditions. The finding would not definitively establish the diagnosis of PV.

The clinical scenario strongly suggests PV given the elevated haemoglobin, normal oxygen saturations (ruling out hypoxic drive), and presence of splenomegaly (the left upper quadrant mass). In this context, JAK2 mutation testing is the most appropriate initial investigation to confirm the diagnosis.

His regular medications include lansoprazole, ramipril, metformin, simvastatin and glimepiride. He drinks approximately 10 units of alcohol per week.

explanation_text:
In chronic myeloid leukaemia there is an increase in granulocytes at different stages of maturation +/- thrombocytosis

Acute myeloid leukaemia - blood tests will reveal immature blood cells (blasts).

Acute lymphocytic leukaemia - far more common in children and blood tests will reveal immature blasts.

question_text:
A 15-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with excessive bleeding following a tooth extraction. He reports a history of easy bruising following minor trauma for as long as he can remember, and his mother has experienced similar symptoms.

On examination, there are multiple bruises on his legs and arms. Blood investigations revealed:


Haemoglobin	120 g/L	135–180
WBC	6 *10 9/L	4.0–11.0
Platelets	197 * 10 9/L	150–400
Activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT)	45 seconds	25-40
Factor VIII assay	50 IU/dl	50 – 150
Von Willebrand factor (vWF)	0.2 IU/ml	0.5- 2.0

What is the most appropriate medication for this patient?
options_json: ["Desmopressin", "Eltrombopag", "Factor IX concentrate", "Factor VIII concentrate", "Vitamin K"]
explanation_text:
Desmopressin is used in the management of Von Willebrand's disease

Desmopressin

is the appropriate choice, as the clinical presentation suggests von Willebrand's disease. The history of easy bruising following minor trauma, coupled with an elevated APTT and reduced Von Willebrand factor (vWF) supports this diagnosis. Desmopressin works by raising the vWF level and acts as a haemostatic agent.

Eltrombopag

is not suitable for this case as it is indicated for the treatment of ITP, not von Willebrand's disease. Given that the clinical features and investigations point towards von Willebrand's disease, eltrombopag would not be beneficial. Raised APTT and reduced vWF are seen in von Willebrand's disease.

Factor IX concentrate

is incorrect because it is utilised in managing haemophilia B. Given that the patient's mother experienced similar symptoms, it is unlikely that the patient suffers from haemophilia B, as it is rare for a female to have this condition. Haemophilia is an X-linked recessive disorder. Raised APTT and normal levels of platelets can also be seen in haemophilia B. Reduced vWF can be seen in von Willebrand's disease.

Factor VIII concentrate

is not an appropriate option. It is used in managing haemophilia A; however, this scenario does not align with a diagnosis of haemophilia A. As the mother suffered from similar symptoms, haemophilia is unlikely because it rarely affects females. Reduced vWF is also not seen in haemophilia.

Vitamin K

would not be an appropriate selection. The clinical picture and investigations, such as raised APTT and reduced vWF do not support a deficiency in vitamin K-related pathways in this instance. In vitamin K deficiency, there will be normal APTT. Vitamin K would be an appropriate option for vitamin K deficiency.

question_text:
A 58-year-old woman presents with progressive fatigue, lightheadedness, and difficulty concentrating over the past several months. She also mentions a tingling sensation in her feet.

Blood results performed are shown below:


Haemoglobin	92 g/L	115–165
MCV	112 fL	80–100
Serum vitamin B12	120 pmol/L	170-700
Serum folate	15 nmol/L	7–20
Reticulocyte count	0.8%	1–2.5

She begins treatment with the administration of the necessary vitamin.

Where in the gastrointestinal tract is this vitamin absorbed?
options_json: ["Duodenum", "Jejunum", "Small intestine", "Stomach", "Terminal ileum"]
explanation_text:
Vitamin B12 is actively absorbed in the terminal ileum

This patient’s symptoms, including fatigue, lightheadedness, difficulty concentrating, and tingling in the feet, are consistent with vitamin B12 deficiency. A raised MCV and low serum vitamin B12 levels confirm the diagnosis. Vitamin B12 is actively absorbed in the

terminal ileum

through a complex process requiring intrinsic factor, a protein secreted by gastric parietal cells. Conditions like pernicious anaemia, which involves intrinsic factor deficiency, impair this process.

The

duodenum

is responsible for absorbing iron, calcium, and magnesium, but it is not involved in vitamin B12 absorption. Conditions such as coeliac disease or duodenal resection can impair nutrient absorption in this region but would not directly cause vitamin B12 deficiency.

The

jejunum

plays a central role in absorbing carbohydrates, fats, proteins, and certain vitamins like folate, but it is not involved in vitamin B12 absorption. The patient’s macrocytic anaemia could suggest folate or B12 deficiency; however, the low serum vitamin B12 levels confirm that the terminal ileum, not the jejunum, is the relevant site for absorption in this case.

Small intestine

is incorrect because, while it plays a major role in nutrient absorption, it is not the specific site for vitamin B12 absorption. The small intestine is primarily responsible for absorbing macronutrients such as carbohydrates, proteins, and fats, along with most vitamins and minerals like folate, iron, and calcium. However, vitamin B12 absorption requires binding to intrinsic factor and occurs specifically in the terminal ileum, a distinct segment of the small intestine.

The

stomach

is critical for producing intrinsic factor, which binds to vitamin B12 and allows absorption in the terminal ileum. However, the stomach itself does not absorb vitamin B12. Conditions like pernicious anaemia impair intrinsic factor production, leading to downstream absorption failure in the terminal ileum, rather than an issue within the stomach itself.

question_text:
A 60-year-old man receives multiple units of packed red blood cells whilst being treated for a bleeding peptic ulcer. He has a history of HIV and is non-compliant with his antiretroviral treatment. His blood tests are normal upon discharge.

He presents to the emergency department a week later with a macular erythematous rash, jaundice, fever and diarrhoea.

On examination, he is tachypnoeic and there is hepatomegaly.


Hb	75 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Platelets	23 * 10 9/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	2.4 * 10 9/L	(4.0 - 11.0)


Bilirubin	34 µmol/L	(3 - 17)
ALP	168 u/L	(30 - 100)
ALT	104 u/L	(3 - 40)

What process aims to avoid the presentation described in this case?
options_json: ["Cross-matching", "Irradiation", "Leukodepletion", "Plasmapheresis", "Platelet apheresis"]
explanation_text:
Irradiated blood products are used to avoid transfusion-associated graft versus host disease

The patient presents with clinical features that are suggestive of transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease (TA-GVHD). These include fever, rash, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, pancytopenia and abnormal liver function tests. TA-GVHD can occur when a patient receives non-irradiated blood products, which may lead to the engraftment of viable donor T-cells. The purpose of irradiating blood products is to damage the DNA within donor T-cells to prevent them from mounting an immune response following transfusion. To mitigate the risk of TA-GVHD, all blood products should undergo

irradiation

. Immunocompromised patients, such as this one, are particularly at risk of TA-GVHD as they are unable to mount an immune response to the foreign cells in the donor blood. Although irradiation also reduces the risk of TA-GVHD in immunocompromised patients, the risk remains higher than in immunocompetent individuals.

Cross-matching

is a critical procedure that ensures compatibility between the blood types of a patient and a donor before transfusion. Incompatible transfusions can precipitate haemolytic reactions, typically manifesting with symptoms including jaundice, abdominal pain and anaemia. However, these reactions generally occur within 24 hours following the transfusion.

Leukodepletion

is a filtration process designed to remove nearly all white blood cells from blood products before they are transfused. Its primary aim is to reduce the risk of cytomegalovirus (CMV) transmission through the removal of monocytes and other blood-borne viruses. It is recommended for patients who are immunocompromised, like ours. CMV infection can present in several ways in immunocompromised patients, including colitis and retinitis. However, the case described is more closely aligned with TA-GVHD.

Plasmapheresis

refers to a technique where plasma is separated from blood cells in a sample. This process can be employed to produce fresh frozen plasma for transfusions or treat plasma in conditions like Guillain-Barre syndrome before it is returned to the patient's circulation. Plasmapheresis does not serve as a preventative measure against TA-GVHD.

Platelet apheresis

involves separating platelets from whole blood. It might be utilised as part of treatment strategies for essential thrombocytopenia or in generating platelet concentrates for transfusion in cases of severe thrombocytopenia. However, platelet apheresis does not play a role in reducing the risk of TA-GVHD.

question_text:
An 18-year-old, with no medical issues, is rushed into the emergency department (ED) following an acute onset of symptoms whilst eating a nut cereal bar.

Her family reports she suddenly had difficulty breathing with an audible wheeze, swelling of her tongue, changes in her voice and developed a widespread rash.

A stat dose of IM adrenaline was given in the ED and all her symptoms rapidly resolve. She is now asymptomatic and her exam is normal.

The likely diagnosis is explained, blood tests taken and a follow-up appointment booked. She is provided with 2 adrenaline auto-injectors with appropriate training.

When would it be most appropriate to discharge this patient?
options_json: ["Minimum of 12 hours after symptom resolution", "Minimum of 2 hours after symptom resolution", "Minimum of 24 hours after symptom resolution", "Minimum of 6 hours after symptom resolution", "Once results of serum tryptase are available"]
answer_text: Minimum of 2 hours after symptom resolution
explanation_text:
A risk-stratified approach should be taken when discharging patients who have presented with anaphylaxis

This patient has presented with a likely anaphylaxis reaction to nuts and has responded well to treatment. Following the Resus Council recommendations for a risk-stratified approach for discharge, this patient would be a candidate for a fast-track discharge i.e.

after 2hours of symptom resolution

. The patient has had a complete resolution of symptoms following a single dose of IM adrenaline, the appropriate adrenaline auto-injector and training have been provided and the patient has adequate supervision in the form of her family on discharge. There are also no red flags mentioned such as previous biphasic reactions, severe asthma, late at night presentation etc.

Discharge follow anaphylaxis should be considered at a

minimum of 12 hours after symptom resolution

for those patients with significant red flags for further complications. These red-flag features include severe reaction requiring > 2 doses of IM adrenaline, patients with severe asthma, if there is the possibility of an ongoing reaction (e.g. slow-release medication), patients presenting late at night or patients presenting to areas where access to emergency access care may be difficult.

Admission following a

minimum of 24 hours after symptom resolution

in anaphylaxis is rare and is normally due to complications secondary to the reaction resulting in significant interventions (i.e. intubation and ventilation) or the patient remaining unsafe for discharge (i.e. unable to be taught adrenaline auto-injector).

Discharge follow anaphylaxis should be considered at a

minimum of 6 hours after symptom resolution

for those patients requiring 2 doses of adrenaline or those with previous biphasic reactions. As these are not concerns for this patient, and they otherwise meet the criteria for a fast-track, this patient can be discharged after 2 hours of symptom resolution.

Although they can assist confirm the diagnosis of anaphylaxis

results of serum tryptase

should not affect the discharge timing of a patient. Instead, a risk-stratified approach using the information previously discussed should determine a patient's suitability for discharge.

A 12-year-old, recently-immigrated boy from Nigeria is referred to the hospital after presenting to his GP with a growth of the jaw. A number of investigations are performed, including a test for the Epstein-Barr virus which comes back positive. A biopsy is taken, which demonstrates a 'starry sky' appearance.

Given the findings and the likely diagnosis, which of the following translocations is most likely implicated?
explanation_text:
Burkitt's lymphoma - t(8:14)

The correct answer is t(8:14). The condition being described here is Burkitt's lymphoma, given the demographic, positive Epstein-Barr virus and the 'starry sky' appearance on microscopy - lymphocyte sheets interspersed with macrophages containing dead apoptotic tumour cells. Burkitt's lymphoma is associated with the c-myc gene translocation, usually t(8:14).

The Philadelphia chromosome is the common name for t(9:22). The presence of this translocation is required for the diagnosis of chronic myeloid leukaemia (although it is not specific enough to be solely sufficient for the diagnosis). It is not implicated in Burkitt's lymphoma.

T(11:14) is implicated in mantle cell lymphoma, which would present typically in much later life (60s) rather than younger patients as seen in Burkitt's.

T(14:18) is implicated in 90% of cases of follicular lymphoma. This, again, would present differently to Burkitt's, with a slow disease course, and a wide range of clinical manifestations.

T(15:17) is linked to acute promyelocytic leukaemia, a subtype of acute myeloid leukaemia. Again, the growth of the jaw, the starry sky appearance and the virus association are all classic of Burkitt's, not this condition.

question_text:
A 23-year-old woman presented with symptoms of itchiness in her mouth and at the back of her throat after consuming peaches on several occasions with some mild swelling which settles down over time.

What is the likely condition in this case?
options_json: ["Angioedema", "Burning mouth syndrome", "Contact cheilitis", "Contact stomatitis", "Oral allergy syndrome"]
explanation_text:
Oral allergy syndrome is strongly linked with pollen allergies and presents with seasonal variation

Oral allergy syndrome is due to allergic antibodies mistaking certain proteins in fresh fruits, nuts or vegetables for pollen. People can experience itchiness in their mouth and throat, often associated with mild swelling, straight after eating fresh fruit or vegetables. This is referred to as oral allergy syndrome.

The best way to prevent an allergic reaction is to identify the food that causes the allergy and avoid it.

Burning mouth syndrome a chronic or recurrent burning in the mouth without an obvious cause. This discomfort may affect the tongue, gums, lips, inside of your cheeks, palate or widespread areas of your whole mouth. This is not described in the scenario.

Allergic contact cheilitis is allergic contact dermatitis which affects the lips. It is due to a type IV hypersensitivity reaction which occurs following contact with an allergen. This is unlikely in this case due to involvement of the back of her throat too.

Contact stomatitis is inflammation or pain of the oral mucosa due to both irritant and allergic substances. It is less common than contact cheilitis and is not associated with itching.

Angioedema is characterised by an abrupt and short-lived swelling of the skin and mucous membranes. This swelling is not itchy and therefore is unlikely in this case.

question_text:
A 25-year-old man is admitted to the haematology ward. He was recently diagnosed with Burkitt's lymphoma and received his first dose of chemotherapy today.

Blood results from today are as follows:


Na+	138 mmol/L	(135 - 145)
K+	6.2 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Bicarbonate	22 mmol/L	(22 - 29)
Urea	10.8 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	162 µmol/L	(55 - 120)
Calcium	1.9 mmol/L	(2.1-2.6)
Phosphate	2.8 mmol/L	(0.8-1.4)

Blood results from yesterday are as follows:


Na+	135 mmol/L	(135 - 145)
K+	3.5 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Bicarbonate	24 mmol/L	(22 - 29)
Urea	4.8 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	72 µmol/L	(55 - 120)
Calcium	2.4 mmol/L	(2.1-2.6)
Phosphate	2.4 mmol/L	(0.8-1.4)

What treatment is required?
options_json: ["Allopurinol", "Calcium gluconate", "Phosphate binder", "Prophylactic dose rasburicase", "Treatment dose rasburicase"]
explanation_text:
Prevention of tumour lysis syndrome: rasburicase is used in preference to allopurinol for high-risk patients, e.g. those with aggressive non-Hodgkin's lymphomas

The patient has clinical tumour lysis syndrome (TLS). TLS is a metabolic syndrome caused by the breakdown of malignant cells. It is most likely to occur just prior to, or at the start of, chemotherapy when the disease is most active. Excessive release of nucleic acids, proteins and intracellular metabolites from the tumour cells overwhelm the normal homeostatic control mechanisms. Hyperkalaemia occurs first and can be life-threatening within 6 hours of the onset of TLS.  Uric acid crystals precipitate into the renal tubules, preventing the excretion of the other TLS metabolites. This creates a downward spiral of acute kidney failure.

The breakdown of tumour cells results in the release of predominantly intracellular molecules (e.g. potassium, phosphate, and uric acid). Hence why high levels of these molecules occur in the plasma. It is important to remember that calcium is a predominantly extracellular ion. Phosphate is a calcium chelator, and thus acute hyperphosphatemia results in hypocalcemia.

Risk factors for TLS include high tumour burden, high-grade tumour with rapid turnover (e.g. Burkitt's, ALL), pre-existing renal impairment, and the use of highly active, cell-cycle specific chemotherapy.

Laboratory TLS is defined by ≥2 of the following occurring 3 days prior or 7 days post initiation of treatment for cancer:

Uric acid ≥ 476 µmol/L or 25% increase from baseline
Potassium ≥ 6.0 mmol/L or 25% increase from baseline
Phosphate ≥ 1.45 mmol/L (adults) or ≥2.1 mmol/L (children) or 25% increase
Calcium ≤ 1.75 mmol/L or 25% decrease from baseline

Thus, this patient fulfils the criteria for laboratory TLS.

Clinical TLS is defined by: laboratory TLS plus at least one of the following:

Creatinine ≥1.5 x the upper limit of normal
Cardiac arrhythmia
Seizure
Sudden death

Therefore, the patient in this clinical scenario has clinical TLS due to the presence of renal impairment.

Treatment dose rasburicase

is correct. The patient has clinical TLS and thus needs emergency treatment with rasburicase. This should be at the higher treatment dose of 200 micrograms/kg. This drug is a recombinant form of mammalian urate oxidase.  It metabolises urate to allantoin, a substance 10x more soluble than uric acid. It acts immediately on any uric acid that is already formed. For this reason, it is the most effective drug used in the management of TLS.

Allopurinol

is incorrect.  This drug reduces the production of uric acid by decreasing the rate of conversion of hypoxanthine to xanthine, and of xanthine to uric acid.  Both hypoxanthine and xanthine are more soluble than uric acid and so less precipitation occurs in the renal tubules. However, it does not increase the rate of breakdown of uric acid that is already present so its therapeutic effect is delayed by 24-72 hours. Thus rasburicase is the preferred agent for the management of TLS due to its immediate therapeutic effect.

Calcium gluconate

is incorrect. Indications for calcium gluconate include severe hyperkalaemia, or symptomatic hypocalcaemia, neither of which are present in this clinical case.

Phosphate binder

is incorrect. Although a phosphate binder could be used in this scenario, the priority is to reduce the levels of uric acid with rasburicase.

Prophylactic dose rasburicase

is incorrect. A low dose of rasburicase (e.g. 3mg) is often used in high-risk patients to prevent TLS. However, the patient, in this case, has established clinical TLS and thus requires a higher treatment dose.

question_text:
A 28-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a 3-day history of progressive right arm weakness, severe abdominal pain, and fever. She has no significant past medical history and takes no regular medications. On examination, she has a temperature of 38.5°C, blood pressure of 145/95 mmHg, and scattered purpuric lesions over her trunk and limbs. Neurological examination confirms a right-sided hemiparesis. Laboratory investigations reveal:


Hb	78 g/L	Female: (115-160)
WBC	12.5 * 109/L	(4.0-11.0)
Platelets	22 * 109/L	(150-400)
Creatinine	156 μmol/L	(45-90)
ALT	78 U/L	(5-40)
Bilirubin	35 μmol/L	(3-21)
LDH	1250 U/L	(135-225)

Blood film shows numerous schistocytes. Coagulation screen is normal.

What is the most likely underlying cause of her condition?
options_json: ["Disseminated intravascular coagulation", "ADAMTS-13 deficiency", "Haemolytic uraemic syndrome", "Catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome", "Malignant hypertension"]
explanation_text:
Acquired inhibition of the protein ADAMTS13 which cleaves vWF multimers is the most common cause of TTP

ADAMTS-13 deficiency

is the correct diagnosis in this case. This patient presents with the classic pentad of thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP): fever, neurological symptoms (right arm weakness), renal impairment (elevated creatinine), microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (low haemoglobin, elevated LDH, schistocytes on blood film), and thrombocytopenia. TTP is caused by a severe deficiency of ADAMTS-13, a metalloprotease that cleaves von Willebrand factor. When ADAMTS-13 is deficient, ultra-large von Willebrand factor multimers accumulate, leading to platelet aggregation and microvascular thrombosis. This explains the patient's neurological symptoms, which result from cerebral microvascular occlusion. The normal coagulation screen is typical of TTP, distinguishing it from DIC. The presence of schistocytes on blood film indicates mechanical fragmentation of red blood cells as they pass through partially occluded vessels. TTP is a medical emergency requiring prompt treatment with plasma exchange to replenish ADAMTS-13 and remove autoantibodies against it, along with immunosuppression.

Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)

can present with microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia and thrombocytopenia, but it typically occurs in the context of severe sepsis, trauma, malignancy, or obstetric complications. A key distinguishing feature is that DIC would show abnormal coagulation parameters (prolonged PT, APTT, low fibrinogen, elevated D-dimer), whereas this patient's coagulation screen is normal. Additionally, the neurological manifestations and fever without an obvious underlying cause make DIC less likely in this scenario.

Haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS)

shares features with TTP, including microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and renal impairment. However, HUS typically presents with predominant renal involvement and is often preceded by a diarrhoeal illness (typically E. coli O157:H7 infection). Neurological manifestations are less common in HUS compared to TTP. The absence of a diarrhoeal prodrome and the prominence of neurological symptoms make HUS less likely in this case.

Catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome (CAPS)

is a rare variant of antiphospholipid syndrome characterised by multiple organ thrombosis developing over a short period. While it can cause microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia and thrombocytopenia, CAPS typically presents with multiple large vessel thromboses rather than the microvascular thrombosis seen in TTP. Additionally, CAPS usually occurs in patients with known antiphospholipid syndrome or systemic lupus erythematosus, which this patient does not have.

Malignant hypertension

can cause a microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia with renal impairment and neurological symptoms. However, the blood pressure in this case (145/95 mmHg) is only mildly elevated and not in the range typically associated with malignant hypertension. Additionally, the severe thrombocytopenia (22 × 10⁹/L) would be unusual for malignant hypertension alone. The constellation of findings is much more consistent with TTP due to ADAMTS-13 deficiency.

question_text:
A 62-year-old man presents with 2-day history of headache, shortness of breath, vomiting and feeling generally weak. He has a background of type 2 diabetes with gastroparesis and ischaemic heart disease. His medications are aspirin, atorvastatin, glyceryl trinitrate, metformin and metoclopramide. He has also recently been commenced on co-trimoxazole for a leg ulcer, according to the sensitivities of previous wound cultures.

On examination, he is tachypnoeic with saturations of 83% and central cyanosis despite 15L oxygen delivered via a non-rebreathe mask. His heart rate is 110/min with blood pressure 120/80 mmHg. He is distressed and anxious but is orientated to time, place and person. Tone, power and reflexes are normal. He has equal, reactive 3mm pupils and normal cranial nerve examination. He has dry, cool skin with a temperature of 37.1ºC.

Investigations:


Hb	150 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Platelets	200 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	13.0 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Na+	140 mmol/L	(135 - 145)
K+	3.8 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Urea	5.5 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	70 µmol/L	(55 - 120)
CRP	65 mg/L	(< 5)

An arterial blood gas on 15 litre/min oxygen shows:

pH	7.51	(7.35 - 7.45)
pO2	50kPa	(10-14)
pCO2	3.0kPa	(4.5 - 6)
Base excess (BE)	+4mmol/L	(-2 - 2)
HCO3	30mmol/L	22 - 26

A departmental chest x-ray is normal.

Which medication is the most useful in managing this patient?
options_json: ["Dicobalt edetate", "Hydroxycobalamin", "Methylthioninium chloride", "Pralidoxime", "Sodium bicarbonate"]
explanation_text:
Normal pO2 but decreased oxygen saturation is characteristic of methaemoglobinaemia

The underlying diagnosis is methaemoglobinaemia, therefore the answer is methylthioninium chloride.

Methaemoglobinaemia occurs when ferrous ions (Fe2+) of haemoglobin are oxidised to the ferric (Fe3+) ions, making them unable to bind oxygen. It can be congenital or acquired due to drug causes. Glyceryl trinitrate, metoclopramide and co-trimoxazole can all cause methaemoglobinaemia. Methylthioninium chloride (methylene blue) can be used to treat drug- or chemical-induced methaemoglobinaemia.

Dicobalt edetate and hydroxycobalamin can be used to treat cyanide poisoning e.g. cyanide salt exposure or smoke inhalation. Cyanide poisoning causes a lactic acidosis, dizziness, hyperventilation, loss of consciousness, coma and death.

Sodium bicarbonate can be used in various overdoses, including tricyclic depressants.

Pralidoxime can be used to treat patients with organophosphate poisoning, which presents with parasympathetic effects.
