question_text:
A 68-year-old woman presents to the respiratory clinic with a 3-month history of persistent dry cough and progressive dyspnoea. She has never smoked. Chest X-ray shows a 3 cm peripheral opacity in the right upper lobe. CT thorax confirms a spiculated mass with no mediastinal lymphadenopathy. A CT-guided biopsy is performed.

What is the most likely histological diagnosis?
options_json: ["Adenocarcinoma", "Carcinoid tumour", "Large cell carcinoma", "Small cell carcinoma", "Squamous cell carcinoma"]
explanation_text:
Lung adenocarcinoma

Adenocarcinoma

is the correct diagnosis in this case. The clinical scenario describes a never-smoker with a peripheral lung lesion, which are both characteristic features of lung adenocarcinoma. Adenocarcinoma is the most common type of lung cancer in non-smokers, although it should be noted that the majority of patients who develop lung adenocarcinoma are still smokers. Adenocarcinomas typically present as peripheral lesions, often with a spiculated appearance on imaging as described in this case. The patient's symptoms of dry cough and progressive dyspnoea are consistent with a peripheral lung lesion that may be irritating airways or causing local parenchymal changes. The absence of mediastinal lymphadenopathy suggests the disease may be at an earlier stage.

Carcinoid tumour

is incorrect. While carcinoid tumours can occur in the lung and may present with cough, they are much less common than adenocarcinoma. Carcinoid tumours typically affect younger patients (40-50 years) and may present with carcinoid syndrome (flushing, diarrhoea, wheezing) if metastatic. They are usually well-defined, round or oval masses on imaging rather than spiculated, and are often more centrally located.

Large cell carcinoma

is incorrect. Although large cell carcinomas can present as peripheral lesions, they are typically anaplastic, poorly differentiated tumours with a poor prognosis. They are strongly associated with smoking history, which this patient does not have. Large cell carcinomas may secrete β-hCG and are less common than adenocarcinoma.

Small cell carcinoma

is incorrect. Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) typically presents as a central mass with early mediastinal spread. It is strongly associated with smoking, with over 95% of cases occurring in smokers. SCLC is often associated with paraneoplastic syndromes such as SIADH or Cushing's syndrome. The peripheral location and non-smoking history make SCLC unlikely in this case.

Squamous cell carcinoma

is incorrect. Squamous cell carcinomas typically present as central lesions, often with cavitation, and are strongly associated with smoking. They can cause hypercalcaemia due to parathyroid hormone-related protein (PTHrP) secretion and are frequently associated with finger clubbing and hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy. The peripheral location and non-smoking history make squamous cell carcinoma an unlikely diagnosis in this scenario.

question_text:
A 22-year-old woman presents with widespread bruising and bleeding gums. She also complains of increasing lethargy over the last week.

Blood results are as follows:


Hb	96 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	28 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	1.4 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Neuts	0.1 * 109/L	(2.0 - 7.0)


Prothrombin time (PT)	28 secs	(10-14 secs)
Activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT)	64 secs	(25-35 secs)
Fibrinogen	0.6 g/L	(2 - 4)
D-Dimer	80,640 ng/mL	(< 400)

A CT scan is performed:


CT head	Right-sided intracerebral haemorrhage

What mutation would be expected on genetic analysis?
explanation_text:
Acute promyelocytic leukaemia - t(15;17)

t(15;17)

is correct. The presence of pancytopenia with DIC should immediately alert you to the possibility of acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APML). Acute promyelocytic leukaemia is characterised by t(15;17), which results in the fusion of the promyelocytic leukaemia (PML) gene at 15q22 with the retinoic acid α-receptor (RARA) gene at 17q21. It is a haematological emergency which requires prompt diagnosis and treatment.

t(11,14)

is incorrect. This translocation is associated with mantle cell lymphoma. Mantle cell lymphoma generally presents with lymphadenopathy and B-symptoms. Bowel involvement is also common (e.g. GI bleeding). Whilst pancytopenia can occur due to marrow infiltration, the presence of a profound coagulopathy, and the absence of B-symptoms and lymphadenopathy favours the diagnosis of APML.

t(14,18)

is incorrect. This translocation is associated with follicular lymphoma. Follicular lymphoma is a low-grade B-cell lymphoma which presents with lymphadenopathy and B symptoms. Whilst pancytopenia can occur due to marrow infiltration, the presence of a profound coagulopathy, and the absence of B-symptoms and lymphadenopathy favours the diagnosis of APML.

t(8,14)

is incorrect. This translocation is associated with Burkitt's lymphoma.  Burkitts's lymphoma is an aggressive high-grade B-cell lymphoma which presents with rapidly enlarging lymphadenopathy and B-symptoms. Bowel involvement is also common (e.g. GI bleeding and obstruction).  The absence of B-symptoms and lymphadenopathy favours the diagnosis of APML.

t(9,22)

is incorrect. This translocation is associated with chronic myeloid leukaemia. This condition is a type of myeloproliferative disorder which would present with leukocytosis and thrombocytosis. The absence of leukocytosis and thrombocytosis favours the diagnosis of APML.

question_text:
A 28-year-old male presents to the emergency department with increasing shortness of breath, nausea, and a frontal headache. He reports he has recently been reviewed in the gastroenterology clinic and started on a medication for a chronic condition, although he cannot remember its name.

On examination, the patient appears very dyspnoeic, with saturations of 80% on air, but good air entry throughout the lungs and no added sounds on auscultation.

Arterial blood gas sampling shows the following:


	Patient's results	Reference ranges
pH	7.35	7.35-7.45 nmol/L
pC02	3.8	4.4-5.9 kPa
pO2	14.0	10.0-14.0 kPa
HCO3	26	22-28 mmol/L
Lac	4	<2 mmol/L

What is the most likely medication the patient has been started on?
options_json: ["Azathioprine", "Dapsone", "Glucocorticoids", "Mercaptopurine", "Metformin"]
explanation_text:
Dapsone + dyspnoea → methaemoglobinaemia

Dapsone is correct as the patient presenting with the typical methaemoglobinaemia presentation of respiratory distress and decreased oxygen saturations despite a normal pO2 on blood gas and respiratory examination. The patient has likely been diagnosed with coeliac disease and started on dapsone for related skin issues, such as dermatitis herpetiformis.

Azathioprine is incorrect as the side effects of this drug would not explain the patient's presentation. Azathioprine can cause bone marrow suppression, hypersensitivity and acute pancreatitis. These do not match the patient's presentation of dyspnoea with decreased saturations but a normal pO2.

Glucocorticoids can cause immune suppression, but this does not explain the patient's presentation. There is no clear evidence of infection, and if an infection was causing the low saturations it would likely be matched by a low pO2 on arterial blood gas.

The side effects of mercaptopurine include bone marrow suppression and liver toxicity. There is no clear evidence of infection or liver impairment in this patient.

Metformin is incorrect as although it can cause lactic acidosis resulting in renal and liver failure this would not explain the patient's findings of decreased saturation with a normal pO2 on arterial blood gas.

question_text:
A 24-year-old male presented with a one-week history of episodic severe abdominal pain associated with vomiting 4 to 5 times a day and dark red urine. He then suddenly developed rapidly progressive weakness in all four limbs for 3 days before being hospitalised.

Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following urinary tests would be raised?
options_json: ["Urinary delta-aminolevulinic acid", "Urinary coproporphyrin", "Urinary hydroxyproline", "Urinary porphobilinogen", "Urinary uroporphyrin"]
explanation_text:
In acute intermittent porphyria, urinary porphobilinogen is typically raised

Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) is a rare metabolic disorder that is characterised by partial deficiency of the enzyme porphobilinogen deaminase. This enzyme deficiency can result in the accumulation of porphyrin precursors in the body. Measuring the levels of the porphyrin precursor porphobilinogen in urine is essential to confirm a diagnosis of acute porphyria. Acute attacks are always associated with increased production and excretion of porphobilinogen.

Urinary coproporphyrin I excretion is increased in patients with Dubin-Johnson syndrome to a greater degree than in patients with other hepatobiliary disorders. This is therefore the incorrect answer in this case.

Urinary hydroxyproline provides an adequate bone marker and in situations where there are very high rates of bone turnover, such as in Paget's disease of bone, its level is seen to be increased.

Urinary uroporphyrin levels are high in porphyria cutanea tarda, which is the most common type of porphyria due to uroporphyrin decarboxylase deficiency. Porphyria cutanea tarda is a rare disorder characterized by painful, blistering skin lesions that develop on sun-exposed skin, which is not described in this case.

Urinary delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) excretion will also be raised in urine samples from individuals with AIP, but the measurement is less widely available and is not essential.

question_text:
A 65-year-old man was diagnosed with gallbladder adenocarcinoma. He had liver, supra-diaphragmatic, and abdominal lymph node metastases. A partial response was achieved after five cycles of chemotherapy.

He had routine blood tests performed just before coming to his oncology follow-up appointment as he had muscle twitches and cramps.


Calcium	2.7 mmol/L	(2.1-2.6)
Phosphate	1.1 mmol/L	(0.8-1.4)
Magnesium	0.3 mmol/L	(0.7-1.0)
Thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH)	3 mU/L	(0.5-5.5)
Free thyroxine (T4)	14 pmol/L	(9.0 - 18)
Amylase	330 U/L	(70 - 300)
Uric acid	0.3 mmol/L	(0.18 - 0.48)
Creatine kinase	125 U/L	(35 - 250)

What chemotherapy is he likely to have received?
options_json: ["Bleomycin", "Cisplatin", "Doxorubicin", "Irinotecan", "Vincristine"]
explanation_text:
Cisplatin is associated with hypomagnesaemia

Cisplatin

works by causing cross-linking in DNA and results in low magnesium which is seen in this case. Cisplatin induces hypomagnesemia through its renal toxicity possibly by a direct injury to mechanisms of magnesium reabsorption in the ascending limb of the loop of Henle as well as the distal tubule.

Bleomycin

works by degrading pre-formed DNA and can cause lung fibrosis.

Vincristine

inhibits the formation of microtubules with a side effect of reversible peripheral neuropathy.

Doxorubicin

stabilises DNA-topoisomerase II complex inhibits DNA & RNA synthesis. It can cause a side effect of cardiomyopathy which there is no suggestion of here.

Irinotecan

inhibits topoisomerase I which prevents relaxation of supercoiled DNA with myelosuppression being an adverse feature.

question_text:
A 45-year-old female is brought to the emergency department by an ambulance after she was found collapsed on the street by a bystander. Within a few minutes of arrival she developed severe abdominal pain and became severely agitated.

Her respiratory rate is 35 breaths per minute, heart rate 110 beats per minute, temperature 39.3ºC. Her prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time are increased, and her fibrinogen levels are lower than normal. Her D-dimer is positive.


Hb	96 g/l
Platelets	85 * 109/l
WBC	14 * 109/l

Blood smears are sent to the laboratory.

What is most likely to be seen in the blood smears?
options_json: ["Heinz bodies", "Bite cells", "Dacrocytes", "Schistocytes", "Elliptocytes"]
explanation_text:
Schistocytes are seen on blood smears in DIC

Also known as 'consumptive coagulopathy,' DIC is a syndrome in which the coagulation cascade is activated to the point in which normal mechanisms of clotting are exhausted, which in turn produces unchecked haemorrhage.

Typically, haemostasis is maintained by maintaining a balance between clot formation (i.e. coagulation) and breakdown (i.e. fibrinolysis). Thrombin is produced through the activation of the coagulation cascade. Thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin (the final product of clotting). Fibrinolysis is the breakdown of fibrinogen and fibrin. In the presence of thrombin, a substance called plasmin is generated, breaking down formed clots. Fibrin degradation products (FDPs) or fibrin split products (FSPs) are produced as a result. Thrombin plays a key role in hemostasis, in both coagulation and fibrinolysis.

Patients with DIC can present with a wide range of abnormalities in their laboratory values. Typically, prolonged coagulation times, thrombocytopenia, high levels of fibrin degradation products (FDPs), elevated D-dimer levels, and microangiopathic pathology (schistocytes) on peripheral smears are suggestive findings.

The activation of the cascade leads to thrombi formation which causes an accumulation of excess fibrin formation in the intravascular circulation. The excess fibrin strands cause mechanical damage to the red blood cells resulting in schistocyte formation and also thrombocytopenia and consumption of clotting factors.

A bite cell is an abnormally shaped red blood cell with one or more semicircular portions removed from the cell margin. These 'bites' result from the removal of denatured haemoglobin by macrophages in the spleen.  Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency (G6PD), in which uncontrolled oxidative stress causes haemoglobin to denature and form Heinz bodies, is a common disorder that leads to the formation of bite cells.

The Heinz Bodies are seen as antigenic and are quickly phagocytosed. Because the Heinz Bodies are derivatives of haemoglobin, they are located inside the cell, and thus phagocytosis takes a significant 'bite' out of the cell.

Dacrocytes (teardrop cells) are usually characteristic of myelofibrosis and seen with marrow disorders or marrow infiltrations, really because of improper production of blood cells from the bone marrow. In post-splenectomy patients, the number of dacrocytes drastically increases, since the spleen cannot remove the improperly formed cells.

Red cells varying in shape from elongated to oval, and rich in haemoglobin, are called elliptocytes. They can be seen in hereditary disorders, such as hereditary elliptocytosis, or in acquired disorders, such as iron deficiency anaemia, infectious anaemias, thalassaemia, and in newborn babies.

question_text:
A 69-year-old man presents to his GP with tiredness and some weight loss. On examination, he appears generally well but splenomegaly is noted. Blood tests are taken which show the following:


Hb	118 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	652 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	11.6 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)	320 U/L	(140 - 280)
Uric acid	632 µmol/L	(<416)

Genetic testing is carried out and he is found to be positive for JAK2 V617F mutation.

What finding on blood film is classically associated with the likely diagnosis?
options_json: ["'Pencil' poikilocytes", "Howell-Jolly bodies", "Schistocytes", "Spherocytes", "Tear-drop poikilocytes"]
explanation_text:
Myelofibrosis is associated with 'tear drop' poikilocytes on blood film

The diagnosis here is myelofibrosis, given the non-specific presentation, thrombocytosis, anaemia, and raised LDH and uric acid. The mutation also increases the likelihood of this diagnosis. Classically, this condition is associated with 'tear-drop' poikilocytes on blood film.

'Pencil' poikilocytes are usually associated with iron deficiency anaemia, rather than myelofibrosis. Given the other blood results, and the JAK2 V617F mutation, myelofibrosis is more likely.

Howell-Jolly bodies are typically associated with hyposplenism or seen post-splenectomy, rather than with splenomegaly which occurs with myelofibrosis.

Schistocytes are fragmented red blood cells and so are seen in microangiopathic, haemolytic disease. They would not be found in myelofibrosis.

Spherocytes are spherical red blood cells. These may be seen in hereditary spherocytosis, or autoimmune haemolytic anaemia.

question_text:
A 45-year-old man attends ambulatory care with a 2-month history of worsening fatigue. On further questioning he states that whilst he has lost some weight recently, he had attributed this to reduced appetite, stating that he has been feeling full after eating relatively little. On direct questioning he states that on a few occasions over the last 2 weeks he has woken feeling sweaty with damp sheets. On examination the patient has pale conjunctiva and there is a large, firm mass in the left upper quadrant of the abdomen. He is haemodynamically stable, afebrile and there are no signs of respiratory distress.

Initial bloods show:


Hb 105 g/l
Platelets 150 * 109/l
WBC 50 * 109/l

The F1 clerking the patient requested an abdominal CT which has been reported by the radiologist as showing massive splenomegaly.

A blood film has been sent and the patient has been discussed with the on-call haematologist who has arranged a bone marrow biopsy and cytogenetics. However, the results of these investigations are not yet available.

Which of the following findings would support a diagnosis of chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML) rather than myelofibrosis?
options_json: ["t(15;17) translocation", "t(8;21) translocation", "Low leucocyte alkaline phosphatase score", "Raised leucocyte alkaline phosphatase score", "Massive splenomegaly"]
explanation_text:
Leucocyte alkaline phosphatase is low in CML but raised in myelofibrosis

The correct answer here is a low leucocyte alkaline phosphatase (LAP) score.

LAP is found within mature white blood cells (WBCs).

Low LAP levels are found in conditions associated with immature/undeveloped WBCs (e.g. CML), whereas pathologies associated with mature WBCs (such as myelofibrosis) cause high LAP levels.

t(15; 18) translocation is associated with acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APML)

t(8;21) translocation is associated with acute myeloid leukaemia (AML)

the Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) creates a BCL-ABL1 fusion gene that codes for a constitutively active tyrosine kinase receptor. This is associated with 95% of CML cases and is the target for imatinib (a tyrosine kinase inhibitor).

Massive splenomegaly is seen in both CML and myelofibrosis

explanation_text:
Polycythaemia rubra vera - around 5-15% progress to myelofibrosis or AML

Myelofibrosis is the correct answer. The patient has polycythaemia rubra vera as evidenced by a ruddy complexion, polycythaemia and a positive mutation for JAK2V617F. These patients are at risk of developing myelofibrosis or acute myeloid leukaemia.

ALL is incorrect. While there have been occasional case reports of this subset of patients developing acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, it is not a typical complication of this disorder.

CLL, multiple myeloma and NHL are all incorrect answers. While there have been occasional reports of these disorders co-existing with PRV or occurring in the lifespan of the same patient, it is an exceedingly rare occurrence.

question_text: A 48-year-old man is diagnosed with acute myeloid leukaemia and cytogenics are performed. Which one of the following is associated most with a poor prognosis?
options_json: ["Deletions of chromosome 5", "Translocation between chromosome 15 and 17", "Deletions of chromosome 15", "Translocation between chromosome 9 and 14", "Deletions of chromosome 8"]
explanation_text:
Acute myeloid leukaemia - poor prognosis: deletion of chromosome 5 or 7

The correct answer is

Deletions of chromosome 5

. This cytogenetic abnormality is associated with a poor prognosis in acute myeloid leukaemia (AML). Patients with deletions of chromosome 5 or 5q- syndrome often present with severe anaemia and are at a higher risk for developing AML. The prognosis for these patients is generally poor, even when treated with intensive chemotherapy.

Translocation between chromosome 15 and 17

is incorrect because this chromosomal translocation results in the formation of the PML-RARA fusion gene, which is characteristic of acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APL), a subtype of AML. This particular translocation is actually associated with a good prognosis, especially when treated with all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) and arsenic trioxide.

Deletions of chromosome 15

are also incorrect. While deletions in chromosome 15 can occur in some cancers, they are not typically associated with AML or a particularly poor prognosis within this disease context.

Translocation between chromosome 9 and 14

is incorrect as it's more commonly seen in Non-Hodgkin lymphomas rather than AML. Specifically, this translocation has been identified in cases of follicular lymphoma and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma but does not carry the same prognostic significance as deletions of chromosome 5 in AML.

Finally,

Deletions of chromosome 8

, though found in various types of malignancies including some forms of AML, do not carry the same poor prognostic value as deletions on Chromosome 5 for patients suffering from AML.

question_text:
A 73-year-old woman has been referred to the haematology clinic following a 15-month history of intermittent lymphadenopathy affecting her neck. A biopsy is taken and the histology report suggests a likely diagnosis of follicular lymphoma. To aid diagnosis, genetic analysis is performed.

Which of the following genomic alterations is most likely to be found?
options_json: ["T(8;14) causing c-myc gene translocation", "T(9;22) causing the fusion of PML and RARA genes", "T(11;14) causing increased BCL-2 transcription", "T(11;22) causing c-myc gene translocation", "T(14;18) causing increased BCL-2 transcription"]
explanation_text:
The t(14;18) translocation causes increased BCL-2 transcription and causes follicular lymphoma

The t(14,18) translocation is present in approximately 90% of follicular lymphoma. The translocation results in the juxtaposition of the B-cell lymphoma 2 (BCL2) gene on chromosome 18 with the immunoglobulin heavy chain locus on chromosome 14. This leads to the over-expression of the BCL2 gene which normally prolongs cell life in the B-cells. This leads to pathological accumulation of B-cells.

In the majority of cases, follicular lymphoma does not present with B symptoms, but instead with intermittent lymphadenopathy in later life. It is slowly progressive, and patients normally die of other causes. Diagnosis is made by a combination of histological, immunological, and genomic assessment.

The t(8;14) translocation is associated with Burkitt lymphoma.

The t(9;22) translocation is associated with CML.

The t(11;14) translocation is associated with Mantle cell lymphoma.

The t(11;22) translocation is associated with Ewing sarcoma.

A 36-year-old woman presents to her general practitioner with fatigue. She has a past medical history of well-controlled rheumatoid arthritis and takes hydroxychloroquine. She does not smoke cigarettes. She drinks approximately one bottle of wine per week.

The examination is unremarkable and there is no clinical evidence of synovitis.

Blood results demonstrate:


Hb	106 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
MCV	62 fl	(80-100)
MCH	20 pg/cell	(27-32)
Platelets	189 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	6.2 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Neuts	3.5* 109/L	(2.0 - 7.0)


Ferritin	540 ng/ml	(12-30)
Total iron binding capacity	30 µmol/L	(45-82)
Vitamin B 12	550 ng/ml	(200-900)
Serum folate	8 ng/ml	(2.5-20)


Na+	137 mmol/L	(135 - 145)
K+	4.2 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Bicarbonate	24 mmol/L	(22 - 29)
Urea	5.2 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	67 µmol/L	(55 - 120)
TSH	0.4 miU/L	(0.2 - 5.5)
CRP	4 mg/L	(<5)

What is the most likely diagnosis?
options_json: ["Anaemia of chronic disease", "Beta-thalassaemia trait", "Haemochromatosis", "Iron deficiency anaemia", "Sideroblastic anaemia"]
explanation_text:
Disproportionate microcytic anaemia - think beta-thalassaemia trait

Beta-thalassaemia trait is correct. The haematological findings of this condition typically reflect a mild iron deficiency with a microcytosis out of keeping to the degree of anaemia. It is associated with an increase in iron and therefore serum ferritin may be increased and total iron-binding capacity may be decreased.

Anaemia of chronic disease is incorrect. While she does have rheumatoid arthritis and this is a cause of anaemia of chronic disease, the profound microcytosis out of proportion to the degree of anaemia is more in keeping with thalassaemia trait. Furthermore, we are told her disease is well controlled, making chronic active inflammation less likely.

Haemochromatosis is incorrect. The serum ferritin is elevated but this condition is not typically associated with microcytic anaemia. Furthermore, it usually presents post menopause in female patients.

Iron deficiency anaemia is incorrect. The serum ferritin is raised with a normal CRP. This makes iron deficiency unlikely.

Sideroblastic anaemia is incorrect. This is a rare cause of microcytic anaemia. Alcohol use can be an acquired cause. However, the microcytosis is not typically as profound as the one observed in this case and she drinks within the recommended guidelines, making this diagnosis unlikely. It is also associated with the development of hepatosplenomegaly, which is not mentioned here.

A 19-year-old male who emigrated from Ghana as a child presents with an intermittent painful morning erection for the last 5 hours. On examination he has mild splenomegaly. He has never had this problem before and is usually fit and well. Investigations demonstrate:


Hb	115 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
MCV	76 fL	(80-95)

The peripheral blood film shows multiple small red blood cells, a few sickle cells and target cells.

What is the most likely genotype for his condition?
options_json: ["HbAA", "HbSC", "HbSS", "HbSβ0", "Hbβ/β0"]
explanation_text:
Hb SC is a milder form of sickle disease

Most children in the UK are screened for sickle cell disease, leading to early diagnosis and regular follow up. In HbSC patients have the sickle mutation and the HbC mutation - where a lysine replaces glutamic acid on position 6 of the normal beta chain. The presentation is similar to sickle cell disease but with reduced severity and frequency of symptoms. There are varying genotypes associated with different severity of disease:

Genotype	Disease severity
HbAA	Normal
HbAS	sickle cell trait, usually asymptomatic
Hb SC/ Sβ+	moderate sickle cell disease (sickle cell beta + thalassemia indicates the blood has some normal haemoglobin)
Hb SS/ Sβ0	severe sickle cell disease/ Sickle cell beta 0 thalassemia (the zero indicates the blood has no normal haemoglobin)

question_text:
A 62-year-old male presents with a 2-month history of symptoms of fatigue and dyspnoea. The patient is visibly jaundiced and on abdominal examination you notice the spleen is palpable. Blood tests reveal:


Hb	98 g/l
MCV	88 fl
Direct Coombs test	Pos

Which immunoglobulin is most likely mediating this?
options_json: ["IgM", "IgG", "IgA", "IgE", "IgD"]
explanation_text:
Warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia involves IgG-mediated haemolysis

Warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia involves IgG-mediated red blood cell destruction at body temperature with work-induced splenomegaly due to extravascular haemolysis.

Episodes of IgM-mediated haemolysis are precipitated by the cold and characteristically present with symptoms involving the hands and feet.

IgA, IgE and IgD are not common antibody mediators of autoimmune haemolytic anaemia.

question_text:
A 38-year-old man is reviewed post-discharge in the acute medical unit after a recent admission with Streptococcus pneumoniae bacteremia. This is his second episode of Streptococcus pneumoniae sepsis in the last year. He has a past medical history of coeliac disease. He is not on any regular medications. He follows a gluten-free diet strictly but it is otherwise normal and well balanced. He does not smoke cigarettes or drink alcohol.

Clinical examination is unremarkable and he appears well.

Given the clinical history, what is his blood film likely to demonstrate?
options_json: ["Auer rods", "Howell-Jolly bodies", "Hypersegmented neutrophils", "Schistocytes", "Tear-drop poikilocytes"]
explanation_text:
Target cells and Howell-Jolly bodies may be seen in coeliac disease → hyposplenism

Howell-Jolly bodies are the correct answer. The patient presents with recurrent streptococcal bacteremia, which is very unusual in a young person without an underlying cause. Hyposplenism is a recognized complication of coeliac disease, which predisposes patients to infection with encapsulated bacteria such as

streptococcus pneumonia

. A Howell-Jolly body is the finding of basophilic nuclear remnants in circulating erythrocytes and is typical of hyposplenism.

Auer rods is an incorrect answer. This is typical of acute promyelocytic leukaemia.

Hypersegmented neutrophils are not correct. This is typical of B12/folate deficiency. We are told he follows a gluten-free diet strictly and has a well-balanced diet and so malabsorption and poor intake is less likely to be a problem.

Schistocytes are not correct. These fragmented red blood cells are typical of thrombotic microangiopathies.

Tear-drop poikilocytes are not correct. This is a typical blood film appearance of myelofibrosis.

question_text:
A 46-year-old man with a history of alcoholic liver disease presents with tense ascites.

Urgent bloods tests demonstrate the following:

Hb	90 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	31 *109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	4.4 *109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Neuts	2.0 *109/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Lymphs	2.0 *109/L	(1.0 - 3.5)
Mono	0.2 *109/L	(0.2 - 0.8)
Eosin	0.2 *109/L	(0.0 - 0.4)


Prothrombin time (PT)	15 secs	(10-14 secs)
Activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT)	34 secs	(25-35 secs)
Fibrinogen	2 g/L	(2 - 4)

The gastroenterology team advises an ascitic drain and advises that a platelet transfusion is required given the patient's thrombocytopenia.

The haematology team advises a pool of platelets should be administered prior to the procedure and a further pool during the procedure to ensure optimal clotting as far as possible.

The patient undergoes an uneventful transfusion of one pool prior to his procedure, however, during the procedure, it is noted that he is very warm to touch and after drain insertion, he begins to experience rigors.

Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's deterioration?
options_json: ["Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis", "Perforation of abdominal viscera with ascitic drain insertion", "Bacterial contamination of platelet transfusion", "ABO incompatibility of platelet transfusion", "None of the above"]
explanation_text:
Platelet transfusions have the highest risk of bacterial contamination compared to other types of blood products

Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is unlikely given the patient has a normal white cell count on presentation.

Perforation of abdominal viscera with ascitic drain insertion is a rare complication and occurs in less than 1 in 1000 drain insertions when performed in accordance with good clinical practice.

ABO incompatibility of platelet transfusion is very rare and would typically present with haemolysis rather than fever.

Rates of bacterial contamination of platelet transfusion are relatively speaking high, given that platelets are stored at between 20-24ºC. Risk of bacterial contamination of the platelet pool increases with increasing time ex vivo and is the main factor contributing to the short shelf life of platelets.

question_text: Which of the following is deficient in patients with hereditary angioedema?
options_json: ["C1-INH", "C3", "Heat shock protein type 1", "C6", "Histamine degradation protein (HDP)"]
explanation_text:
Hereditary angioedema - C1-INH deficiency

The correct answer is

C1-INH

(C1 esterase inhibitor). Hereditary angioedema (HAE) is characterized by recurrent episodes of severe swelling affecting various body parts, most commonly the extremities, face, and airways. It is caused by a deficiency or dysfunction of C1 esterase inhibitor (C1-INH), which normally regulates the complement cascade and prevents excessive bradykinin production. Without adequate C1-INH, there is uncontrolled activation of the complement system leading to increased vascular permeability and angioedema.

C3

is a central component of the complement cascade but is not specifically deficient in HAE. C3 deficiency would cause different clinical manifestations including recurrent bacterial infections.

Heat shock protein type 1

is not involved in the pathogenesis of HAE. Heat shock proteins are molecular chaperones that assist in protein folding and cellular stress responses.

C6

is part of the membrane attack complex (MAC) of complement. C6 deficiency is associated with increased susceptibility to Neisseria infections but not with angioedema.

Histamine degradation protein (HDP)

is a fictional entity. While histamine is involved in some forms of angioedema (particularly allergic angioedema), HAE is not histamine-mediated, which is why antihistamines are ineffective in treating HAE attacks.

Treatment of HAE focuses on replacing C1-INH (using plasma-derived or recombinant C1-INH concentrates) or using medications that target other parts of the pathway such as bradykinin receptor antagonists or kallikrein inhibitors.

question_text:
A 65-year-old woman with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) attends the clinic for review. She denies weight loss, night sweats, or fevers. On examination, you note a 4cm splenomegaly.

Blood results are as follows:


Hb	96 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	72 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	182.2 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Neuts	1.4 * 109/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Lymphs	170.8 * 109/L	(1.0 - 3.5)

Blood results from the clinic 6 months ago are as follows:


Hb	118 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	152 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	64.6 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Neuts	4.2 * 109/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Lymphs	55.4 * 109/L	(1.0 - 3.5)


Genetic testing	Intact TP53 and with mutated IGHV

What treatment is indicated?
options_json: ["Active surveillance", "Fludarabine, cyclophosphamide and rituximab", "Fludarabine, cytarabine and rituximab", "Ibrutinib", "Venetoclax-obinutuzumab"]
explanation_text:
CLL - treatment: Fludarabine, Cyclophosphamide and Rituximab (FCR)

Fludarabine, cyclophosphamide and rituximab (FCR)

is correct. For fit patients with intact TP53 and with mutated IGHV, chemoimmunotherapy with FCR remains an acceptable initial therapy. Mutations of TP53 are associated with a poor response to chemo-immunotherapy (e.g. FCR) and warrant the use of novel agents such as Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitors (e.g. ibrutinib), or BCL2 inhibitors (e.g. venetoclax). Several recent trials have shown that mutated IGHV cases have a prolonged progression-free survival (PFS) after treatment with FCR.

Active surveillance

is incorrect. Indications for treatment include progressive marrow failure, massive (>10 cm) lymphadenopathy, massive (>6 cm) splenomegaly, progressive lymphocytosis (> 50% increase over 2 months or lymphocyte doubling time < 6 months) or systemic symptoms. The patient, in this case, has a lymphocyte doubling rate < 6 months and has the development of cytopaenias suggestive of significant bone marrow infiltration. The patient in this case, therefore, requires treatment.

Fludarabine, cytarabine and rituximab

is incorrect. It is cyclophosphamide, rather than cytarabine, which is used in the treatment of CLL.

Ibrutinib

is incorrect. The patient does not fulfil any of the indications to initiate treatment. The presence of an IGHV mutation favours treatment with FCR.

Venetoclax-obinutuzumab

is incorrect. The patient does not fulfil any of the indications to initiate treatment. The presence of an IGHV mutation favours treatment with FCR.

question_text:
A 65-year-old man presents with worsening fatigue over the past 12 months. A systematic enquiry was otherwise unremarkable.

Blood results are as follows:


Hb	94 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	156 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	19.2 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Neuts	14.2 * 109/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Lymphs	2.0 * 109/L	(1.0 - 3.5)
Mono	2.4 * 109/L	(0.2 - 0.8)
Eosin	0.6 * 109/L	(0.0 - 0.4)


Blood film	Frequent nucleated red blood cell; Frequent myeloblasts (approximately 5% of nucleated cells); Tear drop poikilocytosis

What is the most likely diagnosis?
options_json: ["Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia", "Acute myeloid leukaemia", "Megaloblastic anaemia", "Myelodysplasia", "Primary myelofibrosis"]
explanation_text:
Myelofibrosis is associated with 'tear drop' poikilocytes on blood film

Primary myelofibrosis

is correct. The presence of a leukoerythroblastic blood film with frequent tear-drop poikilocytosis is highly suggestive of myelofibrosis.

Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia

is incorrect. The blood film suggests the presence of myeloblasts. Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) is associated with lymphoblasts rather than myeloblasts.

Acute myeloid leukaemia

is incorrect.  Although this remains within the differential diagnosis, the presence of tear-drop poikilocytosis favours the diagnosis of myelofibrosis. However myelofibrosis has the potential to transform to acute myeloid leukaemia, and thus a bone marrow examination is required to further categorise.

Megaloblastic anaemia

is incorrect.  The classic blood film changes associated with this condition include macrovalocytes, and hypersegmented neutrophils. However, a host of other abnormalities can occur including leukoerythroblastosis and tear-drop poikilocytes. It would therefore be important to exclude B12 and folate deficiency in this case.

Myelodysplasia

is incorrect. Typical blood film features in this condition include hyposegmented and hypogranular neutrophils.

question_text:
A 39-year-old woman presents with a strange collection of symptoms over the past six months. She has been seen by multiple specialists, none of whom have been able to find a cause for her symptoms.

Her symptoms include worsening headaches, memory loss, low mood, lethargy, abdominal pain causing paroxysms of intermittent generalised pain, nausea, an unusual taste in her mouth and paraesthesia in her extremities.

She is irritable during your consultation and at times tearful complaining that no one is taking her seriously and confiding that her General Practitioner had referred her for counselling.

Routine blood tests show:

Hb	101g/L
WBC	5.6 10*9/L

explanation_text:
Abdominal pain, constipation, neuropsychiatric features, basophilic stippling → lead poisoning

It is important to keep lead poisoning in mind as a differential, particularly in someone for whom routine investigations are not providing an answer and who clearly has abnormal pathology (demonstrated by her kidney failure and microcytic anaemia).

It can cause a varied and often non-specific array of symptoms. Some more 'classical' features include an unusual taste in the mouth and paraesthesia of the extremities.

Questions may more obviously point to the route of exposure through industrial exposure or contact with lead-based products such as paint or contaminated water.

question_text:
A 30-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with shortness of breath. She has no history of recent surgery, immobilisation or prolonged travel. She has a past medical history of a right sided calf deep vein thrombosis (DVT) two years previously. She is not taking any medications, including the combined oral contraceptive pill. Her family history is significant for an unprovoked DVT in her mother.

On examination, she is tachycardic and tachypnoeic. Her chest is clear and heart sounds are normal. Her calves are both soft and non-tender. She has a normal body mass index.

ECG demonstrates sinus tachycardia.

Her blood results are:


Hb	140 g/L	Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	250 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	6.2 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Na+	140 mmol/L	(135 - 145)
K+	4.0 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Urea	5.5 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	95 µmol/L	(55 - 120)
CRP	<5 mg/L	(< 5)
Prothrombin time (PT)	12 secs	(10-14 secs)
Activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT)	30 secs	(25-35 secs)
Fibrinogen	3.0 g/L	(2 - 4)
D-Dimer	950 ng/mL	(< 400)

CT pulmonary angiogram demonstrated bilateral pulmonary emboli and she was commenced on anticoagulation.

Which of the following best describes the most likely underlying pathology?
options_json: ["Deficiency of protein C", "Deficiency of protein S", "Mutation in prothrombin gene", "Resistance to protein C", "Resistance to protein S"]
explanation_text:
Activated protein C resistance (Factor V Leiden) is the most common inherited thrombophilia

Resistance to protein C occurs in Factor V leiden, which is the correct answer as it is the most common inherited thrombophilia. A history of recurrent unprovoked venous thromboembolism should raise the concern for an inherited thrombophilia. Missense mutation in the Factor V gene makes factor V ten times less sensitive to inactivation by activated protein C, leading to thrombophilia.

Prothrombin G20210A (prothrombin gene mutation) is the second most common inherited cause of thrombophilia (UpToDate).

Mutations in the gene encoding natural anticoagulants antithrombin III, protein C and protein S can lead to thrombophilia but these are less common. These mutations can be either cause a deficiency or loss of function.

answer_text: Continue on the DOAC for 3-6 months
explanation_text:
Cancer patients with VTE - 6 months of a DOAC

NICE updated their guidance in 2020 and now recommend using DOACs for patients with active cancer. Previously, low molecular weight heparin was recommended.

question_text:
A 27-year-old woman has some blood tests taken at her GP as part of an investigation into persistent, mild fatigue. She migrated from Turkey at the age of six and has not had any health problems to date. Her results are as follows:


Hb	105 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Mean cell volume	66fL	(80-100fL)
Platelets	220 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	5.8 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Haemoglobin A2	4.3%	(2.3-3.1%)


Blood film	'Microcytic, hypochromic erythrocytes with basophilic stippling and occasional target cells'

What is the most likely diagnosis?
options_json: ["Alpha-thalassaemia trait", "Haemoglobin H disease", "Beta-thalassaemia trait", "Beta-thalassaemia major", "Sickle cell trait"]
explanation_text:
Disproportionate microcytic anaemia - think beta-thalassaemia trait

This patient has mild anaemia with a disproportionate microcytosis and a raised haemoglobin A2. This is strongly suggestive of beta-thalassaemia trait (also known as beta-thalassaemia minor). In this condition, one of the two inherited copies of the beta-globin gene is defective, usually due to a single point mutation. Beta-thalassaemia trait is often asymptomatic, and Hb is usually normal or only slightly decreased. Blood film findings include morphological changes to the erythrocytes due to the defective beta-globin gene, such as microcytosis and target cells, but reticulocytosis is not common.

Alpha-thalassaemia trait arises from a more heterogeneous range of gene deletions affecting either one or two of the four copies of the alpha-globin gene. This may also manifest as either a normal or slightly reduced Hb with microcytosis, but is not associated with a raised HbA2 percentage.

Haemoglobin H disease refers to a form of alpha thalassaemia where deletions occur in three of the four alpha-globin genes in an individual. Unlike in this patient, one would expect to see more pronounced anaemia, elevated HbH percentage rather than HbA2, blood film reticulocytosis and possible signs and symptoms of haemolysis, such as hepatosplenomegaly and jaundice.

Beta-thalassaemia major presents with severe anaemia, with marked blood film reticulocytosis and anisopoikilocytosis. Paradoxically, HbA2 is often only mildly elevated or normal.

Patients with sickle cell trait have one normal beta-globin allele and one abnormal beta (S) globin allele. Sickle cell trait is often clinically silent and tends to yield normal Hb, HbA2 and MCV levels.

question_text:
A 50-year-old male, who was recently diagnosed with colorectal cancer, is seen in the outpatient department. He is to be started on a combined cytotoxic agent regime, of which one is a topoisomerase inhibitor. As the agent can cause myelosuppression the patient undergoes a thorough workup to rule out any latent infections (including Mycobacterium tuberculosis) and to ensure no other organ pathology is present.

Which is the most likely agent the patient is due to be started on?
options_json: ["Cyclophosphamide", "Docetaxel", "Fluorouracil", "Irinotecan", "Methotrexate"]
explanation_text:
Irinotecan inhibits topoisomerase I which prevents relaxation of supercoiled DNA

Irinotecan is commonly used in the management of colorectal cancer. Irinotecan inhibits topoisomerase I which prevents the relaxation of supercoiled DNA. As such it can cause myelosuppression.

Cyclophosphamide is an alkylating agent and is not commonly used in the management of colorectal cancer. Although it can cause myelosuppression it mechanism of action is via cross-linking of DNA and it does not affect topoisomerase.

Docetaxel's mechanism of action is on the microtubules, preventing depolymerisation and disassembly and therefore decreasing free tubulin. It is commonly used for breast cancer management.

Fluorouracil is used in chemotherapy regimes for the management of colorectal cancer and can cause myelosuppression; it is an antimetabolite. It works by inducing cell cycle arrest and apoptosis.

Methotrexate is also an antimetabolite and is not commonly used in the management of colorectal cancer.

question_text:
A 24-year-old male is admitted with difficulties breathing. He states that he was at a restaurant having dinner when he noticed a rash on his arms, followed by nausea and difficulties with taking in a breath. On examination, there is generalised urticaria and swelling of his tongue and pharynx. There is audible inspiratory stridor. You treat him with intramuscular adrenaline but due to ongoing symptoms, a further dose is given after 5 minutes.

How long will you monitor the patient before considering discharge?
options_json: ["1 hour", "2 hours", "6 hours", "48 hours", "1 week"]
explanation_text:
In anaphylaxis, biphasic reactions can occur in up to 20% of patients

The patient has clearly had an anaphylactic reaction which has been treated appropriately.  A biphasic reaction includes a recurrence of symptoms that develops after the apparent resolution of the initial reaction. Biphasic reactions have been reported to occur in 1%-20% of anaphylaxis episodes.

Resus Council UK guidelines recommend observing the patient for at least 6 hours if a second dose of adrenaline is given.

question_text: A 65-year-old man with a history of metastatic prostate cancer presents to the acute medical unit with three days of worsening mid-back pain and difficulty walking. He reports numbness over his lower abdomen and both legs. Examination reveals brisk knee reflexes and reduced power bilaterally in the lower limbs. His observations are stable. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options_json: ["Start high-dose oral dexamethasone", "Arrange urgent lumbar puncture", "Refer for urgent neurosurgical review only", "Prescribe regular oral morphine for pain relief", "Request non-contrast CT spine"]
explanation_text:
If neoplastic spinal cord compression is suspected, high-dose oral dexamethasone should be given whilst awaiting investigations

Start high-dose oral dexamethasone

is correct because neoplastic spinal cord compression is a clinical emergency requiring immediate intervention to prevent irreversible neurological damage. UK NICE guidelines recommend starting high-dose corticosteroids, typically dexamethasone, as soon as spinal cord compression is suspected—even before imaging—because this reduces oedema around the tumour, thereby minimising further cord injury while awaiting definitive investigation (MRI) and specialist input. This approach can preserve neurological function and improve outcomes, making it the single best initial step.

Arrange urgent lumbar puncture

would not be appropriate here; lumbar puncture does not diagnose or treat spinal cord compression and may even risk coning if there is raised intracranial pressure or mass effect from metastases. It also delays essential treatment; MRI spine is the gold-standard investigation.

Refer for urgent neurosurgical review only

omits a crucial first-line therapy: steroids should be started immediately while awaiting specialist assessment and imaging, as delays may worsen neurological outcome. Referral is necessary but not sufficient on its own.

Prescribe regular oral morphine for pain relief

addresses symptom control but fails to address the underlying oncological emergency. Analgesia alone will not prevent progression of neurological deficits or potential paralysis without addressing spinal cord oedema.

Request non-contrast CT spine

would miss early changes of malignant spinal cord compression; MRI is much more sensitive for soft tissue pathology affecting the spinal canal, as per NICE guidance. CT might be considered if MRI was absolutely unavailable, but steroids must still be started promptly.

question_text:
A 42-year-old woman presents with several days of fever and general malaise. She has no significant past medical history but describes a recent urinary infection from which she is recovering.

On examination, she appears mildly confused. Petechiae are noted on the extremities. Blood tests are taken which demonstrate the following:


Hb	77 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	12 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	9.2 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Na+	138 mmol/L	(135 - 145)
K+	4.2 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Creatinine	134 µmol/L	(55 - 120)

A blood film subsequently shows evidence of schistocytes.

This condition is caused by the inhibition of which protein?
options_json: ["ADAMTS13", "Antithrombin III", "Factor V", "Von Willebrand factor", "WAS protein"]
explanation_text:
Acquired inhibition of the protein ADAMTS13 which cleaves vWF multimers is the most common cause of TTP

The history and findings here are highly suggestive of thrombotic thrombocytopaenic purpura (TTP), a rare condition usually seen in women between the ages of 30 and 50. It is characterised by a pentad of findings - although these are not usually all seen together - microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopaenic purpura, neurological dysfunction, renal dysfunction and fever. It is precipitated by a number of events, including infection as seen in this scenario. It is caused by an acquired deficiency of the protein

ADAMTS13

, which normally breaks down large von Willebrand factor multimers.

Antithrombin III

deficiency is a thrombotic disorder. Antithrombin III normally acts to reduce coagulation and so deficiency, either inherited or acquired, leads to increased coagulation and thrombosis. This scenario is more in keeping with TTP.

Factor V

deficiency is a very rare inherited bleeding disorder and does not fit with the scenario above. In the context of haematology, factor V is more commonly referred to with regards to factor V Leiden - a variant form that leads to hypercoagulability, due to protein C resistance.

Von Willebrand factor

is not deficient in TTP. Rather, ADAMTS13 deficiency actually leads to a failure in breaking down von Willebrand factor multimers.

WAS protein

provides various functions in myeloid and lymphoid cells. In the context of disease, mutations lead to Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome - a rare, X-linked recessive condition that also shows thrombocytopaenia and petechiae. However, as an X-linked recessive condition, it is classically seen in males, and typically within the first few months of life, along with recurrent bacterial infections, eczema and bloody diarrhoea. This does not fit with the scenario above.

question_text:
A 45-year-old presents with fatigue, bruising, and gum bleeding. He reports feeling unwell and is experiencing frequent nosebleeds.

On examination, he is pale, has multiple bruises and has clear hepatosplenomegaly.

Blood tests:


Hb	80 g/L	(115 - 160)
WBC	36 * 10 9/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Platelets	18 * 10 9/L	(150 - 400)
Activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT)	45 secs	(25-35 secs)
Prothrombin time (PT)	22 secs	(10-14 secs)
Fibrinogen	1.1 g/L	(2 - 4)
Blood film	Promyelocytes & Auer rods present

Supportive treatment, including the administration of blood products, is initiated.

What additional treatment is most appropriate for this patient?
options_json: ["All-trans retinoic acid", "Allogeneic stem cell transplantation", "Azacitidine-based chemotherapy", "Hydroxyurea", "Radiation therapy"]
explanation_text:
APML is treated with all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) to force immature granulocytes into maturation to resolve a blast crisis prior to more definitive chemotherapy

The most appropriate treatment for this patient is

all-trans retinoic acid

(ATRA). Given the clinical presentation and laboratory findings consistent with acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APML), ATRA should be administered immediately, alongside blood products for disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) if present, as has occurred here. ATRA induces differentiation of abnormal promyelocytes, reducing the risk of DIC and other complications associated with APML. This therapy targets the underlying pathophysiology of APML by promoting the maturation of malignant cells, leading to improved outcomes and decreased risk of bleeding.

Allogeneic stem cell transplantation

is inappropriate as the initial treatment for APML. It is sometimes used in relapsed or refractory disease but is not a first-line therapy due to its associated risks and the availability of effective frontline treatments.

Although

azacitidine

is a hypomethylating agent frequently employed in treating myelodysplastic syndromes and specific acute myeloid leukaemias, it isn't the preferred initial therapy for APML. These chemotherapies are crucial in APML management but typically follow induction therapy with ATRA to solidify remission.

Using

hydroxyurea

alone is not the recommended initial treatment for APML. While hydroxyurea can help reduce cell proliferation and manage leukocytosis in APML, it does not address the underlying cause of the disease.

Radiation therapy

alone is an incorrect choice for the initial treatment of APML. While radiation therapy can be effective in certain types of leukaemia, it is not the preferred option for APML. Unlike other types of leukaemia, where radiation may target specific areas of disease involvement, APML primarily affects the bone marrow and bloodstream, making it less amenable to localised radiation therapy.

question_text:
A 55-year-old man presents with three months of urinary hesitancy. He has no past medical history. Both of his sisters developed breast cancer before the age of 30. He is of Ashkenazi Jewish heritage.

On digital rectal examination, there is an irregular, craggy prostate.

What gene likely has a mutation?
options_json: ["APC", "BRCA1", "BRCA2", "MLH1", "P53"]
explanation_text:
BRCA2 mutation is associated with prostate cancer in men

BRCA2

is correct. The patient presents with obstructive urinary symptoms and a frankly abnormal prostate exam. This suggests prostate cancer is the cause. The history of multiple siblings with early-onset breast cancer suggests a family history of the BRCA mutation. It is BRCA2 rather than BRCA1 that confers an increased risk of prostate cancer in men. This mutation is more common in those with Ashkenazi Jewish heritage.

APC

is incorrect. A mutation in this gene is associated with Gardener syndrome which causes multiple colonic polyps along with skull osteomas, thyroid cancer, and epidermoid cysts. Prostate cancer is not a feature and so this is not correct.

BRCA1

is incorrect. This is associated with early-onset breast cancer but it is BRCA2 rather than BRCA1 that causes an increased risk of prostate cancer.

MLH1

is incorrect. This encodes a DNA mismatch repair protein. A mutation in this gene causes 'Lynch syndrome', which is a hereditary colorectal cancer syndrome. It is not a cause of prostate cancer.

p53

is incorrect. A mutation in this gene is associated with Li-Fraumeni syndrome. This causes a high incidence of sarcomas and leukaemia rather than prostate cancer.

question_text:
A 23-year-old woman is admitted to the acute medical unit with an acute history of diffuse abdominal pain and constipation. She also reports burning pains in her legs associated with hyperaesthesia. A psychiatric review has also been requested as the patient is experiencing auditory hallucinations, with no history of mental health diagnoses. On examination she is tachycardia and proximal muscle weakness is also noted. She has no significant past medical history, although has recently changed her diet in a bid to lose weight.

Which single investigation is likely to be diagnostic?
options_json: ["Delta-aminolevulinic acid", "Faecal total porphyrins", "Plasma total porphyrins", "Urine porphobilinogen", "Urine total porphyrins"]
explanation_text:
In acute intermittent porphyria, urinary porphobilinogen is typically raised

This patient is presenting with classic features of acute intermittent porphyria. Abdominal pain and constipation are the most common symptoms, however neuropathic pain, proximal muscle weakness and neuropsychiatric symptoms can also manifest. An elevated urine porphobilinogen is diagnostic for the condition, and ideally should be tested from a single volume urine sample. The other listed investigations are important in helping to distinguish subtypes of porphyria, but are individually are not diagnostic.

Delta-aminolevulinic acid is widely thought to be the agent behind the pain experienced in porphyria attacks. Although it is likely to be elevated, it is not as sensitive as porphobilinogen in diagnosis the condition.

Faecal total porphyrins are indicated in patients with increased porphobilinogen. This aids the differentiation of acute intermittent porphyrias from hereditary coproporphyria and variegate porphyria; faecal porphyrins would be significantly elevated in the latter.

Plasma total porphyrins can be normal or elevated in acute intermittent porphyria. However levels will be elevated in variegate porphyria, hence it is a useful investigation in a porphyria work up.

Urine total porphyrins will be elevated in acute intermittent porphyria, however is a less sensitive test compared to urobilinogen.

question_text:
A 67-year-old woman is referred to the haematology clinic. Her GP has noted that her platelet count is persistently elevated and no reactive cause can be found. Bloods taken a week before clinic are as follows:


Hb	15.4 g/dl
Platelets	784 * 109/l
WBC	5.3* 109/l
JAK2 kinase (V617F mutation)	Positive

question_text:
A 67-year-old man presents to the haematology clinic with fatigue and abnormal blood tests. He reports worsening lethargy over the preceding six months, as well as several episodes of profuse epistaxis requiring packing. More recently, he reports his vision becoming increasingly blurry, with a worsening headache.

On clinical examination, you note hepatosplenomegaly and several rubbery lymph nodes in the anterior cervical chain.

His blood tests are as follows:



Hb	95 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Platelets	75 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	20 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)

You order serum electrophoresis, which reveals an abnormal IgM peak.

Which condition is this patient most likely to have?
options_json: ["Multiple myeloma", "Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma (MALToma)", "Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance", "Waldenstrom's macroglobulinemia", "Myelodysplasia"]
explanation_text:
Waldenstrom's macroglobulinaemia - Organomegaly with no bone lesions

This is a difficult question, as all of these options can produce an IgM peak. A careful examination of the case reveals the correct answer.

Waldenstrom's macroglobulinaemia (WM) is a B-cell lymphoma characterised by organomegaly, pancytopenia, and cold autoimmune haemolytic anaemia. The proliferative B-cells produce excessive IgM, and this forms a cornerstone of the diagnosis, alongside a biopsy. The combination of hyperviscosity symptoms (visual disturbance, headache), anaemia, thrombocytopaenia, raised white cell count, and organomegaly with lymphadenopathy with elevated IgM should prompt consideration of WM.

Multiple myeloma is another B-cell tumour and can cause anaemia and thrombocytopaenia. However, the most common monoclonal band associated with it is IgA, followed by IgA and IgD. IgM-producing multiple myelomas are rare. Further, they are not associated with organomegaly, and most commonly feature bone pain. Other symptoms include those linked to hypercalcaemia and renal failure.

Mucosa-associated lymphatic tissue tumours (MALTomas) are another B-cell tumour. While any mucosal tissue can be affected, the most common location is the stomach, where it is strongly associated with

Helicobacter pylori infection

. There are no indications of this in the above case.

Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) is a condition characterised by a monoclonal gammopathy of less than 30g/L, as well as no CRAB symptoms (hypercalcaemia, renal failure, anaemia, bone pain. Since we have anaemia, this is not MGUS. It would also not explain the organomegaly.

Myelodysplasia can cause anaemia, thrombocytopaenia, and organomegaly. However, it would not cause IgM paraproteinaemia or viscosity symptoms.

question_text:
A 66-year-old female presents with fever, weight loss and low-grade pain. After an array of tests are performed and she is diagnosed with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL). Further investigations are undertaken to assess genetic aberrations and levels of prognostic markers in order to aid management.

Which of the following would likely worsen her prognosis?
options_json: ["High levels of serum beta-2 microglobulin", "Being female", "Developing CLL at a younger age", "Deletion of 17p13 region", "Deletion of 13q14 region"]
explanation_text:
del 17p is associated with a poor prognosis in CLL

The prognosis of CLL varies and can range from 2 to 20 years. The variability highlights the importance of assessing prognostic factors and factoring this appropriately in the management of the patient. Fluorescence in situ hybridization tests (FISH) panel tests, flow cytometry and lab markers are used in order to gather information on prognosis.

Deletion of 17p13 is the strongest independent prognostic factor for CLL. The disease progresses more rapidly and tends to be refractory to many conventional treatments.

The most common genetic aberration in CLL is deletion of 13q. It is associated with a more indolent course of the disease improving the prognosis.

Female patients, younger people (<65) and patients with high levels of serum beta-2 microglobulin are associated with having a better prognosis.

question_text: A 40-year-old female has been diagnosed with haemolytic uraemic syndrome after an episode of severe diarrhoea. She has a haemoglobin of 84 mg/dL. Which of the following blood results is most likely to be found?
options_json: ["Low haptoglobin", "Low bilirubin", "Elevated magnesium", "Low urea", "Increased HbF"]
explanation_text:
Low haptoglobin levels are found in haemolytic anaemias

The patient has an intravascular haemolytic anaemia secondary to haemolytic uraemic syndrome. Haptoglobin levels are reduced in intravascular haemolysis because they bind to free haemoglobin released from lysed erythrocytes. The complexes are then removed from the plasma by the hepatic reticulo-endothelial cells. Haptoglobin levels decrease if the rate of haemolysis is greater than the rate of haptoglobin production.

Bilirubin levels are likely to be elevated because of increased metabolism of haem. Magnesium may be low because of diarrhoea or unaffected. Urea would be increased due to acute kidney injury. HbF is found in patients with inherited haemoglobinopathies and not in acquired haemolytic anaemias.

NICE Evidence search

https://www.evidence.nhs.uk/search?q=haemolytic+uraemic+syndrome

question_text:
A 34-year-old man has acute dyspnoea, fatigue, and greyish-blue discolouration of the lips and fingertips. He has no chest pain or fever. His medical history includes coeliac disease, and he was recently started on dapsone for a pruritic, blistering skin rash.

His oxygen saturation is 85% breathing air, which does not improve with supplementary oxygen. Air entry is clear and equal bilaterally, with no added breath sounds.

An arterial blood gas is performed (on 15 L/min oxygen):


pH	7.42	(7.35 - 7.45)
pO2	31.0 kPa	(10 - 14)
pCO2	4.3 kPa	(4.5 - 6.0)
Bicarbonate	25 mmol/L	(22 - 28)
Lactate	1.3 mmol/L	(< 2.0)

Which treatment is he most likely to receive?
options_json: ["Ascorbic acid", "Cyanocobalamin", "Hydroxocobalamin", "Methylthioninium chloride", "Prussian blue"]
explanation_text:
Dapsone + dyspnoea → methaemoglobinaemia

Methylthioninium chloride

is correct. This patient most likely has methaemoglobinaemia, due to acute dyspnoea, cyanosis (greyish-blue lips and fingertips), and low oxygen saturations unresponsive to high-flow oxygen following dapsone use. The arterial blood gas analysis reveals an elevated pO₂ with normal pH and pCO₂, reflecting adequate ventilation but impaired oxygen saturation due to oxidised haemoglobin. Dapsone oxidises haemoglobin iron from Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺, forming methaemoglobin that cannot effectively bind or release oxygen, leading to tissue hypoxia. Methylthioninium chloride (methylene blue) acts as an artificial electron carrier, and is reduced to leukomethylene blue, and then donates electrons to reduce methaemoglobin (Fe³⁺) back to functional haemoglobin (Fe²⁺), rapidly reversing symptoms of methaemoglobinaemia. Many arterial blood gas machines can now report methaemoglobin levels, however, a definitive diagnosis requires a formal laboratory test.

Ascorbic acid

is incorrect because it is a slow-acting reducing agent used in chronic or mild methaemoglobinaemia, not in acute, symptomatic cases like this. This patient has acute dyspnoea, cyanosis, and hypoxia despite high-flow oxygen, which requires fast reversal. Ascorbic acid would be insufficient in this scenario. It may instead be appropriate in mild or chronic methaemoglobinaemia, such as in congenital cases, where patients present with stable saturations and long-standing mild cyanosis without acute respiratory distress or dapsone exposure.

Cyanocobalamin

is incorrect because it is a form of vitamin B12 used to treat B12 deficiency, not methaemoglobinaemia. It does not affect haemoglobin oxidation or oxygen binding. This patient’s presentation is acute, with dyspnoea and cyanosis shortly after dapsone initiation. Cyanocobalamin may be appropriate in pernicious anaemia or B12 deficiency, which typically presents with fatigue, glossitis, macrocytic anaemia, and neurological symptoms such as peripheral neuropathy, paraesthesia, or subacute combined degeneration causing ataxia and spasticity, none of which are seen here.

Hydroxocobalamin

is incorrect because it is used to treat cyanide poisoning, not methaemoglobinaemia. It binds cyanide to form cyanocobalamin, which is excreted renally. This patient’s features, cyanosis, dapsone use, and hypoxia despite oxygen therapy, are typical of methaemoglobinaemia. Cyanide poisoning presents differently, with a sudden onset of confusion, seizures, lactic acidosis, arrhythmias, and cardiovascular collapse. It often occurs after smoke inhalation in enclosed spaces or industrial exposure, neither of which is described in this case.

Prussian blue

is incorrect because it treats thallium or radioactive caesium poisoning by binding these metals in the gut to prevent reabsorption. It does not reverse methaemoglobinaemia or affect oxygen transport. This patient’s presentation is acute and directly linked to dapsone use. Thallium poisoning would present with gastrointestinal symptoms (nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea), painful peripheral neuropathy, alopecia, and cardiac arrhythmias. Radioactive caesium exposure may cause nausea, vomiting, bone marrow suppression, and radiation sickness, none of which are present in this scenario.

question_text:
A 65-year-old man with myelodysplastic syndrome is attending for a blood transfusion.

He begins to feel unwell and breathless mid-way through his transfusion.

His observations are as follows:

Oxygen saturation 88%
Respiratory rate 28/min
Heart rate 112/min
BP 94/57mmHg
Temperature 38.2ºC

He is a regular patient and receives two units of blood every week. He has a history of chronic kidney disease and type 2 diabetes.

You give oxygen and assess the patient. He looks unwell, cyanosed and flushed. There is no angioedema, wheeze or urticaria.

Given the likely diagnosis, what is the most appropriate management?
options_json: ["IM adrenaline and IV fluids", "IV antibiotics, blood cultures and fluids", "IV furosemide", "Paracetamol and resume the transfusion at a slower speed", "Titrate oxygen, give IV fluids and consider escalation of care"]
answer_text: Titrate oxygen, give IV fluids and consider escalation of care
explanation_text:
TRALI is differentiated from TACO by the presence of hypotension in TRALI vs hypertension in TACO

Transfusion reactions are common and whilst some of them are minor and easily managed, there are some life-threatening reactions that can occur.  Though rare, you should always be alert to transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI) and be aware of its severity.

The treatment of TRALI is purely supportive with oxygen but a majority of patients require further respiratory support and are likely to need a higher level of care.  IV fluids can be given to support blood pressure but many patients will also need vasopressors.  The correct answer, therefore, is to

titrate oxygen, give IV fluids and consider escalation of care

.

Transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO) is differentiated from TRALI by the presence of hypertension rather than hypotension and you would not expect the patient to be febrile.  The treatment of TACO would be

IV furosemide

, so this is incorrect.

IM adrenaline and IV fluids

is incorrect.  This would be the treatment for anaphylaxis as per the Resus Council algorithm.  Anaphylaxis is possible but less likely given there is no urticaria or wheeze.

IV antibiotics, blood cultures and fluids

is not correct.  This would be a suitable treatment for sepsis which may present in this way, but given the context of regular transfusion and no other pointers towards infection, this is less likely.

Paracetamol and resume the transfusion at a slower speed

is also incorrect.  This may be appropriate for simple febrile reactions to transfusion but in this case, the hypoxia and hypotension point away from this as patients with simple reactions are usually well and have no other adverse signs except the temperature.

question_text:
A 52-year-old woman presents with fever, sweats and persistent dyspepsia despite omeprazole. She has also lost 5kg in weight over the last 1 year. Prior to this she is normally fit and well with no other past medical or drug history.

She works as a bus driver and her only recent foreign travel was to Ibiza on holiday.

She undergoes an endoscopy which reveals a tumour in the antrum of the stomach.

Which of the following is most likely to have been causative?
options_json: ["Epstein Barr virus", "Helicobacter pylori", "Coeliac disease", "Schistosoma haematobium", "Human T-lymphotropic virus 1"]
explanation_text:
Helicobacter pylori

Helicobacter pylori

infection can lead to gastric lymphoma (MALT). These are typically arise in the antrum of the stomach and can present with systemic features such as fevers and night sweats.

While coeliac disease can predispose to gastrointestinal (GI) tumours, this is rare. Furthermore, coeliac is associated with enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma, a disease of the small intestine.

Epstein Barr Virus (EBV) predisposes to nasopharyngeal cancer and Hodgkin's lymphoma.

Schistosoma haematobium

predisposes to bladder tumours.

HTLV1 predisposes to adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma.

question_text:
A 32-year-old male presents to your clinic for review. He has a history of hereditary spherocytosis and recently underwent splenectomy. Since the operation he's noticed a major improvement in his energy levels.

If a blood film was taken from the patient, what new histological finding would be observed which would have been absent prior to splenectomy?
options_json: ["Schistocytes", "Bite cells", "Heinz bodies", "Spherocytes", "Howell-Jolly bodies"]
explanation_text:
Howell-Jolly bodies are present in hereditary spherocytosis post-splenectomy

Howell-Jolly bodies are remnants of the red blood cell (RBC) nucleus which are normally removed by the spleen. Post-splenectomy these Howell-Jolly bodies persist and can be observed on histology.

Spherocytes would also be present. However, they would have been observed on histology prior to splenectomy.

Schistocytes are sheared RBCs seen in microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia.

Heinz bodies and bite cells are characteristic of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency.

question_text:
A 71-year-old man is admitted to the orthogeriatric ward following a traumatic fall with a neck of humerus fracture and scalp laceration with significant blood loss. He was transfused various blood products over a 24-hour period before becoming haemodynamically stable.

On the following morning ward round, he appears lethargic and unwell, having spiked a temperature of 38.6ºC. He is tachycardic and mildly hypotensive. Intravenous fluid resuscitation is started and blood cultures are sent.

Which of the following is most likely to have caused this reaction?
options_json: ["Cryoprecipitate", "Fibrinogen", "Fresh frozen plasma", "Platelets", "Red blood cells"]
explanation_text:
Platelet transfusions have the highest risk of bacterial contamination compared to other types of blood products

This patient is presenting with symptoms of an infection, with fever, tachycardia and hypotension. These symptoms started shortly after blood product administration. Of the answers listed in the question, platelet transfusion is most likely to cause bacterial contamination. This is because platelets are stored at room temperature between 20-24ºC as too cold temperatures lead to damage to the platelet membranes. These warmer temperatures are much more favourable for bacterial contamination and growth, compared to products stored at colder temperatures.

Red blood cells are stored at temperatures between 2-6ºC. Fresh frozen plasma and cryoprecipitate are stored at temperatures of -30ºC and are thawed just before use. These temperatures make bacterial contamination much less likely.

Fibrinogen is now commonly stored as a powder that is mixed into a solution with sterile water. Therefore, it is unlikely to cause bacterial contamination.

Blood tests show a normal full blood count, ESR and thyroid function tests. Anti-endomysial antibodies are negative. What is the most suitable test to investigate possible food allergy?

question_text:
A 72-year-old man has 8 months of fatigue, constipation, polyuria, and low mood. He has no fever, headaches, or visual disturbance. Two years ago, he had an incidental 12 g/L monoclonal spike on serum protein electrophoresis, with IgG kappa monoclonal proteins on immunofixation. He was asymptomatic at the time, with preserved renal function.

He is tender over the lumbar spine, with no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly.


Hb	120 g/L	(135-180)
Platelets	392 * 10 9/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	5.4 * 10 9/L	(4.0 - 11.0)


Na+	140 mmol/L	(135 - 145)
K+	4.4 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Urea	8.3 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	143 µmol/L	(55 - 120)

Which condition has he most likely developed?
options_json: ["Immunoglobulin heavy chain disease", "Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance", "Multiple myeloma", "Smouldering myeloma", "Waldenström macroglobulinaemia"]
explanation_text:
Non-IgM MGUS may progress to multiple myeloma

Progression of non-IgM MGUS to multiple myeloma

is correct. This patient now has features of end-organ damage, including hypercalcaemia (fatigue, polyuria, low mood, constipation), renal impairment (creatinine 143 µmol/L), anaemia (Hb 120 g/L), and bone tenderness, fulfilling the CRAB criteria for multiple myeloma. Two years ago, he had non-IgM MGUS, defined by an IgG kappa paraprotein and absence of symptoms or organ damage. Non-IgM MGUS can progress to multiple myeloma, which has likely occurred in this patient. The absence of fever, lymphadenopathy, or hepatosplenomegaly further supports multiple myeloma over alternative diagnoses.

Immunoglobulin heavy chain disease

is incorrect. This patient lacks the systemic features typically seen in immunoglobulin heavy chain disease (HCD), such as lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, respiratory symptoms (e.g., chronic cough, bronchiectasis), gastrointestinal signs (e.g., diarrhoea, weight loss), or autoimmunity. HCD is not a known progression from MGUS. In contrast, this patient's features of hypercalcaemia (fatigue, polyuria, low mood, constipation), anaemia, bone tenderness, and renal impairment align more with multiple myeloma.

Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance

is incorrect. MGUS is defined by a monoclonal protein without symptoms or end-organ involvement. This patient now has CRAB features, hypercalcaemia (fatigue, polyuria, low mood, constipation), renal impairment, anaemia, and bone tenderness, indicating progression beyond MGUS. MGUS would only apply if the paraprotein remained stable and the patient remained asymptomatic, which was true two years ago but is no longer applicable.

Smouldering myeloma

is incorrect. Smouldering myeloma is characterised by ≥ 10% bone marrow plasma cells or a monoclonal protein > 30 g/L, but without organ damage. This patient presents with symptomatic hypercalcaemia (fatigue, polyuria, low mood, constipation), renal impairment, anaemia, and bone tenderness, excluding smouldering myeloma. If this patient did not have these features and their monoclonal spike was > 30 g/L, then this could be considered.

Waldenström macroglobulinaemia

(WM) is incorrect. This condition involves an IgM monoclonal gammopathy, while this patient has an IgG kappa paraprotein. WM typically presents with lymphoplasmacytic infiltration and hyperviscosity symptoms such as blurred vision, headache, or organomegaly, none of which are present here. WM may also cause neuropathy or coagulopathy, which this patient does not have. WM would be more likely in a patient with an IgM paraprotein and systemic or hyperviscosity-related symptoms.
