question_text:
A 27-year-old woman with a background of systemic lupus erythematosus has progressed to end-stage renal failure following a period of declining renal function. An urgent renal biopsy was performed which confirmed the presence of lupus nephritis. Her case was discussed in the MDT meeting and she was commenced on various drug treatments to help suppress the immune system. A few days into the course of her treatment she developed gross macroscopic haematuria which the team felt was likely to have been caused by one of the new medications. Mesna was given to treat this side effect.

What is the mechanism of action of the offending medication in this case?
options_json: ["Cross-linking in DNA", "Degrades preformed DNA", "Increases lysosomal pH in antigen-presenting cells", "Inhibits dihydrofolate reductase", "Inhibits microtubule formation"]
explanation_text:
Cyclophosphamide - causes cross-linking in DNA

Cross-linking in DNA is the mechanism by which cyclophosphamide acts as a chemotherapy agent and is used to suppress the immune system in various conditions such as systemic lupus erythematosus, nephrotic syndrome, granulomatosis with polyangiitis and severe rheumatoid arthritis. It has mainly important side effects to be aware of one of which is haemorrhagic cystitis which can result in dysuria and gross macroscopic haematuria. This can be prevented with adequate fluid intake, avoiding night-time dosing and the use of mesna.

Dihydrofolate reductase inhibitors e.g. methotrexate is chemotherapy and immunosuppressive agent which inhibits. They are used to treat cancers and autoimmune diseases.

Increasing lysosomal pH in antigen-presenting cells is how hydroxychloroquine works as a disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug (DMARD) used in rheumatoid arthritis and lupus. Hydroxychloroquine has side effects of retinopathy and ventricular arrhythmias.

Degrading performed DNA is a mechanism by which bleomycin works to treat cancers and can cause lung fibrosis as an adverse effect.

Stabilisation of DNA-topoisomerase II complex and inhibition of DNA & RNA synthesis is how anthracyclines (e.g. doxorubicin) work as a chemotherapy agent. Doxorubicin as an example can cause cardiomyopathy.

question_text:
A 61-year-old man is diagnosed with metastatic colorectal cancer and is started on a chemotherapy regimen that includes irinotecan.

What is the primary mechanism of action of this medication?
options_json: ["Alkylating agent causing cross-linking in DNA", "Inhibition of topoisomerase I preventing relaxation of supercoiled DNA", "Inhibits formation of microtubules", "Prevents microtubule depolymerisation & disassembly", "Stabilises DNA-topoisomerase II complex"]
answer_text: Inhibition of topoisomerase I preventing relaxation of supercoiled DNA
explanation_text:
Irinotecan inhibits topoisomerase I which prevents relaxation of supercoiled DNA

Irinotecan

inhibits topoisomerase I

, an enzyme with multiple functions including relaxation of supercoiled DNA. It is used in the treatment of a variety of cancers. For the treatment of metastatic colorectal cancer, it is often used as part of the FOLFIRI regimen alongside folinic acid and 5-fluorouracil.

Cyclophosphamide is an example of an

alkylating agent

causing cross-linking in DNA.

Vinca alkaloids such as vincristine and vinblastine

inhibit the formation of microtubules

.

Taxanes such as docetaxel function by

preventing microtubule polymerisation and disassembly

.

Anthracyclines such as doxorubicin

stabilise the DNA-topoisomerase II complex and prevent DNA and RNA synthesis

.

question_text: What is the mechanism of action of cisplatin?
options_json: ["Stabilises DNA-topoisomerase II complex", "Causes cross-linking in DNA", "Inhibits ribonucleotide reductase", "Inhibits purine synthesis", "Inhibits formation of microtubules"]
explanation_text:
Cisplatin - causes cross-linking in DNA

The correct answer is that cisplatin causes cross-linking in DNA. Cisplatin is a platinum-containing chemotherapeutic agent that forms covalent bonds with purine bases (particularly guanine) in DNA. This creates both intrastrand and interstrand cross-links, preventing DNA from unwinding and separating during cellular replication. This mechanism ultimately leads to apoptosis of rapidly dividing cells, making it particularly effective against various malignancies, especially testicular cancer, ovarian cancer, and certain lung cancers.

Stabilises DNA-topoisomerase II complex

is incorrect as this is the mechanism of action for different chemotherapeutic agents, specifically the topoisomerase inhibitors such as etoposide and doxorubicin. These drugs work by preventing the re-ligation of DNA strands after they have been cut by topoisomerase II, leading to cell death.

Inhibits ribonucleotide reductase

is incorrect as this is the mechanism of action of hydroxyurea. This enzyme is responsible for converting ribonucleotides to deoxyribonucleotides, which are essential for DNA synthesis. Hydroxyurea is commonly used in conditions such as sickle cell disease and certain myeloproliferative disorders.

Inhibits purine synthesis

is incorrect as this is the mechanism of action of drugs such as methotrexate and mercaptopurine. These agents interfere with the de novo synthesis of purines, which are essential building blocks for DNA and RNA synthesis. These drugs are commonly used in conditions such as acute lymphoblastic leukaemia and rheumatoid arthritis.

Inhibits formation of microtubules

is incorrect as this is the mechanism of action of vinca alkaloids (such as vincristine and vinblastine) and taxanes (such as paclitaxel). These drugs interfere with microtubule formation or breakdown, preventing proper cell division during mitosis. They are commonly used in various malignancies including breast cancer and lymphomas.

question_text:
Tom is a 45-year-old man who has presented with new-onset urinary retention over the past 8 hours. He was previously diagnosed with non-Hodgkin's lymphoma and is currently undergoing chemotherapy treatment for this. He notes that prior to this, his urine had a reddish-tinge.

A 3-way catheter was inserted and blood-stained urine with clots was seen within the catheter bag. Urinalysis showed significant blood but no leukocytes or nitrites were seen. A cystoscopy performed did not show any masses and biopsies taken did not show any malignancy. It was felt that this was a likely side effect of one of these chemotherapy agents.

What is the underlying mechanism of action of the culprit chemotherapy agent?
options_json: ["Inhibition of DNA topoisomerase II", "Inhibits microtubule formation", "Promotes cross-linking of DNA", "Pyrimidine analogue", "Monoclonal antibody against CD20"]
explanation_text:
Cyclophosphamide - causes cross-linking in DNA

The patient has non-Hodgkin's lymphoma and is likely being managed with the chemotherapy regime R-CHOP which consists of rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine and prednisolone.

Given the negative cystoscopy and urine dipstick, it is likely that his haematuria is caused by haemorrhagic cystitis. This is a documented side effect of cyclophosphamide.

Cyclophosphamide functions as an alkylating agent that promotes cross-linking of DNA.

Inhibition of microtubule formation is the mechanism of drugs such as vincristine.

Inhibition of topoisomerase II and DNA/RNA synthesis occurs with anthracyclines such as doxorubicin.

Rituximab is an example of a monoclonal antibody against CD20.

Pyrimidine analogues include drugs such as 5-fluorouracil. They induce cell cycle arrest and apoptosis by blocking thymidylate synthase. These are not commonly used in the management of non-Hodgkin's lymphoma.

Platelets	65 * 109/l
WBC	12.3 * 109/l

question_text:
A 21-year-old man attends the emergency department after noticing blood in his urine. He has been feeling fatigued and generally unwell for the last two days and has been finding himself getting out of breath easily. His housemates had commented yesterday that he was 'turning yellow', but he had assumed they were teasing him for being unwell and had ignored them.

He is normally fit and well and is not on any regular medications. He has however recently started taking primaquine in preparation for a volunteering trip to Tanzania next week.

On examination, he is clearly jaundiced and tachypnoeic. His urine sample is a dark brown and is positive for blood and bilirubin. He is afebrile and normotensive, though is requiring some supplemental oxygen.

You are awaiting the rest of his test results but have received the following from the lab so far:


Hb	115 g/l
MCV	90 fL
Haematocrit	0.3 L/L
Platelets	250 * 109/l
WBC	10.2 * 109/l
Reticulocyte count	2.1%
Peripheral blood film	Presence of schistocytes, spherocytes and bite cells noted

What is the most likely reason for this presentation?
options_json: ["Sickle cell crisis", "Post-infectious haemolytic anaemia", "G6PD deficiency", "Hereditary spherocytosis", "Pyruvate kinase deficiency"]
explanation_text:
Malaria prophylaxis (e.g. primaquine) can trigger haemolytic anaemia in those with G6PD deficiency

This man is presenting with signs and symptoms of a haemolytic anaemia, the most likely cause of which is G6PD deficiency. A number of foods and medications can trigger haemolysis in individuals with G6PD deficiency, an important class of which are quinine-based anti-malarial medications. The temporal link between starting malaria prophylaxis and developing signs of haemolysis makes this the most likely cause.

While a sickle cell crisis can trigger haemolysis, there is nothing to suggest this patient has sickle cell disease, and no sickle cells are present on the blood film.

Post-infectious haemolysis can occur with atypical pneumonias such as

Mycoplasma

(cold-agglutinin disease) and infections that induce hypersplenism such as mononucleosis. There is nothing to suggest an infectious cause in this scenario, however.

Congenital haemoglobin defects such as spherocytosis can also cause haemolysis. While there are spherocytes on this man's blood film, these are present to different degrees in haemolytic anaemias of any cause and as such are not specific.

Pyruvate kinase deficiency is the next most common inherited metabolic disorder after G6PD deficiency. Haemolysis in these patients tends to be triggered in times of significant physiological stress.

question_text:
A 52-year-old woman with a complex medical history, including systemic lupus erythematosus, is admitted to the hospital with severe sepsis and disseminated intravascular coagulation. As part of her critical care management, she receives multiple transfusions.

Initially, she shows signs of improvement; however, her condition suddenly deteriorates, raising concerns about a possible secondary bacterial infection. The team suspects the infection may be linked to contamination from one of the transfused products.

What transfusion is most likely to be associated with this complication?
options_json: ["Cryoprecipitate", "Fresh frozen plasma (FFP)", "Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG)", "Platelet", "Red blood cells (RBC)"]
explanation_text:
Platelet transfusions are at particular risk of bacterial contamination as they are stored at room temperature

Platelet

transfusions are the most likely source of bacterial contamination because they are stored at room temperature (20-24°C) to preserve platelet function and viability. Unlike other blood products stored at colder temperatures, this room-temperature storage creates an environment more conducive to bacterial growth, increasing the risk of contamination. Common bacteria causing contamination include

Staphylococcus epidermidis

and

Bacillus cereus

.

Cryoprecipitate

is not typically associated with bacterial contamination as it is stored at temperatures of -18°C or below until required for use. The sub-zero storage conditions serve as a deterrent to bacterial growth, thereby minimising the likelihood of infection from this blood product.

Regarding

FFP

, it is also an unlikely source of bacterial contamination as it is stored at temperatures ranging from -18°C to -25°C. Such frigid conditions inhibit bacterial activity, thus decreasing the likelihood of infection related to transfusions.

IVIG

is stored under refrigeration between 2°C and 8°C, an environment that does not support either bacterial or fungal proliferation. Moreover, IVIG products are subject to sterile filtration during production to remove microorganisms and assure sterility, making them less susceptible to bacterial contamination compared with platelet transfusions.

RBCs

are incorrect because they are stored between 1 and 6°C, significantly reducing the risk of bacterial contamination compared to products stored at room temperature. Although contamination of RBCs can occur, the risk is significantly lower when compared to products stored at room temperature. The cold storage environment inhibits bacterial growth, making RBC transfusions less likely to be associated with bacterial infections.

question_text:
A 45-year-old woman presents with muscle weakness primarily affecting her legs. She also complains of chest pain. On examination, you note proximal myopathy of the upper limbs (MRC grade 4/5) and lower limbs (MRC grade 3/5). The weakness demonstrates fatiguability, The examination was otherwise unremarkable.

A chest x-ray medicine:


Chest x-ray	Large mediastinal mass

What is the most likely diagnosis?
options_json: ["Dermatomyositis", "Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome", "Lymphoma", "Myasthenia gravis", "Systemic lupus erythematosus"]
explanation_text:
Anterior mediastinal mass + symptoms of myasthenia = thymoma

A mediastinal mass has a wide differential which includes lymphoma, lung cancer, thymoma and infection (e.g. TB).

Myasthenia gravis

is correct. Myasthenia gravis (MG) is an autoimmune neuromuscular disorder characterized by fluctuating motor weakness involving ocular, bulbar, limb, and/or respiratory muscles. The presence of a mediastinal mass associated with proximal myopathy makes MG with a comorbid thymoma the most likely diagnosis.  Furthermore, the fatigable weakness is classic of MG.

Dermatomyositis

is incorrect. Although dermatomyositis can present with a proximal myopathy, the absence of myalgia and skin manifestations makes this a less likely diagnosis. It is important to remember that mediastinal masses can be associated with dermatomyositis which is often a paraneoplastic condition secondary to lung cancer.

Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome

is incorrect. Although this remains within the differential diagnosis (e.g. as a paraneoplastic phenomenon secondary to lung cancer), it is an exceedingly rare condition making this less likely. Furthermore, in Lamber-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, motor power actually improves with repeated testing in contrast to the fatiguability seen in MG. In this case, the presence of fatiguability favours the diagnosis of MG.

Lymphoma

is incorrect. Paraneoplastic neurological syndromes rarely associate with lymphoma, with the exception of cerebellar degeneration and dermatomyositis. The absence of myalgia and skin manifestations makes paraneoplastic dermatomyositis an unlikely diagnosis.

Systemic lupus erythematosus

(SLE) is incorrect. The coexistence of SLE and thymoma is rare. SLE can rarely cause muscle weakness, however, this would usually be a myalgic process resulting in pain. Furthermore, there are no other typical features of SLE present in this case.

question_text:
A 26-year-old woman is diagnosed with coeliac disease after a 1 year history of weight loss and diarrhoea. Tissue transglutaminases are positive and she is commenced on a gluten free diet.

As part of her investigations she is noted to have a low haemoglobin and ferritin levels and a blood film is sent.

Which of the following blood film findings would be suggestive of hyposplenism?
options_json: ["Basophilic stippling and cabot rings", "Rouleaux formation", "Schistocytes and eosinophilia", "Howell-Jolly bodies and siderocytes", "Toxic granulation and Dohle bodies"]
explanation_text:
Howell-Jolly bodies and siderocytes are typical blood film findings of hyposplenism

Hyposplenism is a feature of coeliac disease. Blood film findings include Howell-Jolly bodies and siderocytes.

Basophilic stippling and cabot rings are features of lead poisoning.

Rouleaux formation are chronic inflammation and myeloma.

Schistocytes are a feature of haemolytic anaemia.

Toxic granulation and Dohle bodies are a neutrophil response to infection.

question_text:
A 9-month-old boy is reviewed in the paediatric clinic for poor weight gain and increasing pallor. His parents report he has been lethargic for the past two months. On examination, he has marked hepatosplenomegaly. His initial blood tests are shown below.


Hb	61 g/L	(105 - 135)
MCV	58 fL	(72 - 88)
Platelets	245 x 109/L	(150 - 450)
WBC	9.1 x 109/L	(6.0 - 17.5)

Haemoglobin electrophoresis is performed.

Which of the following results is most likely in this child?
explanation_text:
HbF is markedly raised in beta-thalassaemia major

The correct answer is

HbA 0%, HbA2 4%, HbF 96%

. This clinical presentation is classic for beta-thalassaemia major. The patient is a 9-month-old infant, the age at which fetal haemoglobin (HbF) levels normally decline, unmasking the inability to produce adult haemoglobin (HbA). This leads to a profound, transfusion-dependent microcytic anaemia, as seen in the blood results (Hb 61 g/L, MCV 58 fL). The severe anaemia causes bone marrow expansion and extramedullary haematopoiesis, resulting in hepatosplenomegaly and failure to thrive. In beta-thalassaemia major, there is a severe or complete deficiency of beta-globin chain synthesis. As HbA is composed of two alpha and two beta chains (α2β2), it cannot be produced. The body compensates by continuing to produce HbF (α2γ2) and a small amount of HbA2 (α2δ2). Therefore, haemoglobin electrophoresis will show a complete absence of HbA, a markedly elevated HbF which constitutes the vast majority of haemoglobin, and a normal or slightly raised HbA2.

HbA 94%, HbA2 5%, HbF 1%

is the characteristic pattern for beta-thalassaemia minor (trait). In this condition, there is reduced, but not absent, production of beta-globin chains. This results in a mild and often asymptomatic microcytic anaemia. The key diagnostic feature is a raised HbA2 level (typically >3.5%). This diagnosis is inconsistent with the severe clinical picture of failure to thrive, profound anaemia, and massive hepatosplenomegaly seen in the patient.

HbA 0%, HbS 90%, HbF 10%

is the pattern seen in sickle cell anaemia (HbSS). While this condition also presents in infancy with severe anaemia and splenomegaly, the underlying defect is a qualitative one (a point mutation in the beta-globin gene) rather than a quantitative one. This leads to the production of abnormal haemoglobin S (HbS) instead of HbA. Electrophoresis would therefore show predominantly HbS, with a variable amount of HbF and no HbA. The patient's results show almost exclusively HbF, not HbS.

HbA 60%, HbS 38%, HbA2 2%

represents sickle cell trait (HbAS). This is a heterozygous carrier state where individuals produce both normal HbA and abnormal HbS. They are typically haematologically normal and asymptomatic, except under conditions of extreme physiological stress (e.g., severe hypoxia). This pattern is completely inconsistent with the severe, symptomatic anaemia presented in the question.

HbA 97%, HbA2 2%, HbF <1%

is a normal adult haemoglobin pattern. This finding would be expected in a healthy individual beyond the first year of life. It is entirely incompatible with the severe microcytic anaemia, failure to thrive, and significant hepatosplenomegaly described in this 9-month-old infant, who is clearly suffering from a major haematological disorder.

question_text:
A 58-year-old woman is referred to breast clinic with a hard painless lump in her left breast. She is eventually diagnosed with breast cancer. She undergoes a series of tests and her clinician decides to prescribe anastrozole.

Which of the following side effects should she be warned about before this medication is prescribed?
options_json: ["Deep vein thrombosis", "Endometrial cancer", "Osteoporosis", "Urinary incontinence", "Vaginal bleeding"]
explanation_text:
Aromatase inhibitors (e.g. anastrozole) may cause osteoporosis

Her breast cancer is ER-positive, meaning that it is responsive to oestrogen (about 80% of all breast cancers are). In postmenopausal women, this can be targeted with aromatase inhibitors such as anastrozole.

The most important side effect of this hormonal treatment is osteoporosis. Women should have their bone mineral density formally assessed at the beginning of treatment and at regular intervals thereafter.

Deep vein thrombosis, endometrial cancer, and vaginal bleeding are both side effects of another common drug used to treat breast cancer (tamoxifen).

Anastrozole has not been linked to urinary incontinence.

question_text:
A 77-year-old lady is admitted by the emergency department complaining of difficulty coping at home. She is unable to mobilise independently and has a poor appetite due to difficulty swallowing. She has a diagnosis of oesophageal cancer but is not thought to be a candidate for chemotherapy. Her GP recently started her on nitrofurantoin for a urinary tract infection.

On examination she is a thin, frail lady who is alert and oriented. There is no neurological deficit in the upper limbs. She has weakness of hip flexion and knee extension in both legs, but markedly more so on the right. You are able to elicit some loss of pinprick sensation on the anterior thigh. Her reflexes are brisk with an upgoing plantar on the right.

Her blood results are as follows:


Hb	101 g/l
Platelets	440 * 109/l
WBC	8.4 * 109/l
MCV	99 fL
Na+	136 mmol/l
K+	4.8 mmol/l
Urea	3.7 mmol/l
Creatinine	52 µmol/l

What is the next most appropriate step in this patient's management?
options_json: ["Transfer to hospice", "Refer for physiotherapy", "MRI imaging of the spinal cord", "Check B12 and folate levels", "Stop nitrofurantoin"]
answer_text: MRI imaging of the spinal cord
explanation_text:
Patients with suspected neoplastic spinal cord compression should have an urgent MRI of the whole spine

A patient with new lower limb neurology and a history of cancer should raise the suspicion of metastatic spinal cord compression, which is best demonstrated on MRI.

Although nitrofurantoin and B12 deficiency could cause a peripheral neuropathy, both are less urgent problems than cord compression.

question_text:
A 38-year-old female patient presents to the emergency department with severe abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting. She also reports reduced sensation in the bilateral lower limb extremities. She appears highly agitated and labile in mood. Her partner reports that this has happened about 6 times before and various suspected diagnoses were made for these past episodes but no definite diagnosis was ever made. She reports that her mother also gets such episodes. These past suspected diagnoses include acute appendicitis, renal calculi, acute intestinal obstruction. They were all found to be negative.

What is the likely diagnosis to account for this clinical presentation?
options_json: ["Acute intermittent porphyria", "Porphyria cutanea tarda", "Lead poisoning", "Neurotic disorder", "Multiple sclerosis"]
explanation_text:
Acute intermittent porphyria typically presents with abdominal, neurological and psychiatric symptoms

Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) typically presents with abdominal, neurological and psychiatric symptoms.

Porphyria cutanea tarda presents with photosensitive bullae.

Lead poisoning is possible to account for this presentation but it doesn't account for the family history. AIP is more likely given the family history.

Neurotic disorder may be possible but physical causes need to be ruled out before considering a psychiatric diagnosis.

Multiple sclerosis doesn't usually present with gastrointestinal symptoms.

question_text:
A 55-year-old man has 9 months of progressive fatigue, weight loss, early satiety, and vague abdominal pain. He has no fevers or night sweats.

His vital signs are normal but he appears pale. He has marked splenomegaly extending 8 cm below the costal margin. There is no lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, or jaundice.

Investigations:


Hb	112 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Platelets	530 * 10 9/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	63.6 * 10 9/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Neuts	58.2 * 10 9/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Lymphs	3.4 * 10 9/L	(1.0 - 3.5)
Mono	0.5 * 10 9/L	(0.2 - 0.8)
Eosin	1.5 * 10 9/L	(0.0 - 0.4)

A blood film is requested.

Which feature is most likely to be seen?
options_json: ["Auer rods", "Fragile cells that break when smeared on a glass slide", "Granulocytes at different stages of maturation", "Lymphocytes at different stages of maturation", "Tear-drop poikilocytes"]
answer_text: Granulocytes at different stages of maturation
explanation_text:
In chronic myeloid leukaemia there is an increase in granulocytes at different stages of maturation +/- thrombocytosis

Granulocytes at different stages of maturation

is correct. This 55-year-old man has progressive fatigue, weight loss, early satiety, pallor, and massive splenomegaly with no lymphadenopathy or hepatomegaly. His blood tests show marked leukocytosis, mainly due to neutrophilia and eosinophilia, along with anaemia and thrombocytosis. These findings strongly suggest chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML), a myeloproliferative disorder characterised by uncontrolled proliferation of the myeloid lineage. On a blood film, this would typically show granulocytes at various stages of maturation, such as myelocytes, metamyelocytes, band cells, and mature neutrophils, demonstrating a “left shift'. The eosinophilia and thrombocytosis further support a myeloid, rather than lymphoid, malignancy. These findings explain the splenomegaly (due to extramedullary haematopoiesis) and chronic symptoms, which are typical of CML.

Auer rods

is incorrect because these are seen in acute myeloid leukaemia (AML), not CML. Auer rods are needle-like inclusions in myeloblasts and indicate blast proliferation. AML presents acutely with symptoms of marrow failure such as infections, bleeding, and severe anaemia. This patient has a more chronic course, with thrombocytosis rather than thrombocytopenia and no circulating blasts reported. Auer rods may be seen in cases of acute leukaemia, particularly acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APL), often with pancytopenia and a more abrupt onset.

Fragile cells that break when smeared on a glass slide

is incorrect because these “smudge cells” are associated with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL), not CML. Smudge cells are remnants of fragile lymphocytes and are seen in lymphoid rather than myeloid malignancies. CLL typically presents with raised lymphocyte counts, minimal symptoms, and often lymphadenopathy. In contrast, this patient has neutrophilia and eosinophilia, no lymphadenopathy, and marked splenomegaly—features that do not align with CLL. Smudge cells may be seen in older adults with incidentally diagnosed lymphocytosis and typical CLL features.

Lymphocytes at different stages of maturation

is incorrect because this pattern suggests a lymphoid disorder such as CLL, whereas this patient’s clinical and haematological findings are consistent with a myeloid proliferation. CML results in increased granulocytes, not lymphocytes. This patient has raised neutrophils and eosinophils, not lymphocytes. Lymphoid maturation patterns may be seen in CLL or in reactive lymphocytosis (e.g. viral infections), neither of which explains the massive splenomegaly, thrombocytosis, or prolonged systemic symptoms seen here.

Tear-drop poikilocytes

is incorrect as these are associated with myelofibrosis, a condition marked by marrow fibrosis and extramedullary haematopoiesis. While myelofibrosis can cause splenomegaly and anaemia, it typically leads to thrombocytopenia, not thrombocytosis as seen here. It also commonly presents with hepatomegaly, which is not reported. Tear-drop cells may be seen in advanced myeloproliferative disorders with bone marrow failure, but are not typical in early-phase CML, which better matches this patient’s presentation.

question_text:
A 34-year-old woman attends the ambulatory emergency care unit for further investigation for a suspected deep vein thrombosis (DVT). This is subsequently confirmed by ultrasound. She reports that several members of her family on her mother's side have had thrombotic episodes and been diagnosed with Factor V Leiden. Otherwise, she does not smoke, has no history of immobilisation, does not take any oral contraceptive and a urine human chorionic gonadotropin is negative.

What is the prevalence of her underlying disorder?
explanation_text:
Activated protein C resistance (Factor V Leiden) is the most common inherited thrombophilia

The most common inherited cause of thrombophilia is activated protein C resistance (Factor V Leiden) which has a prevalence of 5%. The prevalence of other inherited causes thrombophilia are listed below.

Antithrombin III deficiency has a prevalence of 0.02%.

Protein C deficiency has a prevalence of 0.3%.

Protein S deficiency is also a rare cause and has a prevalence of 0.1%.

Prothrombin gene mutation is the second most common inherited cause of thrombophilia with a prevalence of 1.5% however this is still more rare than Factor V Leiden.

question_text: Each one of the following is associated with polycythaemia vera, except:
options_json: ["Splenomegaly", "Hyperviscosity", "Raised ESR", "Hypertension", "Pruritus"]
explanation_text:
Polycythaemia rubra vera is associated with a low ESR

The correct answer is

Raised ESR

. Polycythaemia vera (PV) is a myeloproliferative neoplasm characterised by an increase in erythrocytes, leukocytes and platelets. This results in hyperviscosity of blood but does not typically lead to a raised Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR). ESR is a nonspecific measure of inflammation, and it's usually low in PV due to the increased number of red blood cells that reduce the relative proportion of plasma and thus sedimentation.

Now, let's discuss each of the incorrect answers:

Splenomegaly

is indeed associated with polycythaemia vera. It occurs as a result of extramedullary haematopoiesis and congestion due to increased blood volume. Splenomegaly can be present in up to 75% of patients at diagnosis.

Hyperviscosity

is also associated with PV. The overproduction of red blood cells leads to an increase in blood viscosity which can cause symptoms such as dizziness, headaches and visual disturbances. Hyperviscosity also increases the risk of thrombotic events.

Hypertension

can be seen in patients with PV. The increased blood volume and viscosity can contribute to high blood pressure. Moreover, renal artery stenosis secondary to thrombus formation may also cause hypertension.

Lastly,

Pruritus

, especially after bathing or showering, is a common symptom of polycythaemia vera. It's thought to be caused by histamine release from proliferating mast cells within the bone marrow or by increased basophils in the peripheral circulation.

question_text:
A 64-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a history of progressively worsening facial, neck, and upper chest swelling over the past few weeks, which has acutely intensified in the last 48 hours. He is experiencing dyspnoea, chest and head tightness, hoarseness of voice, and dysphagia.

On examination, he exhibits distended neck veins, facial swelling, and engorged veins on his upper chest and arms. Imaging identifies an apical lung tumour compressing the superior vena cava (SVC).

What is the most common presenting symptom of this man's condition?
options_json: ["Distended neck veins", "Dyspnoea", "Facial swelling", "Headache", "Hoarseness"]
explanation_text:
SVC obstruction - dyspnoea is the most common symptom

The diagnosis in this scenario is SVC obstruction, which is likely due to compression of the SVC by a mediastinal mass, such as lung cancer. This aetiology is frequently encountered, with SVC obstruction commonly arising secondary to lung cancer or other mediastinal malignancies. The most prevalent symptom is

dyspnoea

, resulting from compromised venous return from the upper body to the heart. This impediment leads to elevated pressure within the upper venous system and subsequent venous congestion that affects the lungs and airways, manifesting as dyspnoea. Management typically involves treatment of the underlying cause—such as radiotherapy or chemotherapy for malignancy—and may include the insertion of an SVC stent to re-establish blood flow.

While

distended neck veins

are a classic feature, they are not usually the initial presenting sign of SVC obstruction. They arise from hindered venous drainage from the head, neck, and upper extremities, leading to visible engorgement of the veins. Nonetheless, dyspnoea presents more frequently due to its direct association with impaired respiratory function.

Hoarseness

is not a predominant symptom of SVC obstruction but remains a significant clinical finding when present. It can result from compression of the recurrent laryngeal nerve or irritation caused by adjacent oedema or venous congestion, which induces alterations in voice quality. Although hoarseness can be striking and important when considering SVC obstruction, it often emerges subsequent to more salient symptoms like dyspnoea.

Similarly,

facial swelling

is not typically the foremost symptom observed in SVC obstruction despite its noticeable presence in clinical examinations. Facial and neck swelling develop owing to escalated venous pressure consequent upon SVC compression; however, this presentation is less frequent than other manifestations associated with this condition.

Lastly, while

headaches

may arise due to increased intracranial pressure stemming from impeded venous drainage, they do not represent the most common symptoms of SVC obstruction. Headaches may ensue as an ancillary complaint, particularly if the obstruction persists for an extended duration and exerts substantial effects on intracranial dynamics. Nevertheless, symptoms directly related to obstructed blood flow and respiratory compromise such as dyspnoea tend to predominate.

question_text:
A 44-year-old man attends the genetic clinic after being diagnosed with prostate cancer. He has no other medical history, does not smoke, and is not on any regular medication. His family history is notable for pancreatic cancer in his maternal relatives.

What gene mutation is most likely to be present in this man?
options_json: ["ALK", "BRCA2", "C-KIT", "EGFR", "KRAS"]
explanation_text:
BRCA2 mutation is associated with prostate cancer in men

BRCA2

is associated with prostate, breast, and pancreatic cancer in men. The man has early-onset prostate cancer with a significant family history of pancreatic cancer making a BRCA2 gene mutation the most likely to be present. Depending on the personal and family history of malignancy, specific screening is advised when a BRCA2 mutation is found, i.e. prostate-specific antigen screening from the age of 40 in all men. The BRCA2 gene is located on the long arm of chromosome 13.

An

ALK

gene mutation is associated with adenocarcinoma lung carcinoma. ALK gene mutation-associated lung cancers are associated with younger age and no or little smoking history/exposure. The ALK gene is found on chromosome 2.

A

C-KIT

is a gene mutation associated with gastrointestinal stromal tumours (GIST) and acute myeloid leukaemia. The c-KIT gene is found in chromosome 4. The most common site of GISTs are the stomach and jejunum/ileum. GI bleeding is the most common presentation of GISTs.

Renal cell carcinoma and non-small cell lung carcinoma are associated with

EGFR

gene mutations. The EGFR gene is found on chromosome 7. EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as osimertinib combined with chemotherapy have been shown to increase progression-free survival.

KRAS

gene mutations are associated with pancreatic cancers but not prostate cancer. A BRCA2 mutation would be more likely in this case given the personal history of prostate cancer. The KRAS gene is situated on chromosome 12.

A 67-year-old woman with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) is seen in the haematology clinic for routine follow. She has lost 11% of her body weight over six months but otherwise remains asymptomatic. On examination, splenomegaly is noted extending 8cm as well as small, stable lymphadenopathy.

Her most recent two blood tests are shown below.

Bloods (current):


Hb	141 g/L	Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	181 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	49.3 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Neuts	3.9 * 109/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Lymphs	44.9 * 109/L	(1.0 - 3.5)
Mono	0.4 * 109/L	(0.2 - 0.8)
Eosin	0.1 * 109/L	(0.0 - 0.4)

Bloods (6 months ago):


Hb	146 g/L	Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	191 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	24.1 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Neuts	4.2 * 109/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Lymphs	19.5 * 109/L	(1.0 - 3.5)
Mono	0.3 * 109/L	(0.2 - 0.8)
Eosin	0.1 * 109/L	(0.0 - 0.4)

What is the most appropriate management for this woman?
options_json: ["Continue monitoring", "Doxorubicin, bleomycin, vinblastine, dacarbazine (ABVD)", "Fludarabine, cyclophosphamide and rituximab (FCR)", "Hydroxycarbamide", "Rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine (R-CHOP)"]
explanation_text:
CLL - treatment: Fludarabine, Cyclophosphamide and Rituximab (FCR)

This woman has presented with several indications for treatment (splenomegaly, significant weight loss, increasing lymphocyte count). The treatment of CLL is with FCR.

Monitoring is appropriate in the absence of any indications for treatment. This woman has presented with massive splenomegaly >6cm, weight loss >10% over six months, and a lymphocyte count that has doubled over six months. Any of these is an indication for treatment.

ABVD therapy is indicated for Hodgkin's lymphoma rather than CLL, which is instead treated with FCR.

Hydroxycarbamide is used for a variety of haematological disorders including chronic myeloid leukaemia but is not used in CLL and is therefore incorrect.

R-CHOP is used to treat non-Hodgkin's lymphoma rather than CLL. It is therefore not the correct answer in this case.

question_text:
A 64-year-old women attends oncology clinic following a diagnosis of oestrogen receptor (ER) positive breast cancer. Her consultant decides to commence treatment with anastrozole, an aromatase inhibitor.

Of the following, which is a potential complication associated with this treatment?
options_json: ["Endometrial cancer", "Hypercalcaemia", "Ischaemic heart disease", "Osteoporosis", "Venous thromboembolism"]
explanation_text:
Aromatase inhibitors (e.g. anastrozole) may cause osteoporosis

In the management of oestrogen receptor (ER) positive breast cancer, two classes of oral anti-oestrogen drugs are predominantly used.

Aromatase inhibitors (AIs) such as anastrozole and letrozole reduce peripheral oestrogen synthesis. This accounts for the majority of oestrogen synthesis in post-menopausal women, and therefore aromatase inhibitors are used in this group.

The major adverse effect of aromatase inhibitors is osteoporosis. In postmenopausal women, aromatase inhibitors increase bone loss at a rate of 1- 3%/year.  Bone mineral density should be checked both prior to commencing and throughout treatment.

AIs are not associated with any of the other side effects listed.

The other class of anti-oestrogen medications is Selective oEstrogen Receptor Modulators (SERM), such as tamoxifen. This is used to treat both pre- and post-menopausal women with ER positive breast cancer.

Adverse effects include venous thromboembolism, endometrial cancer, cerebral ischaemia and hypertriglyceridaemia.

The abdomen is soft and non-tender, the body mass index is 23 kg/m² and there is bilateral weakness of ankle dorsiflexion.

question_text:
A 14-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with facial swelling. He lives in social care, and one of his carers called an ambulance after noticing his face had started to swell over the last 24 hours. On arrival, the crew administered adrenaline with minimal effect.

On examination, he has diffuse swelling of his face, in particular his lips and tongue. There is no rash seen. He does not report any itching.

The following day the swelling had improved. He was discharged with follow-up in the immunology clinic 2 weeks later.

At the clinic, what investigation is most appropriate to identify the diagnosis?
options_json: ["C1", "C2", "C3", "C4", "Mast cell tryptase"]
explanation_text:
Hereditary angioedema - C4 is the best screening test inbetween attacks

The build-up of angioedema over a period of 24 hours, particularly with the absence of itch and skin changes such as weals means this is atypical for an allergic reaction. The appearance of lip and tongue swelling is suggestive of isolated angioedema.

This makes a diagnosis of hereditary angioedema more likely. This is further evidenced by the lack of a good response to adrenaline.

C4

is the best screening test for hereditary angioedema in between attacks. A result of low C4 would support the diagnosis.

C1

is incorrect. Instead, it is measuring the C1 inhibitor (C1-INH) level which is appropriate for the diagnosis of hereditary angioedema.

C2

is incorrect. Although levels are also frequently low between attacks, C2 is less reliable compared to C4.

C3

is incorrect. C3 is often low in autoimmune disease but should be normal in hereditary angioedema.

Mast cell tryptase

is incorrect. This is the investigation of choice when an anaphylactic reaction is likely. Guidance is that levels should be taken at the time of the reaction, as soon as possible after emergency treatment has commenced, with a second level taken ideally within one to two hours (but no later than four). The absence of itch, rash and response to adrenaline all make anaphylaxis less likely in this case.

question_text: A 55-year-old man is admitted to hospital with fever and malaise. Blood tests show significant leukocytosis and the haematology team notes immature myeloid cells on the blood film. The main differential diagnoses are chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML) and a leukaemoid reaction. Which additional finding would most support a diagnosis of CML over a leukaemoid reaction?
options_json: ["Low leucocyte alkaline phosphatase score", "High leucocyte alkaline phosphatase score", "Presence of toxic granulation in neutrophils", "Marked left shift in neutrophil nuclei", "Raised C-reactive protein"]
explanation_text:
Differentiating chronic myeloid leukaemia from leukaemoid reactions: leukocyte alkaline phosphatase score is low in CML, high in leukaemoid reaction

Low leucocyte alkaline phosphatase score

is characteristic of chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML) and helps differentiate it from a leukaemoid reaction, where the score is typically high. In CML, malignant granulocytes have reduced enzyme activity, which leads to a low LAP score despite high white cell counts. This finding is clinically important because both conditions can present with marked leukocytosis and immature myeloid cells, but management differs significantly. Recognising this laboratory feature enables appropriate further investigations such as BCR-ABL testing for definitive diagnosis.

High leucocyte alkaline phosphatase score

is seen in leukaemoid reactions rather than CML. It reflects increased enzyme activity in reactive neutrophils responding to infection or inflammation. While this result supports a non-malignant cause for leukocytosis, it does not help confirm CML.

Presence of toxic granulation in neutrophils

suggests an acute inflammatory or infectious process, common in severe infections that trigger a leukaemoid reaction. It is not typical of CML and thus argues against this diagnosis.

Marked left shift in neutrophil nuclei

, meaning more band forms and less nuclear segmentation, occurs predominantly during intense marrow response to infection—a hallmark of the leukaemoid reaction rather than CML. While some left shift may be seen in CML, it tends to be more prominent with reactive causes.

Raised C-reactive protein

indicates systemic inflammation or infection but lacks specificity for distinguishing between malignant (CML) and reactive (leukaemoid) causes of leukocytosis. Both conditions can present with elevated CRP if there is concurrent infection or tissue injury.

question_text:
An 18-year-old woman presents to her GP concerned about her heavy periods. She reports she often needs to change her tampon every hour and she is finding this very inconvenient. She has previously been offered hormonal contraception but wants to avoid this option.

A gynaecological examination is normal.

After various blood tests, she is eventually diagnosed with von Willebrand disease.

Considering the patient's age and underlying condition, what is the most appropriate management option for her menorrhagia?
options_json: ["Desmopressin", "Gene therapy", "Hysterectomy", "Intrauterine device (copper coil)", "Terlipressin"]
explanation_text:
Desmopressin is used in the management of Von Willebrand's disease

Desmopressin

is the correct answer. It can be given intranasally and only needs to be taken when the patient is on her period. It can also be given intravenously or by subcutaneous injection, for example in anticipation of major surgery or post-trauma.

Gene therapy

is incorrect, as there is not currently any such option for treating von Willebrand disease. Some research is ongoing into potential gene therapies but it is currently at very early experimental stages. One of the challenges is the very large size of the von Willebrand factor gene which cannot fit into commonly used viral vectors.

Hysterectomy

is not an appropriate first-line treatment for menorrhagia, especially in a woman so young who is unlikely to have completed her family. There are many more treatment options for menorrhagia that are reversible, cost-effective and avoid the risks associated with surgery.

An

intrauterine device (copper coil)

would be a choice that is mindful of the patient's wish to avoid hormonal contraception, however can often make periods heavier therefore would not be an appropriate treatment. The patient has not expressed any need for contraception, so the copper coil would not be meeting any of her treatment needs but rather might give her worsening of her symptoms.

Terlipressin

is also incorrect. Although it sounds similar in name to desmopressin, and is also a vasopressin analogue, it is an IV medication used for treating variceal bleeding and is not used for von Willebrand disease.

question_text: A 52-year-old is found to have chronic myeloid leukaemia following investigation for splenomegaly. Which one of the following best describes the function of the BCR-ABL fusion protein?
options_json: ["Epidermal growth factor receptor", "Phospholipase C", "CD52 co-receptor", "Tyrosine kinase", "Fibroblast growth factor receptor"]
explanation_text:
Chronic myeloid leukaemia - imatinib = tyrosine kinase inhibitor

The correct answer is

Tyrosine kinase

. The BCR-ABL fusion protein, a result of the Philadelphia chromosome translocation (9;22)(q34;q11), functions as an abnormally active tyrosine kinase. This leads to continuous cell division and proliferation, characteristics of chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML). Tyrosine kinases are enzymes that can transfer a phosphate group from ATP to a protein in a cell, specifically on the tyrosine residue. This process is called phosphorylation and it plays an important role in signalling pathways that control cell growth, differentiation and survival.

The first incorrect answer is

Epidermal growth factor receptor

(EGFR). While EGFR does play a significant role in cell growth and proliferation, it is not directly related to the BCR-ABL fusion protein or CML. Mutations or overexpression of EGFR are more commonly associated with non-small-cell lung cancer and colorectal cancer.

The second incorrect option is

Phospholipase C

. Phospholipase C is an enzyme that cleaves phospholipids just before the phosphate group. It plays a role in signal transduction pathways but does not have direct involvement with BCR-ABL or CML.

CD52 co-receptor

is another incorrect option. CD52 is a protein found on the surface of mature lymphocytes, but not myeloid cells. Alemtuzumab, an anti-CD52 monoclonal antibody, may be used for the treatment of certain types of leukaemias and lymphomas, but it has no relevance to the pathophysiology of CML or function of BCR-ABL.

Finally,

Fibroblast growth factor receptor

(FGFR) is also not correct. FGFRs are part of the tyrosine kinase family but they bind fibroblast growth factors rather than being associated with BCR-ABL or CML. Mutations in FGFRs have been implicated in various forms of cancer including bladder and gastric cancers.

question_text:
A 32-year-old woman is seen in ambulatory care with a 2-day history of shortness of breath and right-sided chest pain. There is no history of fever or cough. She has a past medical history of a left lower limb deep vein thrombosis (DVT) 3 years ago. She is a current smoker with a 15-pack-year history. Other than taking paracetamol for her chest pain there are no other regular medications.

She is afebrile. Her heart rate is 121bpm and regular with a blood pressure of 134/88mmHg. On auscultation, her chest is clear with saturations of 93% on air and there are normal heart sounds. Her calves are soft and non-tender, and there is no pitting oedema.


Investigations:


Hb	160 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Haematocrit	0.54 L/L	Male: (0.4-0.54) Female: (0.37-0.47)
Platelets	223 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	9.1 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Troponin	26 ng/mL	(0-14)
CRP	10 mg/L	(< 5)


ECG: sinus tachycardia and T wave inversion in V1-V4.

What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
options_json: ["Activated protein C resistance", "Antiphospholipid syndrome", "Antithrombin III deficiency", "Polycythaemia", "Von Willebrand's disease"]
explanation_text:
Factor V  Leiden mutation results in activated protein C resistance

This woman has a likely diagnosis of a pulmonary embolus (PE). The clinical history, ECG changes and absence of other differentials make the diagnosis likely. ECG changes in PEs can vary. Sinus tachycardia is the most common finding. The classic S1Q3T3 pattern is not specific for a PE and is seen in approximately 20% of patients. T wave inversion in the right precordial leads (V1-V4) is associated with raised pulmonary pressures, of which a PE is a known cause. The raised troponin is likely secondary to right heart strain.

Recurrent venous thromboembolism (VTEs) and no obvious provoking causes (including malignancy, recent surgery or use of the combined oral contraceptive pill) leads toward a diagnosis of thrombophilia. Of all the inherited causes of thrombophilia, Factor V Leiden is the most common and is present in 3-5% of the population. It increases the risks of VTE by 4-5 times. Protein C is a natural anticoagulant which normally binds to and inactivates factor V and VIII. Protein S is also a natural anticoagulant that acts as a co-factor for protein C, helping it inactivate factor V and VIII. In Factor V Leiden, protein C cannot inactive factor V, therefore increasing its pro-thrombotic potential.

Antiphospholipid syndrome is an acquired disorder that is associated with arterial and venous thromboses, thrombocytopenia and foetal loss. Other features include cutaneous manifestations such as livedo reticularis. T-wave inversion and a raised troponin can be suggestive of coronary artery thrombosis. However, the history given is highly suggestive of a PE. Recurrent venous thromboses without any other features of antiphospholipid syndrome make an alternative diagnosis more likely.

Anti-thrombin III binds to and inactivates thrombin. Thrombin acts to activate several factors in the clotting cascade, including the conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin. Anti-thrombin III deficiency can be inherited or acquired (e.g. following trauma or surgery or in

chronic kidney disease) but is less common than Factor V Leiden.

Polycythaemia is an erythrocytosis characterised by raised haemoglobin and haematocrit levels on full blood count. It can be a primary myeloproliferative disorder associated with a JAK-2 mutation, or secondary to tissue hypoxia commonly caused by smoking or high altitude. Polycythaemia is a recognised cause of thrombosis. However, primary polycythaemia is more likely to present in later life (> 60 years), and a haematocrit of > 0.56 is needed to make a diagnosis of secondary polycythaemia.

Von Willebrand factor has a role in platelet adhesion. It also binds to factor VIII, increasing its half-life. Reduction in von Willebrand factor is the pathological basis of von Willebrand's disease characterised by an increased tendency to bleed. Von Willebrand's disease is the most common inherited cause of bleeding.

question_text:
A 64-year-old male presents to the emergency department with sudden onset dyspnoea and drowsiness. He has a background medical history of COPD, end-stage renal failure on dialysis, and type 2 diabetes mellitus. On examination, he is in respiratory distress. He is cyanotic and has accessory muscle use. His peripheral oxygen saturation is 77%.

An arterial blood gas on room air is taken:


pH	7.435	(7.350 - 7.450)
pCO2	6.5 kPa	(4.50 - 6.00)
pO2	12.0 kPa	(11.0 - 14.5)
Hgb	10 g/dL	(11.5 - 18.0)
sO2	95.2%	(94 - 98)
HCO3-	27.2 mmol/L	(22.4 - 25.8)
Lactate	2.8 mmol/L	(0.5 - 2.0)

Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following will be the most effective intervention?
options_json: ["Hyperbaric oxygen therapy", "Methylene blue", "Penicillamine", "Non-invasive ventilation", "100% high-flow oxygen via a non-rebreather mask"]
explanation_text:
Normal pO2 but decreased oxygen saturation is characteristic of methaemoglobinaemia

Methylene blue is the correct answer. This patient likely has methemoglobinaemia and intravenous methylene blue is the first-line treatment. A normal pO2 (and arterial oxygen saturation) but decreased peripheral oxygen saturation is characteristic of methemoglobinaemia and it is referred to as the pO2-saturation gap. Haemodialysis-associated methemoglobinaemia occurs due to the inadequate removal of chloramines which leads to chloramine toxicity.

Hyperbaric oxygen therapy is an incorrect answer. Hyperbaric oxygen therapy may be used in the management of carbon monoxide poisoning, especially when the carboxyhaemoglobin level is >30%. However, the most appropriate initial management of carbon monoxide therapy in the emergency department is 100% high-flow oxygen via a non-rebreather mask.

Penicillamine is an incorrect answer. Penicillamine is used as a chelating agent in the treatment of copper overload in Wilson's disease.

Non-invasive ventilation is an incorrect answer. Non-invasive ventilation will not treat this patient's methemoglobinaemia associated cyanosis. The patient's slightly raised pCO2 is compensated by the increased bicarbonate level. This is likely chronic and does not require intervention with bilevel positive airway pressure (BiPAP) therapy at this time.

100% high-flow oxygen via a non-rebreather mask is an incorrect answer. Supplemental oxygen is an ineffective monotherapy for the treatment of methemoglobinaemia. Although it may be used as an adjunct therapy to methylene blue. Careful consideration should be given to the use of supplemental oxygen in this case as the patient has a background of COPD and there is evidence that he is a chronic CO2 retainer.

question_text:
A 28-year-old woman is receiving a transfusion of fresh frozen plasma (FFP). After 2 hours into the transfusion, she develops shortness of breath. Observations are as follows: heart rate 120bpm, blood pressure 90/65 mmHg, SpO2 90% on air, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and temperature 37.2ºC. On examination, you note bilateral coarse crepitations. The JVP is not raised and there is no evidence of peripheral oedema. There is no evidence of a rash.

What is the most likely cause?
options_json: ["Acute haemolytic transfusion reaction", "Anaphylactic reaction", "Bacterial contamination", "Transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO)", "Transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI)"]
explanation_text:
TRALI is differentiated from TACO by the presence of hypotension in TRALI vs hypertension in TACO

Transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI)

is correct.  TRALI is a serious and potentially fatal complication of blood product transfusion in which a patient develops rapid onset lung injury and non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema due to activation of immune cells in the lung. It is often associated with plasma-rich blood components such as FFP and cryoprecipitate.  The presence of bilateral coarse crepitations is suggestive of pulmonary oedema. Therefore the main two differentials are TACO and TRALI.  The presence of hypotension and the absence of other features of fluid overload (e.g. raised JVP and peripheral oedema) favour the diagnosis of TRALI.

Anaphylactic reaction

is incorrect. These types of reactions are also more common with plasma-rich blood products such as FFP, cryoprecipitate and platelets.  Although anaphylaxis can also present with hypotension, as seen in this vignette, the onset after 15 minutes and the absence of any other anaphylactoid features (e. g. rash, wheeze) makes an anaphylactoid reaction less likely.

Acute haemolytic transfusion reaction

is incorrect. This reaction occurs due to the destruction of donor red cells from the recipient's naturally occurring antibodies (e.g. anti-A and anti-B). This type of reaction does not occur with FFP since it does not contain red cells.

Bacterial contamination

is incorrect. Contamination of blood products with bacteria can cause sudden onset septic shock. The presence of respiratory distress and absence of fever in the vignette makes this a less likely diagnosis. Bacterial contamination is more likely to occur with platelet transfusions since these blood components are stored at room temperature.

Transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO)

is incorrect. TACO is defined as acute or worsening respiratory compromise and/or acute or worsening pulmonary oedema during or up to 12 hours of transfusion. It is more likely to be associated with hypertension than hypotension (in contrast to TRALI). Risk factors include old age, heart failure, and renal dysfunction. In this vignette, the presence of hypotension and the absence of other features of fluid overload (e.g. raised JVP and peripheral oedema) favour the diagnosis of TRALI.

A 32-year-old woman is planned for an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy for recurrent biliary colic. The surgical registrar requests advice due to unexpected anaemia on her pre-operative full blood count. The medical team request a blood film and Direct Coomb's test.


Hb	95 g/L	Female: (115 - 160)
MCV	82fL	(80-100)
Ferritin	200 ng/mL	(20 - 230)
Vitamin B12	300 ng/L	(200 - 900)
Folate	8.4 nmol/L	(> 3.0)


Blood film	Spherocytes seen
Direct Coomb's test	Negative

Which investigation is most appropriate to confirm the underlying diagnosis?
options_json: ["Beutler fluorescent spot test", "EMA binding test", "High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC)", "Osmotic fragility test", "Flow cytometry for CD55 and CD59"]
explanation_text:
The EMA binding test should be used to diagnose hereditary spherocytosis - the osmotic fragility test is no longer widely used

This woman has normocytic anaemia with a normal iron, B12 and folate.

Spherocytes may be present on a blood film in autoimmune haemolysis, transfusion reactions and hereditary spherocytosis. A negative Direct Coomb's test indicates the cause is not autoimmune.

Hereditary spherocytosis is an inherited disorder of the red blood cell cytoskeleton. Due to incomplete penetrance, it leads to a spectrum of disease severity, from asymptomatic to severe haemolytic anaemia requiring frequent transfusions. Severe cases are usually detected in early life, but milder cases may be diagnosed as an adult. Haemolysis can lead to unconjugated hyper-bilirubinaemia which can cause gallstones.

The EMA binding test should be used to diagnose hereditary spherocytosis - the osmotic fragility test is no longer widely used.

High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) is used to test for variants of haemoglobin (e.g. HbS).

The Beutler fluorescent spot test is used to identify enzyme defects to diagnose Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency.

Flow cytometry for CD55 and CD59 is used to diagnose paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria.

question_text:
A 48-year-old woman presents with a right-sided breast lump which has been increasing in size over the past 3 months. She is diagnosed with an oestrogen receptor positive breast cancer following an ultrasound and biopsy. She underwent the menopause at age 44.

The patient is started on anastrozole.

What is the mechanism of this drug in this patient?
options_json: ["Blockade of oestrogen receptors", "Inhibiting recognition of growth signals by cancer cells", "Prevention of androgen conversion into oestrogens", "Prevention of release of luteinising hormone", "Selective inhibition of CDK4 and CDK6"]
answer_text: Prevention of androgen conversion into oestrogens
explanation_text:
Anastrozole and letrozole are aromatase inhibitors that reduces peripheral oestrogen synthesis

Prevention of androgen conversion into oestrogens

is correct. Anastrozole and letrozole are aromatase inhibitors that reduce peripheral oestrogen synthesis. Peripheral oestrogen synthesis is characterised by the conversion of androgens into oestrogens in non-reproductive body tissues including fat, bone and liver. Aromatase inhibitors are used for oestrogen receptor-positive breast cancer. Aromatase inhibitors are used in post-menopausal women where oestrogen is produced from peripheral androgen conversion and not from the ovaries.

Inhibiting recognition of growth signals by cancer cells

is incorrect. Herceptin (trastuzumab) is a HER2 inhibitor targeted therapy. Herceptin works against HER2-positive breast cancers by blocking the ability of the cancer cells to receive chemical signals that tell the cells to grow.

Prevention of release of luteinising hormone

is incorrect. Goserelin is a type of hormone therapy called a luteinising hormone blocker. This means it stops the release of luteinising hormone (LH) from the pituitary gland. This results in the decreased production of oestrogen. LHRH analogues are used in pre-menopausal women to reduce oestrogen production from the ovaries.

Blockade of oestrogen receptors

is incorrect. Tamoxifen is a selective oestrogen receptor modulator (SERM) which acts as an oestrogen receptor antagonist and partial agonist. It is used in the management of oestrogen receptor-positive breast cancer. Tamoxifen can be used in both in pre- and post-menopausal women.

Selective inhibition of CDK4 and CDK6

is incorrect. Abemaciclib is an antitumor agent and dual inhibitor of cyclin-dependent kinases 4 (CDK4) and 6 (CDK6) that are involved in the cell cycle and promotion of cancer cell growth in case of unregulated activity.

question_text:
A 14-year-old girl with known sickle cell disease presents to the emergency department feeling unwell. Her mother is concerned she has become very pale and lethargic.

She complains of a headache, lethargy, cough, myalgia and fever starting just over a week ago.

On examination, the observations are within normal limits. The patient appears pale. Abdominal, respiratory and cardiovascular examinations are otherwise unremarkable.

Significant blood results are shown below:


Hb	67 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	110 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	3.3 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Bilirubin	5 µmol/L	(3 - 17)

What is the most likely diagnosis?
options_json: ["Acute chest syndrome", "Aplastic crisis", "Haemolytic crisis", "Sequestration crisis", "Vaso-occlusive crisis"]
explanation_text:
Aplastic crises in sickle cell disease are associated with a sudden drop in haemoglobin

Aplastic crisis

is correct. This patient describes a recent illness compatible with parvovirus B19 infection. This is then followed by significant pancytopenia, most notably a severe drop in haemoglobin suggesting an aplastic crisis.

Acute chest syndrome

is incorrect. This would present with chest pain, cough, wheeze, dyspnoea and tachypnoea. Imaging would show pulmonary infiltrates. Acute chest syndrome is a type of vaso-occlusive crisis occurring within the lung circulation.

Haemolytic crisis

is incorrect. This is rare and would present with severe anaemia and jaundice due to sudden haemolysis. The normal bilirubin points away from haemolysis.

Sequestration crisis

is incorrect. This would present with abdominal pain, signs of haemodynamic compromise and hepatomegaly/splenomegaly. Pooling of blood in the spleen occurs, leading to severe anaemia and haemodynamic collapse.

Vaso-occlusive crisis

is incorrect. These could affect different organs, but would typically present with the development of acute pain due to microvascular occlusion. Other presentations include dactylitis, cerebral infarction, mesenteric ischaemia, avascular necrosis of the femoral head or priapism.

question_text: A 61-year-old presents for review. She has been having atypical lower back pain for the past two months. An x-ray of her lumbar spine reported raised the possibility of spinal metastases but there is no current evidence of a primary tumour. A series of tumour markers were sent. Which one of the following is most associated with raised levels of CA 15-3?
options_json: ["Pancreatic cancer", "Colorectal cancer", "Breast cancer", "Ovarian cancer", "Hepatocellular carcinoma"]
explanation_text:
CA 15-3 is a tumour marker in breast cancers

The correct answer in this case is

breast cancer

. CA 15-3 (cancer antigen 15-3) is a protein that is produced by normal breast cells and can be found at higher levels in the blood of individuals with breast cancer. It is primarily used as a marker to monitor the response to treatment in patients with advanced breast cancer, although it may also be elevated in other malignancies and benign conditions. It should be noted that CA 15-3 is not recommended for screening or early diagnosis of breast cancer due to its low sensitivity and specificity.

Regarding the other options:

Pancreatic cancer

typically presents with elevated levels of CA 19-9, which is a carbohydrate antigen that can also be raised in gastrointestinal malignancies such as cholangiocarcinoma and colorectal cancer. However, CA 19-9 has limited utility as a diagnostic tool due to its low sensitivity and specificity.

Colorectal cancer

can present with elevated levels of carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), which may also be raised in other malignancies such as pancreatic, gastric, and lung cancers. CEA is most commonly used for monitoring disease progression or recurrence after treatment rather than for initial diagnosis.

Ovarian cancer

is associated with raised levels of CA 125, a glycoprotein that can also be elevated in endometriosis, pelvic inflammatory disease, and during menstruation. As with other tumour markers mentioned earlier, CA 125 has limited utility as a diagnostic tool due to its low sensitivity and specificity.

Finally,

hepatocellular carcinoma

(HCC) often presents with increased serum levels of alpha-fetoprotein (AFP). AFP can also be elevated in germ cell tumours and during pregnancy. While AFP has some utility as a diagnostic tool for HCC, it is primarily used for monitoring response to treatment and detecting recurrence.

question_text: A 29-year-old man presented to the hospital after he had two episodes of bright red urine in the morning. He is very worried and tells the attending doctor that he has never had such an episode before. He has just started working at an engineering firm and is planning to get married in a few months. He reports feeling tired for the past few months but thought this was due to his job which required him to travel to construction sites every day. He has no significant family history. He had an appendectomy when he was a child but other than that he has never been admitted to the hospital. A blood test reveals a hemoglobin concentration of 11.5 g/dL and a reticulocyte of 14% of red blood cells. Which of the findings is the most likely to be reported upon flow cytometry of a blood sample from this patient?
options_json: ["C3 negative cells", "CD55 negative cells", "CD59 negative cells", "C5 to C9 negative cells", "CD55 and CD59 negative cells"]
explanation_text:
Flow cytometry for CD59 and CD55 is the gold standard test for paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria

This patient presented with the signs and symptoms consistent with a diagnosis of paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH). This condition is an acquired and chronic form of intrinsic hemolytic anemia. Patients can present with hematuria, or even simply symptoms of anemia. Venous thrombosis is also a common occurrence. The classic triad is hemolytic anemia, pancytopenia, and venous thrombosis. Flow cytometry is the gold standard laboratory investigations and shows CD55 and CD59 negative red and blood cells.

1: A deficiency of C3 is a complement deficiency disorder. Since C3 plays an important role in the activation of both the classical and alternative complement pathways, a C3 deficiency confers a higher risk of acquiring recurrent bacterial infections.

2: It is true that this will be present in this patient's cells. However, PNH patients will also have a deficiency of CD59.

3: It is true that this will be present in this patients' cells. However, PNH patients will also have a deficiency of CD55.

4: This would indicate terminal complement deficiency. This condition involves a deficiency of the complements forming the membrane attack membrane. C5 to C9 deficiency confers a high risk of infection with Neisseria organisms.

5: The gold standard in the diagnosis of PNH is flow cytometry, and patients usually have a deficiency of both CD55 and CD59 on their red as well as their white blood cells. Eculizumab is a humanized monoclonal antibody which has been approved for the treatment of PNH. It works mainly via the inhibition of the terminal complement cascade.

question_text:
A 61-year-old man is diagnosed with follicular lymphoma following a six-month history of night sweats and weight loss.

The decision is made to begin chemotherapy with R-CHOP (rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisolone).

Which pathogen should be screened for before starting this chemotherapy regimen?
options_json: ["Epstein Barr virus", "Hepatitis B virus", "Human herpesvirus 8", "Human immunodeficiency virus", "Toxoplasma gondii"]
explanation_text:
Patients starting rituximab should be screened for hepatitis B before starting treatment

Hepatitis B virus

is the correct answer. The R-CHOP regimen contains rituximab, a monoclonal antibody that binds to CD20, an antigen expressed on B cells. Depletion of B cells leads to an impaired humoral immune response, increasing the risk of Hepatitis B reactivation. Accordingly, Hepatitis B is routinely screened for in patients being considered for rituximab therapy due to the high risk of viral reactivation, with subsequent fulminant hepatitis and death. Current infection with Hepatitis B virus is considered a contraindication to rituximab therapy.

Epstein Barr virus

is incorrect. Although Epstein-Barr virus is known to cause lymphomas in immuno-compromised patients, historical infection is essentially ubiquitous (95% of adults worldwide) and does not affect decisions to initiate rituximab therapy.

Human herpesvirus 8

is incorrect. Although human herpes virus 8 is known to cause Kaposi's sarcoma in severely immunosuppressed patients, infection would not contraindicate chemoimmunotherapy with rituximab.

Human immunodeficiency virus

is incorrect. Although HIV screening is widespread and is relevant for the pathogenesis of many lymphomas, this would not affect the decision to give rituximab to a patient with follicular lymphoma being planned for R-CHOP chemotherapy. Hepatitis B is a more correct answer, as a positive test result would directly affect decisions to give chemoimmunotherapy containing rituximab.

Toxoplasma gondii

is incorrect. Screening for toxoplasmosis is not routinely indicated, due to the high prevalence of asymptomatic infection.

question_text:
A 25-year-old man presents with a swollen left upper arm 2 days after being discharged from hospital for observation for a simple, primary pneumothorax. He tells you that he had a cannula in this arm and since discharge it has been swelling up and painful.

Past medical history includes a previous deep vein thrombosis (DVT) 4 years ago. His father is on apixaban due to multiple unprovoked DVTs. The patient is currently on no medications.

On examination there are no signs of infection around the previous cannula site. His left bicep is swollen, tender and slightly red compared to the right bicep.

Blood results are as follows:


Hb	155 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	300 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	5.0 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Na+	140 mmol/L	(135 - 145)
K+	4.2 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Urea	5.5 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	90 µmol/L	(55 - 120)
CRP	1 mg/L	(< 5)


ESR	6 mm/hr	Men: < (age / 2)
Women: < ((age + 10) / 2)
Prothrombin time (PT)	12 secs	(10-14 secs)
Activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT)	34 secs	(25-35 secs)
Fibrinogen	3 g/L	(2 - 4)
D-Dimer	910 ng/mL	(< 400)
Ferritin	150 ng/mL	(20 - 230)
Vitamin B12	500 ng/L	(200 - 900)
Folate	6.8 nmol/L	(> 3.0)
Reticulocytes	1.2 %	(0.5 - 1.5)

Ultrasound doppler of the upper limb reveals a large 10cm thrombosis of the brachial vein.

What is the most likely cause of this thrombophilia?
options_json: ["Antithrombin III deficiency", "Factor V Leiden", "Protein C deficiency", "Protein S deficiency", "Von Willebrand's disease"]
explanation_text:
Activated protein C resistance (Factor V Leiden) is the most common inherited thrombophilia

Factor V Leiden is the correct option as this is the most common inherited thrombophilia in the UK population. In this case the positive family history and tendency to clot in a young man point towards an inherited thrombophilia. A mutation in the factor V gene makes the pro-coagulant factor V less sensitive to inactivation by activated protein C, thus leading to clot formation. The simple primary pneumothorax in this question is an unrelated, incidental finding.

Antithrombin III deficiency is incorrect as this is a less common cause of inherited thrombophilia.

Protein C and protein S deficiency are incorrect options as these are rarer causes of thrombophilia in the UK population, compared to factor V Leiden.

Von Willebrand's disease is incorrect as this has the opposite effect; leads to an increase in bleeding tendency, not clot formation.

question_text:
A 28-year-old mechanic presents with itching and tingling in his lips and mouth. Upon further questioning, he ate an apple a few minutes before the tingling in his lips and mouth began. Moreover, he has not reported any difficulties swallowing since and no vomiting or diarrhoea. The above presentation happened to him last week when he ate the same type of apple, and the tingling and itchiness resolved within a few minutes.

He has a past medical history of hay fever in the spring months well-controlled with antihistamines. His father has a condition which he does not know the name of, which results in sporadic swelling of the skin around the eyes and recurrent abdominal pain.

On examination his lips are erythematous and mildly swollen. There is no swelling or rashes elsewhere and he is not wheezing upon listening to his lungs. All his observations are within normal limits.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
options_json: ["Allergic contact dermatitis", "Anaphylaxis", "Apple allergy", "Oral allergy syndrome", "C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency"]
explanation_text:
Itching and tingling of the lips, tongue and mouth are the most common symptoms of oral allergy syndrome

Oral allergy syndrome (OAS) is the correct option as the case above describes the typical history of pollen-food allergy, with the raw apples being coated with the allergen. This is most commonly associated with birch pollen allergy as described above with the 'springtime hay fever'. OAS is the most likely choice in this case due to the red, swollen, tingling and itchy lips and mouth triggered by raw apples and the lack of systemic upset.

Anaphylaxis is incorrect as there is no wheezing, hives or hypotension described in this case.

Apple allergy is incorrect as the symptoms are localised as in OAS; whereas with specific food allergy you would expect systemic symptoms such as vomiting and diarrhoea. Moreover, anaphylaxis is a more common complication of food allergy compared to OAS.

Allergic contact dermatitis is incorrect as this condition is a type IV allergic reaction mediated by T lymphocytes and arises 48-72 hours after allergen exposure. In this case the exposure to allergic symptoms is a few  minutes and thus is a type I, IgE mediated allergic reaction in the Gell-Coombs classification.

C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency is incorrect as even though his father sounds like he suffers from this condition, it sounds like a birch-pollen allergy with comorbid OAS in the case described above, due to the raw apple being the allergen trigger.
