question_text:
A 43-year-old man attended ambulatory care following a general practitioner (GP) referral for anaemia. He has a past history of hypothyroidism for which he takes levothyroxine 75 micrograms once daily. Routine bloods were done at his GP surgery after he attended for a diabetes check as he has a significant family history of this back in India. These were as follows:


Hb	110 g/L	(135-180)
MCV	60 fL	(80-96)

He denies blood loss, melaena, haematemesis, haematuria or per rectum bleeding. There is no history of weight loss recently and has recently made dietary changes given his concern about diabetes. He drinks around 12 units of alcohol a week.

What is the best investigation to determine the underlying pathology?
options_json: ["Blood film", "Haemoglobin electrophoresis", "Iron studies", "Liver function tests including gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT)", "Thyroid function tests"]
explanation_text:
Disproportionate microcytic anaemia - think beta-thalassaemia trait

Here we have a case of asymptomatic, disproportionate microcytic anaemia in a man of Asian descent. The most likely cause of this is beta thalassaemia trait.

Whilst all of the above options are reasonable investigations to request, the haemoglobin electrophoresis is the diagnostic test of choice for beta thalassaemia trait. It would typically show reduced or absent haemoglobin A, increased haemoglobin A2 (>3.5%) and increased haemoglobin F.

Now to look at the other options.

Blood film would help point to a cause e.g. poikilocytosis or anisocytosis in iron deficiency.

Iron studies would be essential in his workup as it is the most common cause of microcytic anaemia. However, the disproportionate nature of the MCV should point to a potential other cause. In addition, he doesn't have many risk factors for significant iron loss. In beta thalassaemia trait, iron deficiency can co-exist, but typically it would be normal. It is unlikely to be as severe as the MCV would suggest.

Liver function tests including a GGT would be useful in macrocytic anaemia to see if alcohol would be the main contributor to a patients anaemia.

Thyroid functions tests would be useful to exclude this as a contributor. Hypothyroidism could cause a normocytic or macrocytic anaemia typically.

question_text:
A 38-year-old presents having noticed a testicle lump. A CT is performed confirming a likely diagnosis of testicular cancer with spread to the paraaortic lymph nodes.

He undergoes an orchiectomy and is started on adjuvant chemotherapy. Following his first chemotherapy, he reports episodes of severe muscle cramps as well as generalised weakness. Blood tests confirm significant hypomagnesaemia and so he is commenced on replacement therapy prior to his next round of chemotherapy

What drug has likely been included in this patient's chemotherapy resulting in this specific electrolyte imbalance?
options_json: ["Bleomycin", "Cisplatin", "Cyclophosphamide", "Cytarabine", "Vincristine"]
explanation_text:
Cisplatin is associated with hypomagnesaemia

Cisplatin

is a chemotherapy drug used in several cancers including testicular, ovarian and breast cancer. Cisplatin is known to cause cross-linking in DNA, interfering with DNA replication and therefore destroying faster-proliferating cells, which in theory are cancerous. A well-known side effect of cisplatin is the induction of hypomagnesemia as well as hypokalaemia and hypocalcemia, which is thought to be secondary to renal toxicity. Although the full pathophysiology is unknown, direct injury to the mechanism of magnesium reabsorption within the renal system is believed to result in this electrolyte imbalance.

Bleomycin

is another chemotherapy drug also used in the management of testicular cancers as well as several forms of lymphomas. It is believed to affect cancerous cells by inducing breaks within DNA strands. Bleomycin is not associated with renal toxicity or specifically hypomagnesemia; the most serious side effect associated with the drug is pulmonary fibrosis and impaired lung function thought to be secondary to induced sensitivity to oxygen toxicity as well as increased inflammatory processes.

Cyclophosphamide

is used in chemotherapy and as an immunosuppressant for multiple cancers and autoimmune diseases, although not commonly in the treatment of testicular cancer. It acts as an alkylating agent causing DNA crosslinks and causing cell apoptosis. The main adverse effects of cyclophosphamide include haemorrhagic cystitis, and myelosuppression as well as being carcinogenic and therefore increasing the risk of developing other cancers such as lymphomas and transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder. Cyclophosphamide again is not associated with renal toxicity or significant hypomagnesemia.

Cytarabine

is mainly used in the management of leukaemias and lymphomas and is not generally used as an adjuvant to chemotherapy for testicular cancer. Cytarabine is most commonly associated with cerebellar toxicity, especially when used at high doses, which can result in ataxia. Myelosuppression is also associated with cytarabine but it is not known to renal toxicity or hypomagnesemia.

Vincristine

can be used as an adjuvant treatment in testicular cancers as well as in the management of leukaemias and small cell lung cancer. It inhibits the formation of microtubules, disrupting cell replication and causing apoptosis. Again, vincristine is not typically associated with hypomagnesemia and instead is most associated with the adverse effects of peripheral neuropathy and paralytic ileus.

question_text:
A 74-year-old male is seen on the acute medical ward with a history of persistent frontal headaches associated with blurred vision for the past week. On further questioning, the patient reports a history of worsening fatigue and shortness of breath over the preceding 2 months.

The results of preliminary investigations are as follows:


Hb	98 g/l
Platelets	100 * 109/l
WBC	6 * 109/l
Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate	50mm/hr

On examination you note that the patient has enlarged cervical lymph nodes and palpable splenomegaly.

Which of the following conditions is most likely to be the cause of the patient's symptoms?
options_json: ["Hodgkin's lymphoma", "Multiple myeloma", "Acute myeloid leukaemia", "Waldenstrom's macroglobulinaemia", "Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia"]
explanation_text:
Patients with Waldenstrom's macroglobulinaemia often present with issues secondary to hyperviscosity

Waldenstrom's macroglobulinaemia is a form of lymphoplasmacytoid lymphoma (LPL), characterised by a monoclonal IgM paraproteinaemia. This paraproteinaemia leads to systemic symptoms of hyperviscosity such as headaches, visual disturbances and in rarer cases, strokes and ischaemic organ damage.

Many patients often present with issues secondary to this hyperviscosity, as well as the more generalised systemic symptoms and signs common to many haematological diseases.

1) Hodgkin's lymphoma, although likely to cause cervical lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly, is not usually associated with thrombocytopaenia or issues secondary to hyperviscosity

2) Multiple myeloma often causes bony pain in areas of lesions and isn't often associated with lymphadenopathy or organomegaly

3) AML doesn't usually cause lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly.

5) ALL is less common in adults, and although capable of causing lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly, would not usually be associated with symptoms of hyperviscosity

question_text: A patient with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency presents for advice about malaria prophylaxis. He is about to go on a 'gap year' during which he will be travelling abroad for 12 months. Which one of the following medications is it most important that he avoids?
options_json: ["Artemether with lumefantrine", "Mefloquine", "Proguanil", "Doxycyline", "Primaquine"]
explanation_text:
Malaria prophylaxis (e.g. primaquine) can trigger haemolytic anaemia in those with G6PD deficiency

The correct answer is

Primaquine

. The reason for this is that primaquine can cause severe haemolysis in patients with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency. G6PD plays an important role in protecting red blood cells against oxidative stress. Primaquine, an 8-aminoquinoline antimalarial drug, can induce oxidative stress and lead to haemolysis in individuals who are deficient in the enzyme.

Artemether with lumefantrine

is a combination therapy used primarily for the treatment of uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria. It has not been associated with significant haemolysis or adverse effects in G6PD-deficient individuals, making it a safe option for this patient.

Mefloquine

is another antimalarial medication used for both prophylaxis and treatment of malaria. It may be associated with neuropsychiatric side effects but does not pose a significant risk of haemolysis in G6PD-deficient individuals.

Proguanil

, often combined with atovaquone as Malarone, is used for malaria prophylaxis. It works by inhibiting dihydrofolate reductase, which is essential for parasite replication. Proguanil is generally well-tolerated and does not carry a significant risk of haemolytic anaemia in those with G6PD deficiency.

Finally,

Doxycycline

is a tetracycline antibiotic that is also effective as malaria prophylaxis when taken daily. It has not been shown to cause severe haemolysis or significant adverse effects in G6PD-deficient individuals, making it another safe option for this patient.

question_text:
A 48-year-old man presents with fatigue, weight loss, and generalised lymphadenopathy. A biopsy confirms a diagnosis of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.

He is initiated on a chemotherapy regimen that includes rituximab. As part of his pre-treatment evaluation, his oncologist orders several baseline tests to assess for potential complications associated with this therapy.

What should the patient be screened for prior to commencing rituximab treatment?
options_json: ["Cytomegalovirus (CMV)", "Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)", "HIV", "Hepatitis B", "Tuberculosis (TB)"]
explanation_text:
Patients starting rituximab should be screened for hepatitis B before starting treatment

Rituximab, a monoclonal antibody targeting CD20 on B cells, is a cornerstone of treatment for conditions like diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, as in this patient’s case. However, it significantly increases the risk of reactivating latent

hepatitis B

infection due to its immunosuppressive effects on B cells, which are crucial for viral control. For this patient, who is undergoing immunosuppressive therapy, reactivation could lead to severe hepatic injury or even fulminant hepatitis, potentially complicating his cancer treatment and prognosis. Screening for hepatitis B prior to starting rituximab is therefore essential to identify carriers and provide prophylactic antiviral therapy, ensuring safe and uninterrupted treatment.

CMV

reactivation is a concern in profoundly immunosuppressed states, such as post-transplant care or high-dose corticosteroid therapy. However, rituximab does not typically lead to clinically significant CMV reactivation in most patients. Unlike hepatitis B, there is no routine recommendation to screen for CMV before starting rituximab.

EBV

infection or reactivation can be a concern in some rituximab-treated individuals, particularly in post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorders. However, most settings do not require routine screening for EBV before rituximab initiation. Hepatitis B reactivation is a more established and preventable risk, warranting mandatory pre-treatment screening.

HIV

screening, though important in some medical contexts, is not routinely required for rituximab therapy. Rituximab does not directly exacerbate HIV progression, and management of HIV-related immune dysfunction involves antiretroviral therapy rather than adjusting rituximab dosing. Hepatitis B reactivation poses a more immediate risk in rituximab-treated patients.

While

TB

screening is important for patients starting some immunosuppressive treatments, such as TNF-alpha inhibitors (e.g. infliximab or etanercept), it is not routinely required for rituximab. Rituximab's mechanism of action primarily impacts B cells, not the immune pathways central to TB control. There is no established direct association between rituximab and an increased risk of TB reactivation, making hepatitis B screening more critical in this context.

question_text:
A 34-year-old man attends with a fever. There are no localising features on systematic enquiry or examination. He recently completed chemotherapy for Hodgkin's lymphoma. Observations are as follows: heart rate 110 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, blood pressure 125/75 mmHg, oxygen saturation 97% on air, and temperature 38.5ºC. The patient has a PICC line in situ.

Blood results are as follows:


Neuts	0.4 * 109/L	(2.0 - 7.0)

The microbiologist calls the following day to advise that an organism has grown from peripheral blood cultures.

What organism has most likely been cultured?
options_json: ["Candida albicans", "Enterococcus faecium", "Pseudomonas aeruginosa", "Staphylococcus aureus", "Staphylococcus epidermidis"]
explanation_text:
Coagulase-negative, Gram-positive bacteria such as

Staphylococcus epidermidis

is correct. Coagulase-negative, gram-positive bacteria are the most common cause of neutropenic sepsis. This is most likely a consequence of the use of indwelling lines in this cohort of patients.

Candida albicans

is incorrect. Systemic candidiasis is an important complication in neutropenic patients and those undergoing treatment for cancer. This infection has increased persistently over the past three decades and represents a significant cause of morbidity and mortality among high-risk individuals. However, it is much rarer in comparison to gram-positive bacteraemias.

Enterococcus faecium

is incorrect. A progressive increase in infections with multi-drug resistant

Enterococcus faecium

(e.g. vancomycin resistance Enterococcus) has been reported, especially in cancer patients and neutropenic patients. This is potentially driven by selection pressures from broad-spectrum antibiotic use. However, it remains a relatively rare cause of bacteraemias in comparison to

Staphylococcus epidermidis

.

Pseudomonas aeruginosa

is incorrect.

Pseudomonas aeruginosa

has historically been one of the major causes of severe sepsis and death among neutropenic cancer patients. Therefore all patients with prolonged neutropaenia should be on a prophylactic antibiotic which has anti-Pseudomonal cover (e.g. ciprofloxacin). However, this type of infection is very rare in comparison to

Staphylococcus epidermidis

.

Staphylococcus aureus

is incorrect. This is another common cause of infections in neutropenic patients, again most likely secondary to indwelling lines. However, it is less common than coagulase-negative gram-positive infections.

question_text: A patient is started on cyclophosphamide for vasculitis associated with Wegener's granulomatosis. Which of the following is most characteristically associated with cyclophosphamide?
options_json: ["Haemorrhagic cystitis", "Cardiomyopathy", "Ototoxicity", "Alopecia", "Weight gain"]
explanation_text:
Cyclophosphamide may cause haemorrhagic cystitis

The correct answer is

Haemorrhagic cystitis

. Cyclophosphamide, an alkylating agent used in the treatment of Wegener's granulomatosis among other conditions, is most characteristically associated with haemorrhagic cystitis. This potentially severe complication arises due to the toxic metabolite acrolein, which accumulates in the bladder and causes inflammation and bleeding. To minimise this risk, patients are advised to maintain adequate hydration and may also be given mesna, a protective agent that binds acrolein.

Cardiomyopathy

is not typically associated with cyclophosphamide use. While certain chemotherapeutic agents such as anthracyclines (e.g., doxorubicin) are well-known for their cardiotoxic effects leading to cardiomyopathy, cyclophosphamide has a much lower propensity for this side effect.

Ototoxicity

, characterised by hearing loss or tinnitus, is not a common side effect of cyclophosphamide. It is more commonly seen with platinum-based chemotherapy drugs like cisplatin.

The option

Alopecia

could be misleading because while alopecia can occur with many chemotherapeutic agents including cyclophosphamide, it is not the most characteristic association. Alopecia caused by chemotherapy usually regrows after completion of therapy.

Finally,

Weight gain

is not specifically linked to cyclophosphamide use. While some patients undergoing chemotherapy might experience weight changes due to factors such as changes in appetite or activity levels, these are generally non-specific and can occur with any chemotherapy drug rather than being specifically associated with cyclophosphamide.

question_text:
A 32-year-old woman attends general practice complaining of a 12 month history of intermittently heavy periods. On further questioning, she reports nosebleeds up to 6-8 times a week for 2 months, as well as frequent atraumatic bruising. She has had no weight loss or fevers, and denies any abdominal pain or arthralgia.

She has no significant medical or drug history, and takes no regular medications nor any herbal remedies.

She has no family history of bleeding pathologies. She has had no recent travel.

On examination, she has a multiple purpura on her sacrum, which extend down to the buttocks. She does not have any palpable lymphadenopathy nor any hepatosplenomegaly. Urine dip is normal.

Blood tests reveal:


Hb	124 g/L	Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	18*109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	7*109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Prothrombin time (PT)	12 secs	(10-14 secs)
Activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT)	28 secs	(25-35 secs)
ESR	2 mm/hr	Women: < ((age + 10) / 2)

What is the most likely diagnosis?
options_json: ["Henoch-Schonlein purpura", "Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP)", "Von Willebrand disease", "Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura", "Haemolytic uraemic syndrome"]
explanation_text:
ITP should be considered in the presence of symptoms that suggest isolated thrombocytopenia e.g. epistaxis, menorrhagia

Option 1. Incorrect - Henoch-Shonlein purpura (HSP) occurs mainly in children and is typically accompanied by abdominal pain, arthralgia and renal dysfunction, none of which were present here. The blood tests in HSP normally would not display thrombocytopenia, as the mechanism of purpura is different: in HSP the purpura is related to the IgA complex deposition in the small vessels.

Option 2. Correct - ITP classically presents with frequent bruising and easy bleeding. It is a diagnosis of exclusion and relies on other more sinister pathologies to be excluded e.g. myelodysplasia, leukaemia, vasculitides. Therefore a thorough workup should always be performed. Patients with primary ITP are typically well and have no related systemic symptoms.

Option 3. Incorrect - Von Willebrand disease (VWD) is a good differential in a patient presenting with easy bleeding/bruising, and can often present with a normal activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) and thrombocytopenia. However, in VWD, the thrombocytopenia is usually less marked and there will likely be a positive family history.

Option 4. Incorrect - thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura is thrombotic microangiopathy that typically presents with much more severe symptoms of end-organ damage due to vascular occlusion. The pentad of symptoms includes: fever, neurological signs, thrombocytopenia, haemolytic anaemia and renal impairment. This patient only had isolated thrombocytopenia and was generally well.

Option 5. Incorrect - haemolytic-uraemic syndrome is thrombotic microangiopathy that is secondary to certain bacterial infections (shigella, enterohaemorrhagic

E. coli

), therefore the presentation is usually preceded by a period of diarrhoea. The triad of symptoms includes: thrombocytopenia, haemolytic anaemia and renal impairment.

question_text:
A 50-year-old woman attends the Emergency Department with breathlessness, headache and fatigue for the past few days. There is no history of smoking or occupational lung disease. She has difficulty managing her blood pressure and has attended the hospital hypertension clinic in the last six months. Her regular medication includes amlodipine, hydralazine and doxazosin. On examination the patient is breathless with a respiratory rate of 25/min, the chest is clear to auscultation, heart sounds are normal and there is mild symmetrical pedal oedema. Oxygen saturations are 75% on room air with a PaO2 of 11 kPa.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
options_json: ["Aortic dissection", "Atrial septal defect", "Carbon monoxide poisoning", "Methaemoglobinaemia", "Pleural effusions"]
explanation_text:
Normal pO2 but decreased oxygen saturation is characteristic of methaemoglobinaemia

The correct answer is methaemoglobinaemia. Clues to this include the emphasis on the list of hypertension medications - hydralazine is associated with methaemoglobinaemia. The patient has no other noted risk factors for respiratory disease in the stem. Various drugs cause methaemoglobinaemia including sulphur-based drugs, dapsone and local anaesthetics.

The distractor in the question is the pedal oedema which is alluding to the amlodipine. Oedema is a common side effect and not a feature of heart failure.

Carbon monoxide poisoning would cause both low pO

2

and oxygen saturations.

The other options given are not consistent with a difference between pO

2

and oxygen saturations. There are no clues to the diagnosis of a pulmonary embolus. The Wells score would be low.

There is no report of chest pain to support aortic dissection although she is patient with chronic hypertensive.

Atrial septal defects can be diagnosed later in life but would rarely cause this degree of hypoxia. It would be more common to identify it as an incidental examination finding.

Significant pleural effusions are not compatible with the presentation as the examination of the chest was normal.

question_text: Which one of the following cytotoxic agents acts by inhibiting dihydrofolate reductase and thymidylate synthesis?
options_json: ["Methotrexate", "Vincristine", "Bleomycin", "Cyclophosphamide", "Doxorubicin"]
explanation_text:
Methotrexate - inhibits dihydrofolate reductase and thymidylate synthesis

The correct answer is

Methotrexate

. Methotrexate acts as an antimetabolite and inhibits the enzyme dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), which plays a crucial role in the synthesis of purines and pyrimidines, specifically thymidylate. By doing so, methotrexate prevents the formation of DNA and RNA, thereby halting cell division and proliferation, particularly in rapidly dividing cells such as cancer cells.

Vincristine

is not the correct answer because it does not inhibit dihydrofolate reductase or thymidylate synthesis. Instead, vincristine exerts its cytotoxic effect by binding to tubulin, a protein component of the microtubule network. This binding disrupts the formation of mitotic spindles during cell division leading to metaphase arrest and subsequently apoptosis.

Bleomycin

also does not act by inhibiting DHFR or thymidylate synthesis. Its mechanism of action involves binding to DNA and causing strand breaks through free radical formation. The resultant DNA damage triggers apoptosis or programmed cell death.

Cyclophosphamide

too does not inhibit DHFR or thymidylate synthesis. It is a prodrug that undergoes hepatic conversion to form active metabolites. These metabolites cross-link with DNA strands preventing DNA replication and transcription which leads to cell death.

Lastly,

Doxorubicin

doesn't inhibit DHFR or thymidylate synthesis either. It intercalates into DNA strands inducing breaks and disrupting replication and transcription processes. Additionally, it inhibits topoisomerase II enzyme causing further DNA damage leading to apoptosis.

In conclusion, while all options are cytotoxic agents used in chemotherapy regimens for various cancers, only methotrexate specifically acts by inhibiting dihydrofolate reductase and thymidylate synthesis.

question_text:
A 38-year-old woman is seen as part of her oncological surveillance. She has a history of multiple cancers, first diagnosed with osteosarcoma at age 12, treated with chemotherapy and surgery. At 32 years she developed breast cancer and underwent a mastectomy followed by chemotherapy.

Her family history is significant for her mother dying of breast cancer at 34, and her maternal grandfather being diagnosed with a brain tumour in his 40s. Given the early onset of cancers and the pattern across generations, a genetic syndrome is suspected.

What protein mutation is most likely with this syndrome?
options_json: ["BRCA2", "CDKN2A", "NF1", "p53", "PTEN"]
explanation_text:
Li-Fraumeni syndrome is caused by germline mutations to p53 tumour suppressor gene

The tumour suppressor protein likely mutated in this case is

p53

. This patient’s history strongly aligns with Li-Fraumeni syndrome, an autosomal dominant, hereditary cancer predisposition syndrome characterised by early-onset cancers and a family history of malignancies. Individuals with Li-Fraumeni syndrome are at increased risk for a variety of cancers, including osteosarcoma, breast cancer, soft tissue sarcomas, and brain tumours. The presence of multiple primary cancers at a young age, coupled with her family history—her mother dying of breast cancer at 34 and her grandfather’s brain tumour—further supports this diagnosis. The p53 protein is crucial for regulating the cell cycle and inducing apoptosis in response to DNA damage. Mutations in this protein compromise the body's ability to prevent the proliferation of damaged cells, leading to an increased risk of developing cancers throughout an individual’s lifetime.

BRCA2

(breast cancer 2) is incorrect in this case because, while BRCA2 mutations are primarily associated with an increased risk of breast and ovarian cancers, they are not typically linked to the variety of malignancies seen here. Though the patient has a history of breast cancer, BRCA2 mutations are not associated with osteosarcoma, a key part of her cancer history. Additionally, the presence of a brain tumour in her maternal grandfather does not correlate with BRCA2 mutations, which does not explain the broader family cancer history. Instead, Li-Fraumeni syndrome, characterised by a wide range of cancers, including sarcomas, brain tumours, and breast cancer, is a more fitting diagnosis based on this spectrum of malignancies.

CDKN2A

(cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor 2A) is incorrect in this context because, although it is a tumour suppressor gene associated with familial melanoma and some pancreatic cancers, it is not linked to Li-Fraumeni syndrome. Li-Fraumeni syndrome is primarily associated with mutations in the p53 tumour suppressor gene, leading to a broader range of cancers, including sarcomas, breast cancer, and brain tumours. While CDKN2A mutations can increase cancer risk, they do not account for the diverse cancer profile observed in the patient's family history, which suggests a different underlying genetic syndrome.

NF1

(neurofibromatosis type 1) is incorrect in this context because it is primarily associated with neurofibromas, optic gliomas, and other nerve sheath tumours, rather than the spectrum of cancers seen in Li-Fraumeni syndrome. Other common features of NF1 which are not present in this case include axillary freckles, cafe-au-lait spots, lisch nodules and skeletal deformities. While NF1 can increase the risk of various tumours, including some sarcomas, it does not specifically predispose individuals to the same range of malignancies, such as breast cancer and brain tumours, that are characteristic of Li-Fraumeni syndrome. The family history and early onset of multiple cancers in this patient are more consistent with mutations in the p53 tumour suppressor gene.

PTEN

(phosphatase and tensin homolog) is incorrect in this context as it is primarily associated with Cowden syndrome rather than Li-Fraumeni syndrome, which is the more likely diagnosis. Cowden syndrome, a condition caused by mutations in the PTEN gene, predisposes individuals to various cancers, particularly breast, thyroid, and endometrial cancers. Patients with Cowden syndrome may also develop distinct features such as skin lesions like hamartomas, trichilemmomas, and adenomas; mucosal lesions, which can present as cobblestone mucosa (rough, bumpy areas in the mouth); freckling, particularly in sun-exposed areas; and even gastrointestinal polyps. However, the pattern of early-onset sarcoma and breast cancer seen in this patient is more consistent with Li-Fraumeni syndrome, which is not linked to PTEN mutations.

question_text:
A 25-year-old woman attends the haematology clinic with a past medical history of antiphospholipid syndrome. She informs you that she is pregnant at 12 weeks gestation. She has had a previous deep vein thrombosis associated with antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) for which she completed a 6-month course of warfarin.

How should she be managed during pregnancy?
options_json: ["Aspirin and LMWH", "LMWH", "Observation", "Unfractionated heparin", "Warfarin"]
explanation_text:
Antiphospholipid syndrome in pregnancy: aspirin + LMWH

Aspirin and LMWH

is correct. The patient has had a previous VTE associated with antiphospholipid syndrome (APLS) and therefore has an extremely high risk of VTE during pregnancy. Women with VTE associated with antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) should be offered thromboprophylaxis with higher dose LMWH (either 50%, 75% or full treatment dose) antenatally and for 6 weeks postpartum or until returned to oral anticoagulant therapy after delivery. The addition of aspirin is also recommended to reduce the risk of pre-eclampsia.

LMWH

is incorrect. The patient should indeed be started on LWMH however aspirin is also recommended to reduce the risk of pre-eclampsia.

Observation

is incorrect. The patient has a substantial risk factor for VTE and as such needs prophylactic anticoagulation.

Unfractionated heparin

is incorrect. Unfractionated heparin is rarely required during pregnancy. The main indication would be in the management of an acute VTE during labour due to the benefits of using a very short half-life product in a patient with a high risk of bleeding.

Warfarin

is incorrect. Warfarin is teratogenic and is therefore rarely used during pregnancy. The main indication for its use in pregnancy would be high-risk mechanical heart valves.

question_text: Which electrolyte disturbance is cisplatin most associated with?
options_json: ["Hypocalcaemia", "Hyponatraemia", "Hypomagnesaemia", "Hypokalaemia", "Hypercalcaemia"]
explanation_text: Cisplatin is associated with hypomagnesaemia

question_text: A 45-year-old woman is diagnosed with non-Hodgkin's lymphoma. She is a recovering alcoholic and has been left with significant alcohol-related peripheral neuropathy. Which one of the following chemotherapy agents should be avoided if possible, given her past history?
options_json: ["Doxorubicin", "Vincristine", "Chlorambucil", "Docetaxel", "Cyclophosphamide"]
explanation_text:
Vincristine - peripheral neuropathy

The correct answer is

Vincristine

, as it should be avoided if possible in a patient with a history of significant alcohol-related peripheral neuropathy. Vincristine is a vinca alkaloid chemotherapeutic agent that works by inhibiting microtubule formation, leading to cell cycle arrest and apoptosis. A well-known side effect of vincristine is the development or worsening of peripheral neuropathy. In this patient with pre-existing alcohol-related peripheral neuropathy, using vincristine could exacerbate her symptoms and result in further neurological damage.

Doxorubicin

is an anthracycline chemotherapeutic agent that intercalates into DNA, inhibits topoisomerase II, and generates free radicals, ultimately causing DNA damage and cell death. Its primary dose-limiting toxicity is cardiotoxicity rather than neurotoxicity. Therefore, it would not be contraindicated in this patient based on her history of peripheral neuropathy.

Chlorambucil

is an alkylating agent that forms covalent bonds with DNA bases, leading to cross-linking and inhibition of DNA replication and transcription. It can cause myelosuppression but does not typically cause significant neurotoxicity. Thus, it would not be contraindicated in this patient based on her history of peripheral neuropathy.

Docetaxel

is a taxane chemotherapeutic agent that stabilizes microtubules, preventing their depolymerization and leading to cell cycle arrest and apoptosis. While docetaxel can cause some degree of peripheral neuropathy, its risk for neurotoxicity is lower compared to vincristine. It may still be considered for use in this patient but with close monitoring for any worsening of her existing neuropathy.

Cyclophosphamide

is an alkylating agent that cross-links DNA, inhibiting DNA replication and transcription. Its main toxicities include myelosuppression, hemorrhagic cystitis, and secondary malignancies, but it is not known for causing significant neurotoxicity. It would not be contraindicated in this patient based on her history of peripheral neuropathy.

question_text:
A 28-year-old man is being treated on the haematology ward for acute lymphocytic leukaemia. You are contracted because he has developed supra-pubic pain and frank haematuria. On review of his medication, you note that he is receiving cyclophosphamide and wonder if he has developed haemorrhagic cystitis as a result of this medication.

What is the principal mechanism of action of this medication?
options_json: ["Cell cycle arrest and apoptosis", "Cross-linking in DNA", "Decreases DNA synthesis", "Degrades preformed DNA", "Inhibits formation of microtubules"]
explanation_text:
Cyclophosphamide - causes cross-linking in DNA

Cyclophosphamide and cisplatin work by causing cross-linking in DNA. Cyclophospamide is used to treat a variety of cancers and induce immunosuppression in patients prior to stem cell transplant. Haemorrhagic cystitis is a complication of cyclophosphamide treatment. When cyclophosphamide is broken down by the liver it releases a toxic metabolite, acrolein. Acrolein is concentrated in the bladder and causes an inflammatory response which can lead to haemorrhagic cystitis.

The risk of haemorhagic cystitis can be decreased by giving MESNA - a drug which conjugates acrolein and decreases the inflammatory response.

Bleomycin degrades performed DNA rather than causing cross-linking.

Hydroxyurea decreases DNA synthesis by inhibiting ribonucleotide reductase.

5-Fluorouracil (5-FU) is a pyrimidine analogue that works to arrest the cell cycle and cause apoptosis.

Vincristine inhibits the formation of microtubules.

question_text:
A 38-year-old man presents with shortness of breath and headache. He has no significant past medical history and works in a clothes manufacturing factory.

On examination, he appears unwell and anxious. Auscultation of the chest is normal. Physical observations show a respiratory rate of 24 breaths/min, heart rate 78 bpm, blood pressure 132/84 mmHg and oxygen saturation 76% on room air. An arterial blood gas is performed:


pH	7.38	(7.35-7.45)
pO2	12 kPa	(10-14)
pCO2	4.6 kPa	(4.5-6.0)

He is commenced on high-flow oxygen, but his saturations do not improve.

Given the likely diagnosis, what is the most suitable first-line treatment?
options_json: ["Exchange transfusion", "Hydroxocobalamin", "Hyperbaric oxygen", "Methylene blue", "Rivaroxaban"]
explanation_text:
Normal pO2 but decreased oxygen saturation is characteristic of methaemoglobinaemia

This patient's presentation is highly suspicious of methaemoglobinaemia. This a rare condition in which the iron in haemoglobin has been oxidised from Fe

2+

to Fe

3+

. It is typically acquired due to a number of drugs, including sulphonamides and nitrates, but also from exposure to aniline dyes, which are commonly used in the manufacturing of clothes such as jeans. It presents with dyspnoea, headache and anxiety. Textbooks describe 'chocolate-coloured blood'. Importantly, oxygen saturations are low and do not respond to oxygen treatment, whereas arterial pO

2

is normal. Management involves the use of

methylene blue

.

Exchange transfusion

is more commonly used in the treatment of sulfhaemoglobinaemia, rather than methaemoglobinaemia. This may present similarly, with cyanosis. However, peripheral oxygen saturations are more likely to be normal, and patients may have green discolouration of the blood. Exchange transfusion may be used for severe cases of methaemoglobinaemia, but methylene blue is the first-line choice.

Hydroxocobalamin

is used to treat cyanide poisoning, which also presents with hypoxia, headache and sometimes confusion. Its classical features are those of 'brick-red skin' and the smell of 'bitter almonds'. Given the history of exposure to aniline dyes, and the gap between peripheral saturations and pO

2

, methaemoglobinaemia is more likely here.

Hyperbaric oxygen

is sometimes used in the management of carbon monoxide poisoning, which may present similarly with regard to clinical symptoms. However, peripheral oxygen saturations are typically falsely high. Hyperbaric oxygen may be used second-line for methaemoglobinaemia, but methylene blue should be tried first.

Rivaroxaban

is an anticoagulant and may be used to treat pulmonary embolism, which is always an important differential to consider in the context of hypoxia. However, given the unresponsiveness of oxygen saturations to high-flow oxygen, and the normal pO

2

, this is less likely in this scenario.

question_text: Which one of the following causes of primary immunodeficiency is due to a defect in both B-cell and T-cell function?
options_json: ["Di George syndrome", "Chronic granulomatous disease", "Bruton's congenital agammaglobulinaemia", "Leukocyte adhesion deficiency", "Ataxic telangiectasia"]
explanation_text:
Combined B- and T-cell disorders: SCID WAS ataxic (SCID, Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, ataxic telangiectasia)

Ataxic telangiectasia

is the correct answer as it causes a combined B-cell and T-cell immunodeficiency. Ataxic telangiectasia (also known as Louis-Bar syndrome) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the ATM gene, which is involved in DNA repair mechanisms. This condition affects multiple body systems, but notably causes both humoral (B-cell) and cell-mediated (T-cell) immunodeficiency. Patients typically present with progressive cerebellar ataxia, oculocutaneous telangiectasias, recurrent sinopulmonary infections, and have an increased risk of malignancies, particularly lymphomas. Laboratory findings include decreased IgA, IgE, and sometimes IgG levels, as well as lymphopenia with decreased T-cell numbers and function.

Di George syndrome

is incorrect because it primarily affects T-cell function rather than both B and T cells. Di George syndrome (22q11.2 deletion syndrome) results from abnormal development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches, leading to thymic hypoplasia or aplasia. Since the thymus is essential for T-cell development, patients have decreased T-cell numbers and function. However, B-cell numbers are typically normal, although there may be some functional defects due to lack of T-cell help. The classic triad includes congenital heart defects (particularly conotruncal anomalies), hypocalcaemia due to parathyroid hypoplasia, and thymic hypoplasia leading to cellular immunodeficiency.

Chronic granulomatous disease

is incorrect as it is a defect in phagocyte function rather than lymphocyte function. This X-linked or autosomal recessive disorder is caused by mutations in genes encoding components of the NADPH oxidase complex, which is essential for the respiratory burst in phagocytes. This results in an inability of neutrophils, monocytes, and macrophages to kill certain catalase-positive microorganisms. Patients typically present with recurrent bacterial and fungal infections, particularly with *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Burkholderia cepacia*, *Serratia marcescens*, *Nocardia* species, and *Aspergillus* species. Both B-cell and T-cell functions remain intact in this condition.

Bruton's congenital agammaglobulinaemia

is incorrect because it affects only B-cell function. This X-linked disorder is caused by mutations in the Bruton tyrosine kinase (BTK) gene, which is essential for B-cell development. Patients have a profound deficiency or absence of mature B cells and all immunoglobulin isotypes. T-cell numbers and function are normal. Affected males typically present with recurrent bacterial infections after 6 months of age when maternal antibodies have waned. Common pathogens include encapsulated bacteria such as *Streptococcus pneumoniae* and *Haemophilus influenzae*.

Leukocyte adhesion deficiency

is incorrect as it is a defect in phagocyte function rather than lymphocyte function. This autosomal recessive disorder is characterised by mutations in genes encoding proteins involved in leukocyte adhesion to endothelial cells and migration to sites of infection. The most common form (LAD-I) involves mutations in the CD18 gene, which encodes the β2 integrin subunit. Patients typically present with delayed umbilical cord separation, recurrent bacterial infections without pus formation, poor wound healing, and persistent leukocytosis. Both B-cell and T-cell functions are generally preserved in this condition.

question_text:
A 22-year-old female presents to the emergency department with angioedema on 5 occasions in a six month period. No obvious trigger was identified and she does not improve significantly when given IM adrenaline.

Her symptoms are caused by a deficiency of which substance?
options_json: ["Bradykinin", "C1 esterase inhibitor", "Eosinophil peroxidase", "Kallikrien", "Neutrophil elastase"]
explanation_text:
Hereditary angioedema is caused by deficiency of C1 esterase inhibitor

The correct answer is

C1 esterase inhibitor

. This patient's presentation is consistent with hereditary angioedema, a rare but potentially life-threatening condition characterised by recurrent episodes of severe swelling (angioedema). The condition is caused by a deficiency or dysfunction in the C1 esterase inhibitor. This protein plays a crucial role in regulating the complement and contact systems, both of which are involved in immune responses and inflammation. When there's insufficient C1 esterase inhibitor, these systems can be overactive, leading to excessive production of bradykinin. Bradykinin causes blood vessels to dilate and become more permeable, resulting in fluid leakage into surrounding tissues and causing swelling.

Bradykinin

itself isn't deficient in hereditary angioedema; rather, its levels are elevated due to a lack of regulation by the C1 esterase inhibitor. Therefore, while bradykinin plays a significant role in causing symptoms, it isn't the substance that's deficient.

Eosinophil peroxidase

is an enzyme found within eosinophils, a type of white blood cell. It plays a vital role in fighting off certain parasitic infections and also contributes to tissue damage in some allergic reactions. However, it doesn't have any known direct links with angioedema or other symptoms described here.

Kallikrein

, like bradykinin, isn't deficient but rather overproduced due to the lack of regulation by the C1 esterase inhibitor. Kallikreins are proteases that cleave kininogens to release vasoactive kinins like bradykinin.

Lastly,

neutrophil elastase

is an enzyme produced by neutrophils that breaks down proteins during inflammation and fights infection. While it has many functions related to immune response and inflammation, there's no direct link between neutrophil elastase deficiency and recurrent angioedema as described here.

question_text:
A 50-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis is being considered for treatment, which induces the killing of CD20+ B cells. Her medical history includes acute hepatitis B infection, which cleared without treatment 5 years ago. She is asymptomatic from the liver disease perspective, and the blood test results for her liver function tests (LFTs) 2 months ago are shown below.


Bilirubin	8 µmol/L	(3 - 17)
ALP	40 u/L	(30 - 100)
ALT	20 u/L	(3 - 40)
γGT	30 u/L	(8 - 60)
Albumin	40 g/L	(35 - 50)

Which is the most appropriate initial step before starting this therapy?
options_json: ["Begin antiviral prophylaxis", "Check hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) and hepatitis B core antibody (anti-HBc)", "Perform liver biopsy to evaluate for hepatitis B activity", "Recheck LFTs and start rituximab if results are normal", "Test for HBV DNA"]
answer_text: Check hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) and hepatitis B core antibody (anti-HBc)
explanation_text:
Patients starting rituximab should be screened for hepatitis B before starting treatment

Check hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) and hepatitis B core antibody (anti-HBc)

is correct. Rituximab is a monoclonal antibody targeting CD20 on B cells, leading to B cell depletion and immunosuppression. This increases the risk of reactivation of hepatitis B virus (HBV) in patients with resolved or latent infection. Screening with HBsAg and anti-HBc identifies patients with active or prior HBV infection at risk of reactivation. Patients with positive markers should be referred for further evaluation, including viral load testing (HBV DNA).

Begin antiviral prophylaxis

is incorrect. Antiviral prophylaxis (e.g., entecavir or tenofovir) is recommended for patients with active or past HBV infection at risk of reactivation. However, antiviral therapy should not be initiated without confirming HBV status through appropriate screening tests (HBsAg and anti-HBc).

Perform liver biopsy to evaluate for hepatitis B activity

is incorrect. A liver biopsy is not routinely required to evaluate for hepatitis B activity. Non-invasive tests, including serology (HBsAg, anti-HBc) and HBV DNA viral load, are sufficient to assess the risk of reactivation.

Recheck LFTs and start rituximab if results are normal

is incorrect. Liver function monitoring alone is insufficient to prevent HBV reactivation. Proactive HBV screening and, if necessary, prophylactic antiviral therapy are required to prevent reactivation rather than waiting for evidence of liver injury.

Testing for HBV DNA

is incorrect. HBsAg and anti-HBc are recommended for initial assessment, and patients with positive markers should be referred for further evaluation, including viral load testing (HBV DNA). Therefore, testing for HBV DNA should not be an appropriate option as the initial step.

question_text:
A 45-year-old woman attends the acute medical unit with her second DVT this year. Her background is notable for COPD, hypertension and chronic kidney disease stage 4 secondary to membranous glomerulonephritis.

In chronic kidney disease, which of the following contributes most to the increased risk of VTE?
options_json: ["Immobility", "Loss of protein C", "Loss of antithrombin III", "Concurrent cancer", "Lupus anticoagulant"]
explanation_text:
CKD is the most common cause of antithrombin III deficiency

Antithrombin III is an important regulatory molecule that reduces the activity of the intrinsic pathway of the clotting cascade. Loss of antithrombin III, thus, increases coagulability.

Whilst there are hereditary causes of antithrombin III, it is a particularly small protein and is easily lost through the nephron in CKD.

CKD does also increase the risk of concurrent cancers, but not as significantly as the protein loss. Lupus anticoagulant is indeed highly prothrombotic and is associated with antiphospholipid syndrome.

question_text:
A 54-year-old man undergoing treatment for multiple myeloma presents to the cancer assessment unit feeling generally unwell.

His temperature is 38.6ºC, blood pressure is 87/56 mmHg and heart rate is 113/min. He looks diaphoretic and unwell but examination of his heart, lungs and abdomen is unremarkable.

He has had a peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC) line in place for 4-weeks. There is no surrounding erythema but it appears to be blocked.

The haematology lab calls you regarding the following result:


Neuts	0.2 * 109/L	(2.0 - 7.0)

What is the most likely organism to have caused this presentation?
options_json: ["Enterococcus faecalis", "Staphylococcus aureus", "Staphylococcus epidermidis", "Streptococcus pneumoniae", "Streptococcus pyogenes"]
explanation_text:
Coagulase-negative, Gram-positive bacteria such as

These are all gram-positive cocci that are common in clinical practice.

Staphylococcus epidermidis

is a coagulase-negative, gram-positive cocci. It is the most common cause of neutropenic sepsis and is associated with central line infections. This patient's PICC line is blocked. In the context of sepsis without other localising features of infection, this makes 'line sepsis' the most likely cause for this presentation.

Staphylococcus aureus

is a coagulase-positive, gram-positive cocci. It is implicated in skin and soft tissue infections, abscess formation, osteomyelitis and toxic shock syndrome.

Enterococcus faecalis

is the most common species of enterococcus and is most commonly implicated in urinary tract infections, infective endocarditis and intra-abdominal infections.

Streptococcus pneumoniae

is an alpha-haemolytic streptococcus associated with pneumonia, meningitis and otitis media.

Streptococcus pyogenes

is a group A beta-haemolytic streptococci implicated in erysipelas, impetigo, cellulitis, type 2 necrotizing fasciitis and pharyngitis/tonsillitis. It can cause rheumatic fever or post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis and release of erythrogenic toxins to cause scarlet fever.

question_text:
A 56-year-old man presents to his general practitioner with several weeks of urinary frequency and hesitancy. He also describes approximately 20kg of weight loss over the past 2 months. Rectal examination reveals a large, craggy prostate. He is urgently referred for further investigations, including a biopsy which confirms a diagnosis of prostate cancer. At the next consultation, he states that his father and grandfather were both also diagnosed with prostate cancer in their 50s.

What genetic mutation is most strongly associated with this condition?
options_json: ["APC", "BRCA1", "BRCA2", "p53", "RAS"]
explanation_text:
BRCA2 mutation is associated with prostate cancer in men

BRCA2

is the correct answer. Although the BRCA genes are classically associated with breast cancer, they are also implicated in increased risk of numerous other cancers. In women, they are linked to an increased risk of ovarian cancer. In men, they are associated with prostate cancer. BRCA2 is more strongly linked to prostate cancer than BRCA1.

APC

is incorrect. A mutation in this gene is associated with familial adenomatous polyposis. This condition presents with the development of many colonic polyps and typically leads to colorectal cancer - most patients choose to undergo prophylactic colectomy as a result. It is not known to be significantly associated with prostate cancer.

BRCA1

is incorrect. Although this gene is linked with an increased risk of prostate cancer, the association is not as strong as the link between BRCA2 and prostate cancer.

p53

is incorrect. Although this is the most commonly mutated gene in human cancers, it is not specifically associated with an increased risk of prostate cancer.

RAS

is incorrect. Mutations in this family of genes are implicated in numerous cancers. However, this is not specifically associated with an increased risk of prostate cancer.

question_text:
A 34-year-old woman is taken to the emergency department by a friend with a two hour history of headache, shortness of breath and confusion. She is unable to give a coherent history as to what has led to her admission. She has a past medical history of asthma for which she takes a salbutamol inhaler as required.

Her vital signs show oxygen saturations of 84%, respiratory rate of 20/min, heart rate of 93/min, and a temperature of 36.7ºC. Subsequently, an arterial blood gas is done before she is initiated on oxygen.


pH	7.46
pO2	10.1kPa
pCO2	3.5kPa
HCO3	23
Lac	0.7

On examination her airway is patent and chest is clear. The rest of the examination is unremarkable.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
options_json: ["Acute asthma", "Carbon monoxide poisoning", "Cyanide poisoning", "Methaemoglobinaemia", "Organophosphate poisoning"]
explanation_text:
Normal pO2 but decreased oxygen saturation is characteristic of methaemoglobinaemia

This woman has presented with methaemoglobinaemia. This is a due to the conversion of haemoglobin from an Fe2+ state to Fe3+ resulting in a shift in the oxygen dissociation curve to the left (as haemoglobin has a reduced affinity for oxygen). As a result, there is a fall in oxygen saturation on pulse oximetry however the partial pressure of oxygen on an arterial blood gas remains normal.

Acute asthma would not cause the disproportional change seen on oximetry versus the arterial blood gas.

Organophosphate poisoning would not cause the changes noted on oximetry.

Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin and forms carboxyhemoglobin which in turn is unable to to bind oxygen. This is a similar pathological process to methaemoglobinaemia in that both reduce the ability of haemoglobin to bind oxygen. In contrast however, a saturation probe in carbon monoxide poisoning will still detect both haemoglobin saturations and produce a normal reading despite the reality that the patient is hypoxic.

Cyanide causes histotoxic hypoxia whereby the body cannot utilise oxygen from the bloodstream. Oxygen saturations are normal however venous oxygen levels may be raised (due to reduced consumption).

question_text: A 14-year-old girl is admitted to the Emergency Department. Over the past hour she has developed a painless, non-pruritic erythematous rash associated with severe angioedema. She has a past medical history of recurrent abdominal pain. Her symptoms fail to respond to adrenaline and she is therefore intubated to protect the airway. She is discharged from ITU after three days. During outpatient follow-up two weeks later a diagnosis of hereditary angioedema is suspected. What is the most appropriate screening test to perform?
options_json: ["Serum IgE levels", "Serum C3 levels", "Serum tryptase levels", "Serum C4 levels", "Serum C1-INH levels"]
explanation_text:
Hereditary angioedema - C4 is the best screening test inbetween attacks

The correct answer is

serum C4 levels

. Hereditary angioedema (HAE) is a rare autosomal dominant condition caused by a deficiency or dysfunction of the C1 inhibitor protein (C1-INH). This leads to increased activation of the complement and contact systems, resulting in excessive release of bradykinin, which causes angioedema. The most appropriate screening test for HAE is serum C4 levels, as they are typically low in patients with this condition due to increased consumption during uncontrolled activation of the complement system. If serum C4 levels are found to be low, further testing for serum C1-INH levels and function should be performed to confirm the diagnosis.

Serum IgE levels

would not be an appropriate screening test for hereditary angioedema. Elevated IgE levels are commonly seen in allergic conditions such as atopic dermatitis, asthma, and allergic rhinitis but not in HAE. In this case, the patient's symptoms failed to respond to adrenaline, which suggests that her angioedema was not mediated by an allergic mechanism.

Serum C3 levels

can be helpful in evaluating complement deficiencies or disorders involving immune complex formation; however, they are typically normal or only slightly decreased in HAE patients. Therefore, measuring serum C3 levels would not provide definitive information about whether this patient has hereditary angioedema.

Serum tryptase levels

are used as a diagnostic marker for mast cell activation disorders such as systemic mastocytosis or anaphylaxis. Tryptase is released from activated mast cells during these conditions, leading to elevated serum tryptase levels. However, HAE is not related to mast cell activation and thus measuring serum tryptase would not be useful in diagnosing this condition.

Finally,

serum C1-INH levels

can be used to confirm the diagnosis of HAE, but they are not the most appropriate screening test. As mentioned earlier, if serum C4 levels are found to be low, further testing for serum C1-INH levels and function should be performed to confirm the diagnosis. In HAE type 1, there is a deficiency in the quantity of C1-INH produced, while in HAE type 2, there is a defect in the function of C1-INH despite normal or elevated protein levels.

question_text:
A 17-year-old woman presents to the clinic with fatigue. She has recently moved to the UK from Greece. She states that she has a 'blood disorder' which runs in her family however she can not remember the specifics of it. She has never had a blood transfusion. An examination is unremarkable and in particular, there is no evidence of hepatosplenomegaly.

Blood results are as follows:


Hb	105 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
MCV	55 fL	(80 - 100 fL)
Ferritin	80 fL	(> 15 micrograms/L)
Platelets	162 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	6.8 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)


Hb electrophoresis	Raised HbA2

What is the most likely diagnosis?
options_json: ["Alpha thalassaemia trait", "Beta thalassaemia major", "Beta thalassaemia trait", "HbH disease", "Sickle cell disease"]
explanation_text:
Disproportionate microcytic anaemia - think beta-thalassaemia trait

Microcytic anaemia has a variety of causes including iron deficiency anaemia, thalassaemia, and rarely sideroblastic anaemia. A normal ferritin level as in this case makes iron deficiency unlikely. It is important to remember that a low ferritin confirms iron deficiency, however, a normal or raised ferritin does not exclude iron deficiency since it is an acute phase protein.

Disproportionate microcytic anaemia is suggestive of beta thalassaemia. In iron deficiency, the MCV and Hb are usually proportionally decreased.  The patient's ethnic origins and mild disproportionate microcytic anaemia make

beta thalassaemia trait

the most likely diagnosis.  This can be confirmed with high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) or Hb electrophoresis confirming a raised HbA2.

Beta thalassaemia major

can also present with disproportionate microcytic anaemia however the anaemia would be marked, and the patient would be transfusion dependent.

Alpha thalassaemia trait

can also present with a mild disproportionate microcytic anaemia however the raised HbA2 on electrophoresis is more suggestive of beta thalassemia trait.  Electrophoresis is normal in alpha thalassemia trait.

HbH disease

is a type of alpha thalassaemia which occurs due to a deletion of three out of four of the alpha globulin alleles.  This would present with a more severe anaemia and evidence of HbH on electrophoresis.

Sickle cell disease

would present with a history of vaso-occlusive crisis and Hb electrophoresis would show evidence of HbS.

A 71-year-old woman who is known to have multiple myeloma is admitted with confusion. Blood tests show the following:


Corrected calcium	2.91 mmol/l

Which one of the following is the most significant cause of the raised calcium level?
