question_text: Which one of the following is not a recognised feature of methaemoglobinaemia?
options_json: ["Dyspnoea", "'Chocolate' cyanosis", "Anxiety", "Reduced pO2 but normal oxygen saturation on pulse oximetry", "Acidosis"]
answer_text: Reduced pO2 but normal oxygen saturation on pulse oximetry
explanation_text:
Normal pO2 but decreased oxygen saturation is characteristic of methaemoglobinaemia

The correct answer is

Reduced pO2 but normal oxygen saturation on pulse oximetry

. Methaemoglobinaemia is a condition characterised by an elevated level of methaemoglobin in the blood. Methaemoglobin is a form of haemoglobin that does not bind oxygen, and its increased presence can lead to tissue hypoxia. However, it does not cause reduced pO2 but normal oxygen saturation on pulse oximetry. In fact, pulse oximetry may overestimate oxygen saturation due to the absorption characteristics of methaemoglobin.

Discussing the incorrect answers:

Dyspnoea

is indeed a recognised feature of methaemoglobinaemia. It occurs due to inadequate oxygen supply to tissues leading to shortness of breath.

'Chocolate' cyanosis

refers to the brownish colouration of the skin and mucous membranes seen in methaemoglobinaemia. This happens because methaemoglobin imparts a chocolate-brown colour to the blood.

Anxiety

can be seen in patients with methaemoglobinaemia as it's a non-specific symptom related to hypoxia and dyspnoea. Patients may feel anxious due to difficulty breathing or fear from their abnormal skin colouration.

Acidosis

, specifically metabolic acidosis, can occur in severe cases of methaemoglobinaemia due to lactic acid build-up from tissue hypoxia. The body responds to low oxygen levels by shifting metabolism towards anaerobic pathways, which produces lactic acid as a byproduct causing acidosis.

question_text:
A 56-year-old woman presented to the breast clinic with a breast lump. On examination, there was a palpable irregular, 3 cm, non-tender lump in the left upper quadrant. She was subsequently diagnosed with ductal carcinoma in situ of the left breast. She was referred to the oncology team and commenced on anastrozole.

What is the mechanism of action of the medication?
options_json: ["Binds to human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) receptors", "Breaks down oestrogen receptors", "Luteinising hormone-releasing hormone (LHRH) agonist", "Oestrogen receptor antagonist", "Reduces peripheral oestrogen synthesis"]
explanation_text:
Anastrozole and letrozole are aromatase inhibitors that reduces peripheral oestrogen synthesis

In postmenopausal women, oestrogen is produced from peripheral tissues and lipids via the enzyme aromatase. Therefore, aromatase inhibitors such as anastrozole and letrozole which

reduce peripheral oestrogen synthesis

are frequently used to treat breast carcinoma in this group of patients.

Trastuzumab is a monoclonal antibody that

binds to HER2 receptors

on the cancer cells, thereby suppressing the growth and proliferation of the tumour. It is effective in HER2-positive breast cancers.

Fulvestrant is a type of selective oestrogen receptor degrader that binds to and

breaks down oestrogen receptors

. Unlike tamoxifen, it does not have agonistic effects on the oestrogen receptor, instead, it leads to downregulation of the receptor.

Goserelin is an

LHRH agonist

that suppresses oestrogen production by the ovaries. It can be used as adjuvant therapy in premenopausal women.

Tamoxifen is an

antagonist (and a partial agonist) of oestrogen receptor

. It is useful in oestrogen-receptor positive breast cancers and particularly in patients who have not gone through menopause.

question_text:
You are seeing a 35-year-old male in the emergency department who was involved in a road traffic accident. He has been successfully stabilised by the trauma team.

His records show that he is under the local oncology team following a recent diagnosis of Hodgkin's lymphoma stage 1B. His records also mention that he is cytomegalovirus (CMV) IgG positive but IgM negative. He has no known allergies.

Blood tests revealed a haemoglobin level of 68 g/L and it has been decided that he requires a blood transfusion.

What modification is most important when ordering blood products for this patient?
options_json: ["CMV-seronegative red cells", "Irradiation", "Leucocyte depletion", "Washed red cells", "Whole blood"]
explanation_text:
Irradiated blood products are used to avoid transfusion-associated graft versus host disease

Cytomegalovirus (CMV)-seronegative red cells: this patient's blood results suggest a previous infection by CMV (IgG positive and IgM negative). Therefore, CMV-negative products are not normally given to such patients. Furthermore, routine leucocyte depletion in the UK makes CMV transmission via blood unlikely.

Irradiation: all patients with Hodgkin's lymphoma (regardless of disease stage) must be given irradiated blood products to prevent transfusion-associated graft versus host disease (taGVHD), for the rest of their life. Irradiated blood destroys all nucleated cells (such as leucocytes), therefore, eliminating the risk of taGVHD.

Leucocyte depletion: since 1999, all allogenic blood components in the UK must be subjected to a leucocyte depletion process. The UK definition of leucodepletion is as follows (taken from the Joint United Kingdom (UK) Blood Transfusion and Tissue Transplantation Services Professional Advisory Committee):

'UK specification for leucodepletion is that more than 90% of leucocyte-depleted components from relevant processes should have less than 1 Ã— 106 leucocytes and more than 99% of components should contain less than 5 Ã— 106 leucocytes, both with 95% confidence'.

Therefore, this is inadequate to prevent the life-threatening risk of taGVHD.

Washed red cells: red blood cells are washed to reduce the presence of plasma proteins, including anti-IgA that can cause anaphylactic reactions in susceptible individuals. It does little in the way of depleting leucocytes and preventing taGVHD.

Whole blood: this is useful for trauma settings associated with major bleeding. However, giving such a transfusion to a patient with Hodgkin's lymphoma carries the risk of life-threatening taGVHD and, therefore, should not be used.

question_text:
A 64-year-old female is brought to the Emergency Department by her family, who are concerned about her increasing confusion over the past 2 days. On examination she is found to be pyrexial at 38ºC. Blood tests reveal:


Hb	9.6 g/dl
Platelets	65 * 109/l
WCC	11.1 * 109/l
Urea	23.1 mmol/l
Creatinine	366 µmol/l

What is the most likely diagnosis?
options_json: ["Wegener's granulomatosis", "Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura", "Haemolytic uraemic syndrome", "Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura", "Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis"]
explanation_text:
HUS or TTP? Neuro signs point towards TTP

The combination of neurological features, renal failure, pyrexia and thrombocytopaenia point towards a diagnosis of thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura

question_text:
A 43-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with confusion and fever. She is 4 weeks pregnant. She drinks 21 units of alcohol weekly.

On examination, her Glasgow coma scale is 14/15 without any localizing neurological signs. Her temperature is 38.4ºC and her blood pressure is 142/82 mmHg.

Blood tests:


Hb	88 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	24 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	6.7 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Urea	5.2 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	88 µmol/L	(55 - 120)
CRP	4 mg/L	(< 5)
Haptoglobin	2 mg/dl	(30-200)
LDH	754 U/L	(140-280)


Blood film	schistocytes

What is the underlying pathophysiological mechanism of the likely diagnosis?
options_json: ["Acquired inhibition of ADAMTS13", "Alcohol induced bone marrow suppression", "Antiplatelet antibodies", "Binding of Shiga-toxin to globotriaosylceramide", "Cytokine driven haemophagocytosis"]
explanation_text:
Acquired inhibition of the protein ADAMTS13 which cleaves vWF multimers is the most common cause of TTP

Acquired inhibition of ADAMTS13

is correct. The patient presents with fever and confusion in association with thrombocytopenia and evidence of microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (anaemia, low haptoglobin and schistocytes). These findings point to a diagnosis of thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). Pregnancy is a secondary cause of this condition, which is caused by acquired inhibition of ADAMTS13. This is a metalloproteinase responsible for breaking large multimers von Willebrand factor (vWF) into smaller sub-units. The increased amount of circulating vWF results in platelet adhesion and thrombosis. Platelets are used up in creating thrombi and paradoxically, the overall amount of circulating platelets is subsequently reduced, resulting in a tendency to bleed.

Binding of Shiga-toxin to globotriaosylceramide

is incorrect. This is the cause of the haemolytic uraemic syndrome. This is usually caused by infection with bacteria producing Shiga-toxin. It is another cause of microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia and is a cause of fever and confusion. However, it is almost always associated with severe renal dysfunction, which is absent in this case. Additionally, there is often evidence of a preceding diarrhoeal illness.

Alcohol-induced bone marrow suppression

is incorrect. While alcohol excess can cause bone marrow suppression and resultant anaemia and thrombocytopenia, it would not typically cause a fever or microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia.

Antiplatelet antibodies

is not the right answer. This is the cause of immune thrombocytopenic purpura. This is a cause of isolated thrombocytopenia rather than anaemia. Additionally, it would not be associated with fever.

Cytokine driven haemophagocytosis

is incorrect. This has been implicated as the cause of thrombocytopenia in sepsis. While this patient has a fever, the white cell count and CRP are normal, making a pyogenic infection, less likely (although not impossible). This would not cause microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia or schistocytes on the blood film.

question_text:
A 35-year-old male presents with a four-day history of painless visible haematuria, mostly occurring in the morning.

His past medical history includes asthma and a previous right-sided pulmonary embolism. He is a slim teetotaller and works as a teacher.

A recent sexual health screen was normal and there is no family history of cancers.

Which of the following investigations is the gold standard for the likely underlying diagnosis?
options_json: ["Flow cytometry", "Guthrie's test", "Ham's test", "Sucrose lysis test", "Urine cultures"]
explanation_text:
Flow cytometry for CD59 and CD55 is the gold standard test for paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria

Patients with haematuria and unexplained or unusual sites of thrombosis, or with a raised LDH (indicating haemolysis), abnormal cell counts or aplastic anaemia, should be screened for PNH (paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria). PNH is a rare acquired disorder characterised by intravascular haemolysis due to deficiency of decay-accelerating factor, a protein normally present on red blood cells. The mechanism by which this also leads to venous thrombus formation is not fully understood.

Flow cytometry is now the gold standard investigation in PNH and is, therefore, the correct answer.

The sucrose lysis test was historically used for screening. It involves placing the patient's red blood cells in a low-ionic-strength solution and observing for haemolysis. It has now been replaced by flow cytometry which is both more sensitive and more specific.

Ham's test (acid-induced haemolysis, named after Dr Thomas Ham) used to be the next investigation of choice if the sucrose lysis test was positive, but it is no longer used and is therefore incorrect.

Urine cultures are an excellent first choice of investigation for patients presenting with urinary symptoms. However, in this case, they are not the single best answer as they are unlikely to lead to the underlying diagnosis of PNH.

Guthrie's test, also known as the heel prick test, is done in neonates on their fifth day of life to screen for metabolic disorders. It is an inappropriate choice of investigation in an adult patient.

question_text:
A 28-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a one-week history of fatigue and shortness of breath. His past medical history is significant for an allogenic haematopoetic stem cell transplant 3 months ago.

Blood results are as follows:


Hb	72 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	46 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	2.2 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)

You plan to transfuse him 2 units of blood. The laboratory call to ask if any special requirements are indicated.

What special requirements do you advise the laboratory?
options_json: ["CMV negative blood", "Irradiated", "Leukodepleted", "No special requirements indicated", "Washed"]
explanation_text:
Irradiated blood products are used to avoid transfusion-associated graft versus host disease

Irradiated blood

is required in individuals with severe immunodeficiencies, those with a history of Hodgkin's lymphoma, patients who have been exposed to certain drugs (e.g. bendamustine and fludarabine), and following stem cell transplant. Following autologous stell cell transplantation irradiated blood is required for 3 months (6 months if total body irradiation is performed). In contrast, those who have had an allogeneic stem cell transplant require irradiated blood for a minimum of 6 months and until they are also off immunosuppression, have a lymphocyte count >1, and have no evidence of chronic graft versus host disease (GvHD).

Historically, immunocompromised patients who have not been infected with CMV (CMV negative) received CMV negative blood due to the possible life-threatening complication of infection. However recent studies have shown that leukodepletion is just as effective as CMV IgG negative blood components. Therefore

CMV IgG negative blood

is no longer required in this cohort.

The following groups of patients require CMV-negative blood:

Intra-uterine transfusions.
Neonates up to 28 days post expected date of delivery.
Pregnancy.

With very few stated exceptions (e.g. granulocytes), from November 1999 all allogeneic blood components produced in the UK have been subjected to a leukocyte depletion process. This was primarily a vCJD risk reduction measure, however, it has resulted in other added benefits including reduced incidence of non-febrile haemolytic transfusion reactions, TRALI, and transfer of CMV. All blood products in the UK are

leukodepleted

(with very few exceptions eg granulocytes). This is therefore not a special requirement.

Washed red cells

can be requested for patients who have recurrent febrile or allergic reactions to standard packed red cells.

question_text:
A 23-year-old woman has presented to her GP after developing swelling of her face 2 days ago.

She has never had an allergic reaction in the past but mentions that her older brother is under the immunology clinic after having five unexplained episodes of sudden-onset facial and lip swelling without any clear trigger. He has apparently tested positive for a 'genetic problem' but she is unable to give any further details.

The swelling has now cleared but she is keen on further investigations.

Based on the likely diagnosis, which is the most appropriate screening test to perform?
options_json: ["Bradykinin", "Mast cell tryptase", "C1 esterase inhibitor", "C3", "C4"]
explanation_text:
Hereditary angioedema - C4 is the best screening test inbetween attacks

The episodic attacks of unexplained facial and lip swelling in her brother which are apparently of genetic origin are suggestive of hereditary angioedema. This condition is inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion. Assuming that this was inherited from a parent (rather than being a

de novo

mutation), there is a 50% probability that she is also affected. This condition is commonly associated with low C4 levels. Importantly, C4 tends to remain low in between attacks and is relatively cheap to test, hence it is the most appropriate screening tool, even though the specificity of the test is low.

While C1 esterase inhibitor is the most specific test for hereditary angioedema, it is expensive and not widely available in laboratories, hence is not a suitable screening test to perform here. In addition, approximately 15% of cases of hereditary angioedema are classified as 'type 2', where C1 esterase inhibitor is normal in concentration but abnormal in function.

Abnormal C3 levels are not seen in hereditary angioedema.

Raised mast cell tryptase levels are seen in anaphylaxis, not in hereditary angioedema.

While increased bradykinin is the main pathophysiological process behind hereditary angioedema, testing for this peptide is generally not available, hence this is not the correct answer.

question_text:
A 25-year-old man presents with a several-month history of fluctuating abdominal cramps and foul-smelling, greasy loose stools. This is associated with significant weight loss and fatigue.

He is otherwise well and denies any infective symptoms. He has no past medical history and is not on any medications.

Anti-transglutaminase and anti-endomysial antibodies are positive.

What specific blood film abnormality is associated with this condition?
options_json: ["Degmacyte", "Howell-Jolly bodies", "Hypersegmented neutrophils", "Schistocytes", "Spherocytes"]
explanation_text:
Target cells and Howell-Jolly bodies may be seen in coeliac disease → hyposplenism

This patient has presented with the autoimmune disorder, coeliac disease, where patients develop an intolerance to gluten (found in foods such as wheat and barley), resulting in an inflammatory response. The diagnosis is confirmed with positive anti-transglutaminase and anti-endomysial antibodies. A well-recognised complication of coeliac disease is hyposplenism thought to result from functional hyposplenism and splenic atrophy. As such, a blood film in coeliac patients often shows

Howell-Jolly bodies

signifying the inability of a damaged spleen to remove these red cell inclusions.

Degmacyte

, also known as 'bite cells', are abnormally shaped mature red blood cells with a portion of the cell margin removed. These removed portions or 'bites' occur due to the mechanical removal of denatured haemoglobin as the cells migrate through the spleen. This denaturing of haemoglobin can result from several processes of oxidative haemolysis such as glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency. These cells are not associated with hyposplenism and are not commonly seen in coeliac disease.

Hypersegmented neutrophils

are normally defined as the presence of neutrophils whose nuclei have six or more lobes or where over 3% of neutrophils have at least five lobes. Hypersegmented neutrophils are associated with the macrocytic, megaloblastic anaemia due to hypovitaminosis such as vitamin B12 or folate deficiency. Although severe coeliac disease can result in some malabsorption, hypovitaminosis is rare and therefore these cells are not associated with the condition.

Schistocytes

are irregularly shaped, fragmented parts of red blood cells, often seen in patients with mechanical haemolysis. Several microangiopathic diseases can result in haemolytic conditions including disseminated intravascular coagulation and thrombotic microangiopathies. Again, these cells are not associated with coeliac disease.

Spherocytes

are sphere-shaped red blood cells rather than normal bi-concave disk-shaped cells. They are found in hereditary spherocytosis and immunological-mediated haemolytic anaemia. The spleen mistakes these sphere-shaped cells as damaged and therefore removes them resulting in the associated anaemia. They are not seen in coeliac disease.

question_text: A 54-year-old woman is reviewed in oncology clinic following debulking surgery for primary peritoneal cancer. She is known to have two liver metastases. She underwent surgery one month ago and has come in for review prior to adjuvant chemotherapy. During her chemotherapy treatment, which tumour marker would be most appropriate to monitor disease progression?
options_json: ["CA 15-3", "CA 19-9", "CA 125", "Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG)", "S-100"]
explanation_text:
Ovarian cancer - CA 125

CA 125 is the tumour marker most associated with primary peritoneal cancer as well as ovarian cancer and can be used to monitor response to chemotherapy, alongside regular CT scans. It can also be raised in various other cancers.

The other tumour markers are more appropriate for other cancers.

Source:

Sturgeon, C. M., L. C. Lai, and M. J. Duffy. 'Serum Tumour Markers: How to Order and Interpret Them.' BMJ (2009): 852-58.

question_text:
A 68-year-old man with a 10-year history of polycythaemia vera presents to haematology clinic with increasing fatigue, weight loss, and night sweats over the past 3 months. On examination, he has marked splenomegaly. He has been managed with regular venesection and aspirin. Recent blood tests show:


Hb	98 g/L	(135-180)
WBC	3.2 × 10^9/L	(4.0-11.0)
Platelets	85 × 10^9/L	(150-400)
Blood film	Teardrop red cells, nucleated red cells, myelocytes	

What is the most likely diagnosis?
options_json: ["Acute myeloid leukaemia", "Myelofibrosis", "Hairy cell leukaemia", "Essential thrombocythaemia", "Chronic myeloid leukaemia"]
explanation_text:
Polycythaemia rubra vera - around 5-15% progress to myelofibrosis or AML

Myelofibrosis

is the correct diagnosis in this case. The patient has a long-standing history of polycythaemia vera (PV) and has now developed constitutional symptoms (fatigue, weight loss, night sweats), splenomegaly, and pancytopenia with characteristic peripheral blood film findings. Approximately 5-15% of patients with PV will progress to post-polycythaemic myelofibrosis over time. This transformation is characterized by progressive bone marrow fibrosis leading to ineffective haematopoiesis. The peripheral blood typically shows leukoerythroblastic features including teardrop poikilocytes (dacryocytes) and nucleated red cells, which are present in this case. The splenomegaly results from extramedullary haematopoiesis as the bone marrow function deteriorates. The development of cytopenias in a patient previously requiring venesection for polycythaemia is particularly suggestive of this transformation.

Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML)

is another possible complication of PV, occurring in approximately 5-15% of patients, particularly those treated with certain cytotoxic agents. However, AML typically presents with a rapid onset of symptoms, often with blast cells visible on the peripheral blood film, and frequently with more profound cytopenias. The absence of blast cells in the described blood film makes AML less likely than myelofibrosis in this scenario.

Hairy cell leukaemia

is an uncommon B-cell malignancy that can present with pancytopenia and splenomegaly. However, it is not a known progression of polycythaemia vera. Hairy cell leukaemia would typically show characteristic 'hairy cells' on blood film examination, which are not described here. The leukoerythroblastic blood picture is not typical of hairy cell leukaemia.

Essential thrombocythaemia

is another myeloproliferative neoplasm but is characterized by thrombocytosis rather than thrombocytopenia. It would be extremely unusual for PV to transform into essential thrombocythaemia. The patient's low platelet count (85 × 10^9/L) makes this diagnosis implausible.

Chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML)

is a myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by the Philadelphia chromosome. While it can present with splenomegaly and constitutional symptoms, it typically shows leukocytosis with a characteristic left shift in granulocyte precursors. CML is not a known transformation of polycythaemia vera, and the patient's leukopenia rather than leukocytosis makes this diagnosis unlikely.

question_text: A 62-year-old woman who is known to have metastatic breast cancer presents with increasing shortness of breath. She is currently receiving a chemotherapy regime. On examination she has a third heart sound and the apex beat is displaced to the 6th intercostal space, anterior axillary line. Which one of the following chemotherapeutic agents is most likely to be responsible?
options_json: ["Paclitaxel", "Docetaxel", "Bleomycin", "Dactinomycin", "Doxorubicin"]
explanation_text:
Anthracyclines (e.g. doxorubicin) may cause cardiomyopathy

The correct answer is

Doxorubicin

. Doxorubicin is an anthracycline chemotherapeutic agent that is known to cause dose-dependent cardiotoxicity. This cardiotoxicity can manifest as congestive heart failure, which may explain the patient's increasing shortness of breath, third heart sound, and displaced apex beat. The risk of cardiotoxicity increases with higher cumulative doses of doxorubicin.

Paclitaxel

and

Docetaxel

are taxane chemotherapeutic agents. They are not commonly associated with cardiotoxicity or congestive heart failure. Instead, their main side effects include peripheral neuropathy, myelosuppression (bone marrow suppression), and hypersensitivity reactions.

Bleomycin

is a glycopeptide antibiotic used in chemotherapy. Its primary toxicity is pulmonary fibrosis, which can lead to shortness of breath but would not typically cause a third heart sound or displaced apex beat. The pulmonary fibrosis caused by bleomycin is dose-dependent and irreversible.

Dactinomycin

, also known as actinomycin D, is an antineoplastic antibiotic used in chemotherapy. It does not typically cause cardiotoxicity or congestive heart failure. Its main side effects are myelosuppression (bone marrow suppression) and gastrointestinal toxicity.

question_text:
A 46-year-old woman is being reviewed in the breast cancer multidisciplinary team meeting. After reviewing her history, imaging and histology, the team decide that the best chemotherapy agent to commence her on is docetaxel. She is counselled appropriately regarding the side effects and agrees to start.

What is the mechanism of action of this drug?
options_json: ["Blocks thymidylate synthase", "Cross-links DNA", "Inhibits ribonucleotide reductase", "Prevents microtubule depolymerisation", "Stabilises DNA-topoisomerase II complex"]
explanation_text:
Taxanes such as docetaxel - prevents microtubule depolymerisation & disassembly, decreasing free tubulin

The correct answer is the prevention of microtubule depolymerisation. By doing so, and preventing disassembly, docetaxel leads to a decrease in free tubulin. A common adverse effect of docetaxel is neutropaenia.

Blocking thymidylate synthase refers to the action of fluorouracil, a pyrimidine analogue that induces cell cycle arrest and apoptosis. Adverse effects include myelosuppression, mucositis and dermatitis.

Cross-linking DNA is the method of action of cyclophosphamide, an alkylating agent. It is known for causing haemorrhagic cystitis, which can be prevented with adjunctive use of the drug mesna.

Inhibition of ribonucleotide reductase refers to the action of hydroxyurea, thereby decreasing DNA synthesis. Side effects include myelosuppression.

Stabilisation of the DNA-topoisomerase II complex refers to the action of doxorubicin and the anthracycline class. These are known to lead to cardiomyopathy.

question_text:
A 30-year-old female presents with a painless rash on both lower limbs and prolonged gum bleeding this morning whilst brushing her teeth.

She has no medical history nor any regular medication.

She is apyrexial and her vital signs are within the normal ranges. Clinical examination revealed multiple lower limb petechiae measuring 1-4mm in size. There were no lesions nor active bleeding in the oral cavity. Clinical examination was otherwise normal.

Blood tests show:


Hb	126 g/L	(115 - 160)
Platelets	26 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	7.2 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)


Clotting screen	Normal
U&Es	Normal
HCV, HBV, HIV	Negative


Peripheral blood smear	True thrombocytopenia
Pregnancy test	Negative

Which is the most appropriate initial treatment for her condition?
options_json: ["Intravenous corticosteroids", "Intravenous immunoglobulins", "Observation only", "Oral prednisolone", "Platelet transfusion"]
explanation_text:
First-line treatment for ITP is oral prednisolone

This is a typical presentation of an uncomplicated case of primary immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP). Reversible causes of ITP have been excluded by the investigations. From the options provided the appropriate first-line treatment for this case will be oral prednisolone. Corticosteroids help suppress the immune-mediated destruction of platelets.

Intravenous immunoglobulins is a second-line therapy for minor bleeding, or first-line (along with other agents) for severe bleeding. This patient only has features suggesting minor bleeding.

Intravenous corticosteroids are unnecessary in this patient, as she has no contraindications to receiving treatment via the oral route, nor any features of severe/critical bleeding.

Observation only is reserved for asymptomatic adults with a platelet count >=30 * 10

9

/L. This patient has a platelet count <30 * 10

9

/L and also has petechiae with mild mucosal bleeding, therefore not asymptomatic, and requires treatment due to increased bleeding risk with the low platelet count.

Platelet transfusions are reserved for those with life- or organ-threatening bleeding and may be used to control active bleeding for surgery; however, they are ineffective as a treatment for ITP due to continued immune-mediated platelet destruction. This is not the appropriate choice for this case, as there is no evidence of significant active bleeding.

question_text: A patient develops methaemoglobinaemia after being prescribed isosorbide mononitrate. Which substance is most likely to be depleted?
options_json: ["Pyruvate kinase", "Hyponitrite reductase", "Pyridoxine 5-dehydrogenase", "Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase", "NADH"]

question_text: Which of the following is most associated with thymomas?
options_json: ["Myelodysplasia", "Thrombocytopenia", "Acute myeloid leukaemia", "Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia", "Red cell aplasia"]

question_text: A woman is prescribed docetaxel as part of her chemotherapy for breast cancer. What is the mechanism of action of docetaxel?
options_json: ["Inhibits RNA synthesis", "Stabilizes DNA-topoisomerase II complex", "Prevents microtubule disassembly", "Inhibits formation of microtubules", "Causes cross-linking in DNA"]
explanation_text:
Taxanes such as docetaxel - prevents microtubule depolymerisation & disassembly, decreasing free tubulin

Like other taxanes the principal mechanism of action is the prevention of microtubule disassembly.

question_text:
A 22-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with confusion and lethargy.

Her blood pressure is 90/70 mmHg, heart rate 110/min, and temperature 39.4ºC.

On examination, she is pale, there is sternal tenderness with petechiae on her arms and legs and there is hepatosplenomegaly. Her cannula site is bleeding.


Hb	78 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	30 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	25 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
PT	27 secs	(10-14 secs)
APTT	45 secs	(25-35 secs)
Fibrinogen	0.4 g/L	(2 - 4)

The patient is resuscitated with blood products and transferred to ICU.

What chromosomal translocation is most likely to be identified on further testing?
explanation_text:
Acute promyelocytic leukaemia - t(15;17)

This patient presented with signs and symptoms suggestive of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). High white cell count, bony tenderness, and hepatosplenomegaly with DIC indicate acute leukaemia. The presence of DIC without any underlying cause in a young patient suggests acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APML). APML is associated with

t (15:17) translocation

involving the promyelocytic leukaemia (PML) gene and retinoic acid receptor alpha (RARA) gene, which gives rise to an abnormal retinoic acid receptor, inhibiting the differentiation of myeloblast. All-trans-retinoic acid is used for the treatment of APML which induces PML-RARA proteolysis and stimulates the differentiation of myeloblasts.

T11:14

is a translocation between the cyclin D1 locus on chromosome 11 and the lg heavy chain locus on chromosome 14 and it is characteristic of mantle cell lymphoma.

T14:18

is a translocation between the long arm of chromosome 18 near the BCL2 gene and the lg heavy chain gene on chromosome 14, leading to overexpression of the apoptosis inhibitor protein Bcl-2. It is commonly associated with follicular lymphoma.

T16:16

are recurring chromosomal rearrangements commonly associated with the M4Eo subtype of acute myeloid leukaemia.

T9:22

is a translocation of the ABL gene from chromosome 9 to 22 resulting in the formation of the Philadelphia chromosome, which encodes a protein with high tyrosine kinase activity that inhibits apoptosis and accelerates mitogenesis. It is a typical finding in chronic myeloid leukaemia.

question_text: A 58-year-old man is reviewed in clinic. Six months ago he had a Whipple procedure for pancreatic cancer and is currently undergoing chemotherapy. Which one of the following blood tests is most useful in monitoring his disease?
options_json: ["CA 15-3 levels", "Faecal elastase", "CA 125 levels", "Amylase levels", "CA 19-9 levels"]
explanation_text:
Pancreatic cancer - CA 19-9

The correct answer is

CA 19-9 levels

. CA 19-9, or carbohydrate antigen 19-9, is a tumour marker that is often elevated in pancreatic cancer. Monitoring CA 19-9 levels can provide useful information about the progression of disease or the response to treatment in patients with pancreatic cancer. However, it's important to note that while an increase in CA 19-9 levels may suggest disease progression, a decrease does not necessarily confirm successful treatment. Furthermore, some patients with pancreatic cancer do not have elevated CA 19-9 levels.

CA 15-3 levels

are typically used to monitor breast cancer rather than pancreatic cancer. While this marker can be elevated in other malignancies including pancreatic cancer, it is not as specific or sensitive as CA 19-9 for monitoring this disease.

Faecal elastase

is a test used to assess exocrine pancreatic function and can help diagnose chronic pancreatitis or cystic fibrosis. It would not be useful for monitoring the progression or treatment of pancreatic cancer.

CA 125 levels

are commonly used to monitor ovarian cancer. Like CA 15-3, this marker can also be elevated in other types of malignancies including pancreatic cancer but it is less specific than CA 19-9 for this purpose.

Finally,

Amylase levels

can be increased in acute pancreatitis and other conditions causing acute abdominal pain but they are not useful for monitoring the progress of a known case of pancreatic cancer. Elevated amylase levels might occur if the tumour obstructs the pancreatic duct but they would not provide reliable information about how well the patient's cancer responds to chemotherapy.

question_text:
A 31-year-old woman with known sickle cell disease presents to her GP feeling acutely lethargic. She has also noticed palpitations and shortness of breath on exertion. She has previously been fit and well. However, her daughter has been unwell over the past few days with fevers, malaise and a facial rash.

Blood test results 3 months ago:


Hb	116 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	178 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	6.3 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)

Blood test results today:


Hb	71 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	110 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	4.1 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)


Reticulocytes	0.1 %	(0.5 - 1.5)

What is the most likely complication which has occurred here?
options_json: ["Acute chest syndrome", "Acute splenic sequestration", "Aplastic crisis", "Community acquired pneumonia", "Haemolytic crisis"]
explanation_text:
Aplastic crises in sickle cell disease are associated with a sudden drop in haemoglobin

The correct answer here is

aplastic crisis

in sickle cell disease. There are multiple clues to this, including the symptoms of anaemia, the exposure to parvovirus B-19 (which is the most common trigger) and the drop in haemoglobin with a low reticulocyte count. This implies acute bone marrow failure.

Haemolytic crisis

and

acute splenic sequestration

would also cause a sudden drop in haemoglobin levels in sickle cell patients. However, in these conditions, you would expect a raised reticulocyte count, given that the problem is with red blood cell survival rather than red blood cell production.

Acute chest syndrome

is an acute respiratory complication of sickle cell disease. However, that would not explain the blood results.

Community-acquired pneumonia

would cause respiratory symptoms but would not account for the blood results noted here.

question_text:
A 34-year-old female presents due to the development of a purpuric rash on the back of her legs. Her only regular medication is Microgynon 30. She also reports frequent nose bleeds and menorrhagia. A full blood count is requested:


Hb	11.7 g/dl
Platelets	62 * 109/l
WCC	5.3 * 109/l
 
PT	11 secs
APTT	30 secs
 
Factor VIIIc
activity	Normal

What is the most likely diagnosis?
options_json: ["Drug-induced thrombocytopenia", "Henoch-Schonlein purpura", "Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura", "Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura", "Antiphospholipid syndrome"]

question_text:
A 40-year-old female patient diagnosed with sickle cell anaemia had complicated recurrent hospital admissions with a recent episode where she suffered from acute severe pain affecting both her arms, pain when breathing in and out as well as extreme tiredness.

She was seen in the haematology clinic as an outpatient to optimise the management of her underlying condition to reduce the incidence of such complications.

Which of the following medications should this patient be commenced on?
options_json: ["Deferoxamine", "Folic acid", "Hydroxycarbamide", "Penicillin V", "Vitamin D"]
explanation_text:
Sickle cell patients should be started on long term hydroxycarbamide to reduce the incidence of complications and acute crises

Hydroxycarbamide reduces the frequency of painful episodes and the risk of life-threatening illness or death. However, it can also increase your risk of infections. It is advised not to be taken in pregnancy.

Hydroxycarbamide essentially makes your red blood cells bigger, stay rounder and more flexible. Therefore, less likely to turn into a sickle shape. This is achieved by increasing a special kind of haemoglobin called haemoglobin F.

Folic acid taken regularly in anaemia raises haemoglobin levels and helps provide a healthy reticulocyte response. However, the use of folic acid in patients with sickle cell disease is not well supported by primary literature.

Deferoxamine is an iron chelation therapy used in sickle cell disease to enhance iron excretion and removes excessive tissue iron in regularly transfused patients with sickle cell disease.

Vitamin D deficiency has been shown in 98 per cent of patients with sickle cell disease. As a result of low bone density, patients may develop osteonecrosis, chronic inflammation and related pain. Therefore whilst vitamin D supplementation is important, hydroxycarbamide has a more crucial role in reducing the incidence of complications and acute crises.

Penicillin V helps prevent life-threatening infections, particularly in patients who have undergone a splenectomy, which is not the case here.

question_text:
A 61-year-old man is referred by his family physician to a haematologist after he presented with a right-sided painless neck lump. The lump started small and has been slowly increasing in size. More recently a second lump has appeared which prompted the family physician to refer the patient.

The patient has also been complaining of lethargy, night sweats and has lost significant weight. Thyroid function tests are normal and the patient does not have a significant family history. There is no recent travel or contact history. Biopsy of the nodes and cytogenetic analysis show a translocation causing increased B-cell lymphoma 2 (BCL-2) transcription which confirms the diagnosis. Unfortunately, the patient's condition cannot be treated with imatinib.

Which of the following translocation does this patient have?
explanation_text:
The t(14;18) translocation causes increased BCL-2 transcription and causes follicular lymphoma

This patient presented with the signs and symptoms suggestive of non-Hodgkin lymphoma. This is supported by the signs and symptoms of weight loss, night sweats, and painless lymphadenopathy. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma is one class of lymphoma, with the other class being Hodgkin lymphoma. There are several types of Hodgkin lymphoma which are actually neoplasms of mature B cells, and very rarely of T cell origin. In this case, a cytogenetic analysis revealed a translocation causing increased BCL-2 transcription. This is associated with the t(14;18) translocation which causes follicular lymphoma.

2: t(11;14) is associated with Mantle cell lymphoma, which is a type of non-Hodgkin lymphoma. There is a translocation of cyclin D1 on chromosome 11 and heavy-chain Ig on chromosome 14. Mantle cell lymphoma is characteristic of being CD5 positive. It is known to be an aggressive tumor with late presentation and therefore poor prognosis.

3: t(15;17) is associated with the acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) subtype of acute myeloid leukemia (AML). AML usually presents in patients above 65 years of age. The therapeutic importance of knowing the APL subtype is that it responds to all-trans retinoic acid (vitamin A).

4: t(12;15) is associated with the development of breast cancer, more specifically secretory breast carcinoma. This type of breast cancer is known to be rare and the clinical outcome following is usually good.

5: t(11;22) is a translocation which occurs in Ewing sarcoma. This is a malignant bone tumour which often occurs in individuals under 15 years of age.  The disease is known to be very aggressive and is associated with the development of early metastases.

question_text:
A 69-year-old male patient presents to the oncology clinic with a 3-months history of right upper quadrant discomfort, weight loss and anorexia. Ultrasound liver raises the suspicion of a hepatocellular carcinoma.

Which carcinogen had he likely been exposed to?
options_json: ["Nitrosamine", "Aflatoxin", "Aniline dye", "Arsenic", "Benzene"]
explanation_text:
Exposure to aflatoxin is a risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma

Exposure to aflatoxin is a risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma.

Exposure to nitrosamine is a risk factor for gastric and oesophageal carcinoma.

Exposure to aniline dye is a risk factor for transitional cell carcinoma.

Exposure to arsenic is a risk factor for lung malignancy and liver angiosarcoma.

Exposure to benzene is a risk factor for leukaemia.

question_text:
A 60-year-old male is brought in by his concerned son. The patient is known to have advanced, non-small cell lung cancer and is currently under review for palliative radiotherapy. Over the last 2 days, he has experienced increasing weakness of his legs confining him to his bed.

On direct questioning, he reports ongoing chest discomfort, breathlessness and sweating at night for several months. He has also noticed some difficulty passing urine associated with the weakness.

On exam, he has global reduced power of the legs with increased ankle and knee reflexes.

His observation are seen below

HR 80 /min
BP 142/80 mmHg
RR 25 /min
Oxygen sats 95%
Temperature 37.6 ºC

What is the most appropriate initial management for this patient?
options_json: ["Broad spectrum antibiotics", "High-dose oral dexamethasone", "IV mannitol", "Urgent MRI whole spine", "Urgent referral for radiotherapy"]
explanation_text:
If neoplastic spinal cord compression is suspected, high-dose oral dexamethasone should be given whilst awaiting investigations

This patient has presented with possible cord compression and therefore urgent high-dose dexamethasone must be given to reduce possible oedema and prevent further swelling and spinal injury. The patient's features of lower motor neurone signs and increased reflexes, along with an established diagnosis of lung cancer means he is at risk of possible spinal metastases and should be managed as such until proven otherwise. Spinal cord compression is an oncological emergency and so dexamethasone should be given whilst arranging investigations, ideally a whole MRI spine within 24hours of presentation.

Although the patient is at increased suspectable given his cancer there is no clear indication of infection. Night sweating is a common feature of varies cancers and is not necessarily a sign of infection and the patient's urinary issues are likely due to neurogenic bladder secondary to spinal cord compression. The patient denies any specific infective symptoms and is haemodynamically stable making the likelihood of sepsis low, particularly when compared to the risk of spinal cord compression. IV antibiotics can be considered especially if further evidence of infection is found (e.g. raised inflammatory markers, positive urine dip) but for now high dose steroids in the form of dexamethasone is the priority.

IV mannitol is often used in patients presenting with another oncological emergency, raised intracranial pressure, which can occur due to brain metastases. Although brain metastases present with neurological signs it would be very usual for this to occur without local cerebral symptoms such as headache, vomiting, altered mental state etc. Also, high dose dexamethasone would be the recommended first treatment before considering mannitol in these cases anyway.

A whole MRI spine is an important aspect of management and should ideally be carried out within 24 hours in suspected spinal cord compression however dexamethasone should be given whilst this investigation is being arranged. Spinal cord compression is time-critical and the commence dexamethasone should be a priority.

A referral for radiotherapy may be appropriate at a later stage however this is not the initial management. Confirmation of spinal metastases and an oncological opinion must be sought prior to radiotherapy, all of which can take time. Dexamethasone can be given immediately within the emergency department and can improve outcomes by reducing further spinal cord compression.

question_text:
A 34-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a one-week history of fatigue. There is no evidence of bleeding on systematic inquiry or examination. He has recently completed a course of anti-malarial prophylaxis for travel to Uganda.

Blood results are as follows:


Hb	84 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Reticulocytes	322 * 109/L	(50-100)
Platelets	182 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	10.8 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)


Blood film	Polychromasia; Frequent blister cell
Thick and thin blood films	No abnormality detected
Direct antiglobulin test (DAT)	Weakly positive for IgG (1+)

What is the most likely diagnosis?
options_json: ["Auto-immune haemolytic anaemia", "G6PD deficiency", "Hereditary spherocytosis", "Malaria", "Methemoglobinemia"]
explanation_text:
Malaria prophylaxis (e.g. primaquine) can trigger haemolytic anaemia in those with G6PD deficiency

Anaemia with reticulocytosis is suggestive of haemolysis or bleeding. The lack of any obvious bleeding source favours haemolysis in this case. The differential diagnosis for haemolysis is wide including immune and non-immune mediated mechanisms.

The presence of blister cells highly suggests G6PD deficiency since these are a result of oxidative damage which occurs with this condition. They would not be expected with any of the other causes of haemolysis.

G6PD deficiency

is correct. The presence of haemolysis with blister cells on the blood film is highly suggestive of G6PD deficiency. Furthermore, several antimalarials (e.g. primaquine) are well-known precipitants of a haemolytic crisis in those with G6PD deficiency.

Auto-immune haemolytic anaemia

is incorrect. A positive DAT is associated with autoimmune haemolytic anaemia. However, it is important to remember that this is a non-specific test and can be positive due to a variety of other reasons. The presence of blister cells and exposure to primaquine favours the diagnosis of G6PD deficiency.

Hereditary spherocytosis

is incorrect. Although this condition can also present with haemolysis, one would expect to find spherocytes on the blood film.

Malaria

is incorrect. Although this remains within the differential diagnosis, the absence of malaria parasites on thick and thin blood films makes this an unlikely diagnosis.

Methemoglobinemia

is incorrect. Although methaemoglobinaemia can occur as a consequence of primaquine exposure, it would present with hypoxia, cyanosis, and cardiovascular instability rather than anaemia.

question_text:
A 60-year-old man with a medical history of Hodgkin's disease underwent an emergency appendectomy. He received 4 units of packed red blood cells during the procedure. On the 14th postoperative day, he returned complaining of abdominal pain, fever and diarrhoea. Physical examination showed a maculopapular rash on his trunk, scleral icterus, and hepatomegaly. Laboratory studies showed.


Hb	90 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	110 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	2.2 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Total Bilirubin	9 mg/dL	(0.1 - 1.2)
Alanine transaminase	2000 U/L	(7-56)
Aspartate transaminase	1800 U/L	(10-40)


Hepatitis A IgM	Negative
Hepatitis B RNA	Negative
Hepatitis C IgM	Negative

Which of the following measures could have prevented the development of this condition?
options_json: ["Irradiation of blood products", "Screening for hepatitis", "Using blood only from a family member", "Using fresh blood for transfusion", "Using leucocyte depleted blood products"]
explanation_text:
Irradiated blood products are used to avoid transfusion-associated graft versus host disease

This patient is having transfusion-associated graft versus host disease (TA-GvHD), which is a rare but lethal transfusion complication. The pathology of this condition is the failure of the recipient to eliminate donor-derived T-cells, which then recognize HLA class II in recipient and cause excessive release of cytokines.

There are three major risk factors for this condition.

1.       Volume and age of transfused blood.

2.       Depressed immune function especially, that involving T-cells and cell-mediated immunity. Hodgkin's disease is a risk factor which this patient has.

3.       Similar HLA haplotype sharing.

TA-GvHD is a delayed reaction that occurs 2-6 weeks after transfusion. The patient presents with diarrhoea, liver damage, and rash. Laboratory studies show pancytopenia. A biopsy of skin or bone marrow can be diagnostic. A biopsy specimen of the skin will show abundant necrotic keratinocytes. Bone marrow shows marked hypocellularity with macrophage infiltration.

There is no treatment, so prevention by using gamma-irradiated blood products in high-risk patients is the key.

This patient has tested negative for viral hepatitis thereby screening for these would not have prevented his condition.

Since similar HLA haplotype sharing is a risk factor, receiving blood from relatives increases the risk of TA-GvHD. But do note that it can occur with a transfusion from unrelated individuals also.

Using fresh blood is not the correct answer as the number of T-cells in the blood reduces drastically over time, so the use of recently drawn blood increases the risk of TA-GvHD.

Leucodepletion reduces the number of leucocytes in the blood to less than 5 million/unit. Leucodepletion cannot prevent TA-GvHD, as current technology is not adequate and probably because the critical number of T-cells required to cause TA-GvHD may be small.

question_text:
A 23-year-old male medical student presents with swollen lips for the last 20 minutes. He is concerned he is having an anaphylactoid reaction. Upon further questioning, he ate some strawberries directly before the swelling began.

He has got this same reaction a dozen times before with strawberries and it has always settled after taking an antihistamine. He has not taken an antihistamine this time as he had run out. There is no vomiting or diarrhoea.

He has a past medical history of well-controlled asthma on salbutamol inhalers and hay fever in the spring months well-controlled with antihistamines. There is no family history of atopy.

On examination his lips are erythematous and mildly swollen. There is no swelling or redness elsewhere and he can talk to you in full sentences and is not short of breath. All his observations are within normal limits.

He is given an antihistamine and kept in for observation.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
options_json: ["Anaphylaxis", "Hay fever", "Oral allergy syndrome", "Strawberry allergy", "C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency"]
explanation_text:
Oral allergy syndrome is strongly linked with pollen allergies and presents with seasonal variation

Oral allergy syndrome (OAS) is the correct option as the case above describes the typical history of pollen-food allergy, with the raw strawberries being coated with the allergen. This is most commonly associated with birch pollen allergy as described above with the 'springtime hay fever'. OAS is the most likely choice in this case due to the red and swollen lips triggered by raw strawberries and the previous history of symptoms resolving with antihistamines.

Anaphylaxis is incorrect as there is no wheezing, hives or hypotension described in this case.

Hay fever is incorrect as this is not a reaction to pollen in the air, but more localised to the mouth from eating of the strawberries.

Strawberry allergy is incorrect as the symptoms are localised as in OAS, whereas with specific food allergy you would expect systemic symptoms such as vomiting and diarrhoea. Moreover, anaphylaxis is a more common complication of food allergy compared to OAS.

C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency is incorrect as there is no family history reported in this case and the swelling in this condition has an obvious trigger which would not be present in the deficiency syndrome. The presentation is also different, with angioedema and abdominal pain most commonly.

question_text:
A 25-year-old man is admitted to the Haematology ward, after experiencing fever and rigors at home. He had completed his first cycle of ABVD chemotherapy for Hodgkin's lymphoma the week before.

He is taking prophylactic co-trimoxazole and aciclovir, and has been doing so since starting chemotherapy. Asides from this, he takes no regular medications and has no known drug allergies.

On initial assessment, his observations are temperature 38.1ºC, respiratory rate 24/minute, heart rate 94 beats per minute, oxygen saturations 96% on room air and blood pressure 116/72mmHg.

His blood results are shown below:



Hb	140 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	170 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	1.3 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Neuts	0.4 * 109/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Lymphs	0.6 * 109/L	(1.0 - 3.5)
Mono	0.2 * 109/L	(0.2 - 0.8)
Eosin	0.1 * 109/L	(0.0 - 0.4)



Na+	138 mmol/L	(135 - 145)
K+	3.9 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Bicarbonate	24 mmol/L	(22 - 29)
Urea	4.0 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	70 µmol/L	(55 - 120)

Which of the following antimicrobial regimens should be started, pending further information from blood culture results?
options_json: ["Intravenous co-amoxiclav", "Intravenous vancomycin, gentamicin and metronidazole", "Intravenous piperacillin/tazobactam", "Intravenous meropenem", "Intravenous piperacillin/tazobactam and ambisome"]
explanation_text:
Piperacillin with tazobactam (Tazocin) is the empirical antibiotic of choice for neutropenic sepsis

This patient has suspected neutropenic sepsis. Intravenous co-amoxiclav by itself would not provide sufficiently broad cover for gram negative organisms, and those with inducible beta-lactamase activity, and is therefore not appropriate as an empirical antibiotic for neutropenic patients.

Intravenous vancomycin, gentamicin and metronidazole would be an appropriate empirical regimen for this patient were they to have a severe penicillin allergy.

Intravenous piperacillin/tazobactam is the empirical antibiotic of choice for neutropenic sepsis, in the absence of contraindications.

Intravenous meropenem would would be an appropriate empirical regimen for this patient were they to have a mild penicillin allergy, but is not first line in this scenario. The patient may also have their antibiotic therapy escalated to meropenem, were they to remain febrile after 48 hours.

The Christie guidelines do not recommend initiating anti-fungal therapy in patients presenting with neutropenic sepsis. Were the patient to remain febrile after several days of broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy, it would be appropriate to consider anti-fungal therapy depending on radiological or biochemical evidence.

question_text:
A 32-year-old presents with a 4-day history of lower abdominal pain with vaginal discharge. She reports she was 8 weeks pregnant but had an assumed miscarriage just prior to the onset of her symptoms.

On exam, she appears unwell, with several bruises all over her body as well as bleeding from her nose and mouth. Her lower abdomen is tender and there is foul-smelling discharge per vagina. She is tachycardia, febrile and hypotensive.

Bloods:


Haemoglobin	100 g/L	130-180
White cell count	16Ã—109/L	4.0-11.0 Ã—109
Platelets	60 Ã—109/L	150-400/L
Active Partial thromboplastin time (APTT)	60 seconds	25-40
Prothrombin time (PT)	18 seconds	11-15
Fibrinogen	1.8 g/L	2-4 g/L

Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following would be most present on blood film?
options_json: ["Rouleaux", "Spherocytes", "Howell-Jolly body", "Schistocytes", "Target cells"]
explanation_text:
DIC is associated with schistocytes due to microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia

This patients presentation and blood investigation are in keeping with disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), most likely due to retained products of conception resulting in sepsis. In DIC the haemostasis process between coagulation and fibrinolysis is disrupted resulting in both widespread clottings as well as bleeding. Patient present with low platelets, low fibrinogen, with a raised PT, APPT and INR. In DIC the endothelial layers of the small vessels are damaged resulting in fibrin deposits and platelet aggregation. Red blood cells are damaged as they flow through these vessels resulting in microangiopathic hemolytic anaemia (MAHA) and fragments of cells or schistocytes can be seen on blood film.

Rouleaux are a result of red blood cells stacking on top of each other, a phenomenon that normally occurs when plasma protein concentration is high. They are caused by an increase in cathodal proteins such as immunoglobulins and fibrinogen and therefore are seen in inflammation and infective conditions as well as myeloma and macroglobulinemias. As fibrinogen levels are low in DIC there are not normally seen in the condition.

Spherocytes are, as the name suggested, sphere-shaped red blood cells instead of the normal, bi-concaved shape disks. They are most commonly seen in hereditary spherocytosis, due to gene mutations affecting the proteins which control erythrocyte membrane formation. Spherocytes can be seen in haemolytic anaemia however they are mainly a result of autoimmune haemolytic diseases. In DIC a MAHA process occurs which results in anaemia, and therefore the presents of schistocytes, and not an autoimmune haemolytic process.

Howell-Jolly bodies are the finding of red blood cell nuclear proteins with red blood cells which are normally removed by the spleen. As such Howell-Jolly bodies are seen in patients who have undergone splenectomy or have function asplenia (i.e from sickle cell disease).

Target cells, also known as codocytes, are red blood cells that have a 'bullseye' like appearance with haemoglobin concentrated in the centre and on the periphery with a colourless/pallor area in between the two. Target cells are due to the surface of the red cell increasing disproportionately to its volume and are seen in several conditions including chronic liver disease, sickle cell disease, thalassaemia and post-splenectomy. Target cells are not associated with DIC.

question_text:
A 47-year-old man from northern India presented with a 3-day history of fever with severely painful and cold extremities. He has a background of alcohol dependence. No pulse could be palpable on examination. A diagnosis of symmetrical peripheral gangrene was made.

During the aetiological evaluation, routine blood tests along with thick and thin films were sent.


Hb	120 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Platelets	140 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	11 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)


ESR	70 mm/hr	Men: < (age / 2)
Prothrombin time (PT)	25 secs	(10-14 secs)
Activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT)	40 secs	(25-35 secs)
Fibrinogen	1 g/L	(2 - 4)
D-Dimer	3,000 ng/mL	(< 400)
Ferritin	500 ng/mL	(20 - 230)


Thick and thin film	Pending
Peripheral smear	Schistocytes / helmet cells

What is the diagnosis based on the results?
options_json: ["Acute leukaemia", "Disseminated intravascular coagulation", "Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia", "Viral haemorrhagic fever", "Vitamin B12 deficiency"]
explanation_text:
DIC is associated with schistocytes due to microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia

Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is associated with a number of clinical conditions; generally involving activation of systemic inflammation. The common underlying conditions include sepsis, trauma, malignancies, transfusion reactions, acute pancreatitis, obstetric complications, and severe toxic reactions.

Diagnosis of DIC involves a combination of laboratory tests and clinical evaluation. Laboratory findings suggestive of DIC include a low platelet count, elevated D-dimer concentration, decreased fibrinogen concentration, and prolongation of clotting times such as prothrombin time (PT).

When assessing blood films in these patients, irregular shapes can appear such as 'helmet' cells. Such fragmented red blood cells are referred to as 'schistocytes' and they are indicative of microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (MAHA) or other causes of intravascular haemolysis. This finding is typical for disseminated intravascular coagulopathy (DIC).

Acute leukaemia can reveal too many or too few white blood cells, not enough red blood cells, and not enough platelets. A blood test may also show the presence of blast cells which are immature cells normally found in the bone marrow. Given the normal white blood cell count, the diagnosis of acute leukaemia is unlikely.

Viral haemorrhagic fever (VHF) is a severe, multi-organ disease in which the vascular system is damaged and the body's ability to regulate itself is impaired which can result in DIC. Symptoms of VHF usually include fever but the absence of any headache, myalgia, diarrhoea, vomiting and haemorrhage makes this diagnosis unlikely.

Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) is thrombocytopenia (a low platelet count) that occurs due to the administration of various forms of heparin, an anticoagulant. HIT predisposes to thrombosis because platelets release microparticles that activate thrombin, resulting in thrombosis. The absence of any history of heparin use makes this diagnosis incorrect.

Vitamin B12 deficiency may present as pseudo-thrombotic microangiopathy. Pseudo-thrombotic microangiopathy is anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and schistocytes caused by vitamin B12 deficiency. It usually results in elevated lactate dehydrogenase, reticulocyte count, bilirubin, and platelet count making the diagnosis incorrect here.

question_text:
A 75-year-old man is referred to the haematology department with unexplained anaemia and fatigue. He has no past medical history or history of travel.

On examination, the spleen is palpable and crosses the midline of the abdomen.


Hb	82 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
MCV	101 fL	(80-98)
Platelets	489 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	12.2 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Neuts	10.0 * 109/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Lymphs	2.2 * 109/L	(1.0 - 3.5)
Vitamin B12	250 pg/ml	(180 - 1000)
Folate	5.2 ng/ml	(>4.0)
Na+	138 mmol/L	(135 - 145)
K+	4.2 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Urea	5.4 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	88 µmol/L	(55 - 120)

A bone marrow biopsy fails to obtain a sample.

What blood film finding is most specific for the likely diagnosis?
options_json: ["Auer rods", "Hypersegmented neutrophils", "Schistocytes", "Smudge cells", "Tear-drop poikilocytes"]
explanation_text:
Myelofibrosis is associated with 'tear drop' poikilocytes on blood film

Tear-drop poikilocytes

is correct. The patient presents with fatigue, anaemia with mild macrocytosis and massive splenomegaly (spleen crosses the midline). There is a broad differential for this appearance including haematological and infective causes but the failure to obtain a bone marrow aspirate ('dry tap') suggests myelofibrosis as the cause.

Auer rods

is incorrect. This appearance is found in acute leukaemias such as acute myeloid leukaemia and acute promyelocytic leukemia. Enlargement of the spleen may occur in myeloid leukaemias although it is mainly mild and asymptomatic rather than massive as seen in myelofibrosis. You would not expect the bone marrow biopsy to be a dry tap in acute myeloid leukaemia and it would typically demonstrate myeloblasts.

Hyper-segmented neutrophils

is incorrect. Neutrophil hypersegmentation is defined as the presence of neutrophils whose nuclei have six or more lobes or the presence of more than 3% of neutrophils with >= five nuclear lobes. This is typical of the megaloblastic anaemia associated with B12/folate deficiency. This is incorrect as the B12 and folate levels are normal. It is less commonly seen in myelofibrosis but not as characteristic as teardrop poikilocytes.

Schistocytes

is incorrect. This is a typical blood film finding in a patient with microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia. However, this is more commonly associated with thrombocytopenia rather than thrombocytosis and massive splenomegaly is not a feature.

Smudge cells

is incorrect. This is the typical blood film appearance in chronic lymphocytic leukaemia. You would expect a very elevated lymphocyte count in this condition and it is normal in this case making the diagnosis unlikely.

question_text: What are the most common types of transformations seen in patients with polycythaemia vera?
options_json: ["Myelodysplasia + chronic myeloid leukaemia", "Myelofibrosis + chronic myeloid leukaemia", "Myelodysplasia + myelofibrosis", "Myelofibrosis + acute myeloid leukaemia", "Myelodysplasia + acute myeloid leukaemia"]
explanation_text:
Polycythaemia rubra vera - around 5-15% progress to myelofibrosis or AML

The correct answer is

Myelofibrosis + acute myeloid leukaemia

. Polycythaemia vera (PV) is a chronic myeloproliferative neoplasm characterised by the clonal proliferation of erythroid, megakaryocytic and granulocytic elements in the bone marrow. The most common transformation seen in patients with PV are myelofibrosis (MF) and acute myeloid leukaemia (AML). MF is a disorder of the bone marrow, in which the marrow gets replaced by fibrous (scar) tissue. AML is a type of cancer in which the bone marrow makes abnormal myeloblasts, red blood cells, or platelets.

Discussing each incorrect answer:

Myelodysplasia + chronic myeloid leukaemia

: This option is incorrect because although Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML) is also a type of myeloproliferative neoplasm like PV, it's not a common transformation seen in patients with PV. Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) are conditions that can occur when the blood-forming cells in the bone marrow become abnormal. However, MDS are not commonly associated with transformations from PV.

Myelofibrosis + chronic myeloid leukaemia

: As mentioned previously, CML isn't commonly associated with transformations from PV. While MF is indeed one of the two most common transformations seen in patients with PV, pairing it with CML makes this option incorrect.

Myelodysplasia + myelofibrosis

: Myelodysplasia isn't typically associated with transformations from PV. Although MF is one of the two most common transformations seen in patients with PV, pairing it with Myelodysplasia makes this option incorrect.

Myelodysplasia + acute myeloid leukaemia

: Even though AML is one of the two most common transformations seen in patients with PV, combining it with Myelodysplasia - which isn't typically associated with transformations from PV - makes this option incorrect.

question_text: Burkitt's lymphoma is associated with which one of the following genetic changes:
options_json: ["Cyclin D1-IGH gene translocation", "TEL-JAK2 gene translocation", "Bcl-2 gene translocation", "C-myc gene translocation", "BCR-Abl1 gene translocation"]
explanation_text:
Burkitt's lymphoma - c-myc gene translocation

The correct answer is

C-myc gene translocation

. Burkitt's lymphoma, a type of non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, is most commonly associated with a translocation involving the c-myc gene. This oncogene is usually located on chromosome 8, but in Burkitt's lymphoma, it typically undergoes a translocation to be juxtaposed with one of the immunoglobulin genes on chromosomes 2, 14 or 22. This leads to overexpression of the c-myc protein, which promotes cell growth and proliferation - key features of malignancy.

Cyclin D1-IGH gene translocation

is incorrect as this genetic alteration is most commonly associated with mantle cell lymphoma rather than Burkitt's lymphoma. The cyclin D1-IGH gene translocation results in overproduction of the cyclin D1 protein which promotes cell cycle progression and thus contributes to unregulated cell growth.

TEL-JAK2 gene translocation

is also incorrect. This genetic change has been linked to chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML) and acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL), but not Burkitt's lymphoma. The TEL-JAK2 fusion protein has constitutive tyrosine kinase activity that leads to continuous cell signalling for growth and division.

The option

Bcl-2 gene translocation

is not correct either. While Bcl-2 is an oncogene involved in several types of cancer by inhibiting apoptosis or programmed cell death, its translocation is specifically associated with follicular lymphomas rather than Burkitt's lymphoma.

Lastly,

BCR-Abl1 gene translocation

is incorrect because it's characteristic of chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML). It results in the production of a fusion protein with increased tyrosine kinase activity that stimulates uncontrolled cell proliferation.

question_text:
A 23-year-old woman is reviewed at the genetics clinic after a recent diagnosis of breast cancer. Her mother died at the age of 40 with osteosarcoma, her maternal aunt was diagnosed with breast cancer at the age of 28.

Which of the following is most likely to be affected?
options_json: ["HER2/Neu", "p53", "APC", "HRas", "BRCA 1"]
explanation_text:
Li-Fraumeni syndrome is caused by germline mutations to p53 tumour suppressor gene

The clinical diagnosis of Li-Fraumeni syndrome relies on personal and family history of associated malignancies. The diagnosis of breast cancer in this patient and her aunt, as well as a diagnosis of sarcoma in a first-degree relative strongly points to Li-Fraumeni syndrome. Li-Fraumeni syndrome is caused by germline mutations to the p53 tumour suppressor gene, therefore 2 is the correct answer.

HER2/Neu is associated with the development of several cancers including breast cancer. However, the history of sarcoma in a first-degree relative, in this case, makes p53 the most likely protein affected.

APC is associated with colorectal cancer.

HRas is mainly associated with bladder cancer.

BRCA 1 is associated with breast cancer as well as ovarian cancer. Again, the family history of sarcoma most implicates p53.

question_text:

Which of the following features is associated with a poor prognosis?

She has a past medical history of neuroendocrine cancer of the cervix treated with carboplatin and etoposide. Her last treatment was eight days ago. She has been feeling generally unwell with temperatures measured at home at 38.1C. Blood cultures are taken and she is started on neutropenic sepsis protocol. question_text: A 56 year old man is treated with doxorubicin for transition cell carcinoma of the bladder. Which one of the following adverse effects is most characteristically associated with this drug?
options_json: ["Ototoxicity", "Pulmonary fibrosis", "Peripheral neuropathy", "Cardiomyopathy", "Haemorrhagic cystitis"]
explanation_text:
Anthracyclines (e.g. doxorubicin) may cause cardiomyopathy

The correct answer is

Cardiomyopathy

. Doxorubicin, an anthracycline, is most characteristically associated with cardiotoxicity, which can manifest as cardiomyopathy. The mechanism of this adverse effect involves the generation of free radicals and oxidative stress that lead to myocardial damage. Cardiotoxicity may present either acutely during treatment, or chronically months to years after cessation of therapy. It is important to monitor patients receiving doxorubicin for signs of heart failure.

Ototoxicity

is incorrect because it's not typically associated with doxorubicin. This side effect is more commonly linked with aminoglycosides and platinum-based chemotherapy agents such as cisplatin.

Pulmonary fibrosis

is also incorrect as it's not a characteristic adverse effect of doxorubicin. Pulmonary fibrosis is more commonly seen with drugs like bleomycin and amiodarone.

The option

Peripheral neuropathy

while being a common side effect of many chemotherapeutic agents, particularly the taxanes and platinum-based drugs, it's not significantly associated with doxorubicin use.

Finally,

Haemorrhagic cystitis

is incorrect as well. This condition is specifically linked to cyclophosphamide and ifosfamide usage, rather than doxorubicin. It occurs due to toxic metabolites irritating the bladder lining leading to bleeding from the urinary tract.

question_text:
A 34-year-old woman presents to the ambulatory care service with a swollen left leg. This had come on suddenly over the past 12 hours. She denies any trauma to the leg before the onset of the swelling. She reports she is not on the oral contraceptive pill and has not been on any long-distance journeys recently. Her left leg is also painful and is preventing her from walking properly. The patient denies any shortness of breath.

Physical examination reveals a unilateral swollen leg on the left side. This is hot and tender to touch. Her left leg measures 35cm on the left and 30cm on the right side. Chest examination was unremarkable. USS doppler on the left leg confirms the presence of an occlusive thrombosis within the popliteal vein.

The patient notes that her mother suffered from similar symptoms in her adult life and also had to be hospitalized due to shortness of breath and chest pain. Her aunt also suffered from multiple deep vein thromboses and is on anticoagulation.

What is the most likely underlying abnormality causing her presenting complaint?
options_json: ["Activated protein C resistance", "Activated protein S resistance", "Deficiency in antithrombin III", "Deficiency in protein C", "Increased levels of prothrombin"]
explanation_text:
Activated protein C resistance (Factor V Leiden) is the most common inherited thrombophilia

The early age of onset of her deep vein thrombosis (DVT) along with the strong family history seen makes this a likely case of hereditary/inherited thrombophilia. This is a group of conditions that causes the patient to be predisposed to a state of increased coagulability. These will often present with DVTs or pulmonary embolism (PEs) in patients under the age of 40.

The most common cause of this is heterozygous factor V Leiden and is seen to be found in approximately 5-8% of the European population. It is an autosomal dominant condition that results in activated protein C resistance. Resistance to activated protein C prevents the coagulation cascade from deactivating, resulting in increased clot formation.

Deficiency in protein C results in protein C deficiency syndrome. It is less common that Factor V Leiden with a prevalence of approximately 0.2-0.5% in the Caucasian population.

Deficiency in protein S results in protein S deficiency. It is a rare condition with a prevalence of only 0.03-0.13% of the general population.

Deficiency in antithrombin III is caused by a mutation within the antithrombin gene. It is also rare with a prevalence of approximately 1%.

Elevated prothrombin levels are caused by mutations of the prothrombin gene. This is the 2nd most common cause of inherited thrombophilia after Factor V Leiden, making this an incorrect answer.
