question_text:
A 31-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with facial swelling and difficulty breathing. This is her fourth episode of this within the last 2 years, and has previously not been helped by IM adrenaline, but rather has self-resolved within hours/days.

After the attack has subsided, you undertake some blood tests which confirm the diagnosis of hereditary angioedema. She is concerned as she plans to become pregnant, and wants to know what the risk of her passing the condition onto her children is.

What are the chances that a child of hers will be affected by this condition?
options_json: ["0%", "25%", "50%", "50% if the child is male, 0% if the child is female", "100% regardless of the sex of the child"]
explanation_text:
Hereditary angioedema is autosomal dominant

As an autosomal dominant condition, parents with hereditary angioedema have a 50% chance of passing on the condition.

0% is the likelihood of a carrier of an autosomal recessive condition having a child affected by the condition, assuming their partner is not a carrier. It is also the likelihood of a man passing on an x-linked condition to a male offspring.

25% is the likelihood of two carriers of an autosomal recessive condition having a child who is affected by the condition.

50% if the child is male, 0% if the child is female is the likelihood of a female carrier passing on an x-linked recessive condition.

100% is the likelihood of two individuals affected by an autosomal recessive condition having a child who is affected.

question_text:
A 28-year-old woman presents to the haematology clinic with fatigue and intermittent jaundice. She has a family history of similar symptoms. On examination, she has mild jaundice and splenomegaly. Blood tests show:


Hb	98 g/L	Female: (115-160)
MCV	82 fL	(80-100)
MCHC	38 g/dL	(32-36)
Reticulocytes	8%	(0.5-2.5)
Bilirubin	42 μmol/L	(3-17)
LDH	380 U/L	(135-225)

Blood film shows spherocytes. Which test is most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis?
options_json: ["Osmotic fragility test", "EMA binding test", "Direct antiglobulin test", "G6PD enzyme assay", "Ham's acidified serum test"]
explanation_text:
The EMA binding test should be used to diagnose hereditary spherocytosis - the osmotic fragility test is no longer widely used

EMA binding test

is the most appropriate test to confirm hereditary spherocytosis (HS) in this patient. The clinical presentation with fatigue, jaundice, splenomegaly, and a family history of similar symptoms is highly suggestive of HS. The laboratory findings support this with anaemia, elevated MCHC (38 g/dL), increased reticulocytes (8%), elevated bilirubin and LDH indicating haemolysis, and spherocytes on blood film. According to the British Journal of Haematology guidelines, when the diagnosis is equivocal, the EMA binding test is recommended. This test measures the binding of eosin-5-maleimide to band 3 protein in the red cell membrane, which is reduced in HS due to cytoskeletal defects. It has high sensitivity (92-99%) and specificity (95-99%) for HS and has largely replaced older tests in clinical practice.

Osmotic fragility test

was historically used to diagnose HS but is no longer recommended due to its poor sensitivity and specificity. It measures the resistance of red cells to haemolysis in solutions of decreasing osmolarity. While spherocytes typically show increased osmotic fragility, this test is labour-intensive, poorly standardised, and can give false-positive and false-negative results. Modern guidelines no longer recommend it as a first-line investigation for suspected HS.

Direct antiglobulin test (DAT)

is used to detect antibodies or complement bound to the surface of red blood cells, which would indicate immune-mediated haemolysis such as autoimmune haemolytic anaemia. This patient's presentation with family history and spherocytes is more consistent with a hereditary membrane defect rather than an immune process. A negative DAT would be expected in HS, making this test useful to exclude immune haemolysis but not to confirm HS.

G6PD enzyme assay

measures glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase activity and is used to diagnose G6PD deficiency, an X-linked disorder primarily affecting males of African, Mediterranean, or Asian descent. G6PD deficiency typically causes episodic haemolysis triggered by oxidative stress (infections, certain drugs, fava beans) rather than chronic haemolysis. The blood film would show bite cells or blister cells rather than spherocytes, making this test inappropriate for this case.

Ham's acidified serum test

is used to diagnose paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (PNH), a rare acquired disorder caused by a somatic mutation in the PIGA gene. PNH is characterised by complement-mediated intravascular haemolysis, venous thrombosis, and cytopenias. The absence of thrombotic events and the presence of spherocytes on blood film make PNH unlikely in this case. Flow cytometry for CD55 and CD59 has largely replaced Ham's test for diagnosing PNH.

question_text:
A 72-year-old man is referred to the haematology clinic complaining of lethargy and a rapidly growing lump in his right armpit. After a PET-CT and an excisional biopsy, he is diagnosed with diffuse large B cell lymphoma. He is due to start treatment with a monoclonal antibody that targets CD20.

What should the patient be screened for prior to his first infusion?
options_json: ["Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)", "Hepatitis B", "Hepatitis C", "Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML)", "Tuberculosis"]
explanation_text:
Patients starting rituximab should be screened for hepatitis B before starting treatment

The drug in question is rituximab which is a chimeric monoclonal antibody against CD20 which is expressed on B lymphocytes. Other anti-CD20 monoclonal antibodies have been developed but rituximab is currently the standard one used for diffuse large B cell lymphoma. The correct answer is

hepatitis B

as it is the only disease that NICE states patients should be routinely screened for prior to starting rituximab. This is because of a risk of reactivation of the virus.

Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)

is not routinely tested for prior to starting rituximab, therefore this answer is incorrect. It is however linked to the development of Hodgkin's lymphoma, with around 40% of UK cases thought to be due to EBV.

Although there is also a theoretical risk of

hepatitis C

virus reactivation, research has not found evidence of this in practice. Therefore,  routine screening is not currently advised by NICE. Interestingly, hepatitis C virus is itself linked to the development of some B cell lymphoproliferative disorders, such as cryoglobulinaemia, which rituximab is used to treat.

Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy

is screened for prior to commencing natalizumab (a monoclonal antibody that targets α4-integrin) but is not routinely screened for in patients starting rituximab. The risk of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (caused by reactivation of the JC virus) is several times greater in patients receiving natalizumab than those receiving rituximab treatment. Natalizumab is used for the treatment of multiple sclerosis and Crohn's disease.

Whilst

tuberculosis

is screened for in patients starting infliximab (a monoclonal antibody targeting TNFα), routine screening is not currently advised by NICE for patients commencing rituximab treatment. Interestingly, the risk of tuberculosis reactivation is higher in infliximab than other anti-TNFα drugs such as etanercept, possibly due to infliximab binding more strongly to TNFα and also having a longer duration of action than etanercept.

question_text:
A 28-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a two-week history of lethargy and gingival bleeding. He has no significant past medical history. On examination, he is pale, appears unwell, and there is evidence of gingival bleeding.


Hb	66 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	22 * 10 9/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	1.4 * 10 9/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
D-dimer	8000 ng/ml	(< 500)
Prothrombin time	32 seconds	(11-12.5)
Fibrinogen	89 mg/dl	(150-400)


Blood film	Auer rods

What is the most appropriate initial treatment for this patient's likely diagnosis?
options_json: ["All-trans retinoic acid (ATRA)", "Anticoagulation", "Daunorubicin with cytarabine", "Leukapharesis", "Tranexamic acid"]
explanation_text:
APML is treated with all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) to force immature granulocytes into maturation to resolve a blast crisis prior to more definitive chemotherapy

All-trans retinoic acid (ATRA)

is the correct answer. The patient presents with a subacute history of lethargy and gingival bleeding, combined with pancytopenia, which raises the suspicion of a haematological malignancy. Additionally, there is evidence of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), indicated by an elevated d-dimer level, reduced fibrinogen, and an increased prothrombin time. There is a score that quantifies the risk of DIC known as the  ISTH Criteria for Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC). Acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APML) uniquely presents with DIC and is the likely diagnosis here. Auer rods, frequently observed on peripheral blood smears in such cases, were also noted in this patient. The most urgent treatment involves the administration of all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) to induce the maturation of immature granulocytes and resolve a blast crisis before commencing definitive chemotherapy.

Anticoagulation

is incorrect. Current guidelines indicate that the role of heparin, tranexamic acid or other anticoagulant or antifibrinolytic therapies in this setting is uncertain; therefore, their use outside clinical trials is not recommended.

Daunorubicin with cytarabine

is incorrect. While this regimen represents standard cytoreductive chemotherapy for acute myeloid leukaemia, its initiation can be postponed until after genetic confirmation in patients with white blood cell counts below 10 × 10⁹/L. In contrast, ATRA must be initiated immediately based solely on clinical suspicion.

Leukapharesis

is incorrect. This procedure—aimed at reducing white blood cell counts—is no longer recommended as a 1st line option due to the associated risk of triggering fatal haemorrhage. It may still be considered in certain clinical scenarios such as symptomatic hyperleukocytosis or leukostasis.

Tranexamic acid

is incorrect as no evidence supports its efficacy in alleviating bleeding abnormalities related to this condition; hence, it should not be utilised in management.

question_text: A patient with testicular cancer is started on cisplatin therapy. Which of the following side-effects is most characteristically associated with cisplatin?
options_json: ["Liver cirrhosis", "Alopecia", "Peripheral neuropathy", "Haemorrhagic cystitis", "Cardiomyopathy"]
explanation_text:
Cisplatin may cause peripheral neuropathy

The correct answer is

Peripheral neuropathy

. Cisplatin, a platinum-containing chemotherapeutic agent, is widely used in the treatment of numerous malignancies including testicular cancer. Its toxicity profile includes a well-characterised dose-dependent peripheral neuropathy. This presents as sensory symptoms beginning in the distal extremities and may be associated with motor weakness and autonomic dysfunction if severe. The pathophysiology involves damage to dorsal root ganglia neurons, leading to axonal degeneration.

Liver cirrhosis

is not typically associated with cisplatin therapy. Liver toxicity can occur with some chemotherapy agents, but it's more commonly linked to drugs like methotrexate or azathioprine rather than cisplatin.

Alopecia

, while a common side-effect of many chemotherapeutic agents, is not characteristically associated with cisplatin. It can occur but is less common compared to other drugs such as doxorubicin or cyclophosphamide.

Haemorrhagic cystitis

is a known complication of some chemotherapeutic agents, particularly cyclophosphamide and ifosfamide due to their toxic metabolite acrolein. It is not usually seen with cisplatin use.

Lastly,

Cardiomyopathy

is also not typically associated with cisplatin therapy. Anthracyclines like doxorubicin are much more frequently implicated in chemotherapy-induced cardiotoxicity which can lead to cardiomyopathy.

A 23-year-old patient is referred to the department of immunology with recurrent chest infections. He has no significant past medical history otherwise.

The examination is unremarkable.

Blood tests:


IgA	0.1 g/L	(0.6-5.00)
IgG	3.1 g/L	(6.0-16.6)
IgM	0.24 g/L	(0.53 - 2.47)
B cells	250 cells/µL	(100-500)

What is the likely diagnosis?
options_json: ["Chediak-Higashi syndrome", "Common variable immunodeficiency", "Severe combined immunodeficiency", "Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome", "X-linked congenital agammaglobulinaemia"]
explanation_text:
Common variable immunodeficiency -  low antibody levels, specifically in immunoglobulin types IgG, IgM and IgA. → recurrent chest and other infections

Common variable immunodeficiency

is correct. This typically presents with recurrent chest infections and hypogammaglobulinemia.

Chediak-Higashi syndrome

is incorrect. This immune deficiency syndrome is characterized by partial albinism and peripheral neuropathy, which are not present here.

Severe combined immunodeficiency

is incorrect. This typically presents with recurrent viral and bacterial infections in the infant period and it is unlikely the patient would only present now for medical attention. It is also associated with low levels of immunoglobulins.

Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome

is incorrect. This is caused by a defect in the WASP gene. This causes recurrent bacterial infections but is also typically associated with eczema and thrombocytopenia, which are absent here.

X-linked congenital agammaglobulinaemia

is incorrect. This can be difficult to differentiate clinically from CVID but typically B cells are normal in CVID and absent in this condition.

question_text:
A 65-year-old man presents to the emergency department with gingival bleeding, confusion, and fluctuating levels of consciousness. He was diagnosed with polycythaemia rubra vera one month ago and recently commenced chemotherapy. Examination reveals a petechial rash on his chest and upper arms. He has marked hepatosplenomegaly without tenderness or ascites.

The following blood test results are obtained:


Platelets	43 * 10 9/L	(150 - 400)
Prothrombin time (PT)	22 secs	(10-14 secs)
Activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT)	41 secs	(25-35 secs)

What is the most likely cause of this patient's current symptoms?
options_json: ["Acute promyelocytic leukaemia", "Hepatic vein thrombosis", "Hyperviscosity syndrome", "Myelofibrosis", "Tumour lysis syndrome"]
explanation_text:
Polycythaemia rubra vera - around 5-15% progress to myelofibrosis or AML

The patient has manifested signs indicative of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), as evidenced by gingival bleeding and fluctuating levels of consciousness, which may suggest microemboli. Blood test results support the diagnosis of DIC, demonstrating low platelet counts alongside prolonged prothrombin time (PT) and activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT). It is recognised that 5-15% of individuals with polycythaemia vera progress to acute myeloid leukaemia (AML), with an increased risk coinciding with the initiation of chemotherapy.

Acute promyelocytic leukaemia

, a variant of AML, characteristically presents with DIC, rendering it the most appropriate diagnosis in this scenario.

Hepatic vein thrombosis

, also known as Budd-Chiari syndrome, can arise as a complication of polycythaemia vera but would typically manifest with symptoms such as abdominal pain and ascites; these are not present in this patient. Budd-Chiari syndrome may lead to DIC but in this case, AML is more likely.

Hyperviscosity syndrome

is associated with polycythaemia vera but does not typically result in DIC. Common presentations include headaches, spontaneous mucosal bleeding, and visual disturbances.

Myelofibrosis

, another potential sequela of polycythaemia vera affecting 5-15% of patients, usually presents more insidiously with symptoms such as bone pain, fatigue, fever, weight loss, easy bruising and bleeding, along with night sweats'none of which are described in this case. Myelofibrosis infrequently leads to DIC and thus is less likely than acute promyelocytic leukaemia given the current clinical picture.

Tumour lysis syndrome

is an uncommon complication in the context of polycythaemia vera and generally presents with clinical features that are not reported in this case such as nausea, vomiting, haematuria, loin pain and dyspnoea. This syndrome arises when rapid destruction of a large number of cancer cells releases their contents into the bloodstream leading to electrolyte imbalances including hyperphosphataemia, hypocalcaemia and hyperuricaemia. Tumour lysis syndrome does not typically present with DIC.

question_text:
You see a 24-year-old patient in the haematology clinic after referral by her general practitioner for thrombocytopaenia. She feels generally well in herself except for increased fatigue over the last 6 months, and more recently epistaxis. Her episodes of epistaxis often last hours at a time.

She's becoming increasingly frustrated with these episodes of epistaxis as she is a carpenter and it ruins her projects. On examination, there is no evidence of ongoing bleeding during the clinic appointment.

Her platelet count today is:


Platelets	46 * 109/L	(150 - 400)

Which treatment option is most appropriate?
options_json: ["Anti-D immunoglobulin", "Platelet transfusion", "Observation", "Prednisolone", "Splenectomy"]
explanation_text:
First-line treatment for ITP is oral prednisolone

This patient's history is highly consistent with immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) in the absence of drug and infectious causes for thrombocytopenia.

In patients with a diagnosis of ITP first-line treatment varies depending on various factors, including platelet count on presentation and the presence of active bleeding.

Her platelets are over the commonly used cutoff for treatment of 30*10

9

/L, however, her frequent symptoms of prolonged bleeding, the impact on her life, and her injury-prone profession would warrant consideration to initiate treatment of the condition. In this scenario, due to the history of bleeding and high risk of bleeding, observation is an inappropriate answer.

The initial management of ITP is ordinarily high dose corticosteroids in the absence of contraindications. Consideration is later given to splenectomy and immunomodulatory drugs, such as mycophenolate if this fails. Usually, there is a response to steroids within 3 weeks of commencing corticosteroid therapy.

IVIg is an expensive and possibly risk-prone treatment and whilst it may be appropriate for some it is reserved for those in need of rapid improvement in platelet function or contraindications to corticosteroid therapy.

Anti-D immunoglobulin is also a possible therapy for ITP but is used less frequently than corticosteroids in the first instance due to its risk profile and the better availability and familiarity with corticosteroid use.

ITP is primarily a destructive pathology of platelets and as such platelet transfusion has little effect on disease course with short term (minutes to hours) benefits and significant risks involved, this is therefore not an appropriate option especially in haemodynamically stable patients.

A 65-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a one-week history of fatigue and shortness of breath. The examination was unremarkable. In particular, there is no evidence of bleeding on systematic inquiry or examination.

Blood results are as follows:


Hb	82 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Reticulocytes	442 * 109/L	(50-100)
Platelets	162 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	12.8 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)


Bilirubin	66 µmol/L	(3 - 17)
ALP	42 u/L	(30 - 100)
ALT	28 u/L	(3 - 40)
Î³GT	44 u/L	(8 - 60)
Albumin	36 g/L	(35 - 50)

What abnormality would be in keeping with the likely diagnosis?
options_json: ["Low ADAMTS13 level", "Low LDH", "Low haptoglobin", "Negative DAT", "Raised haptoglobin"]
explanation_text:
Haptoglobin binds to free haemoglobin

Anaemia with reticulocytosis is suggestive of haemolysis or bleeding. The markedly raised bilirubin with otherwise normal LFTs is more in keeping with haemolysis, however, it is important to remember that haemorrhage can also result in increased bilirubin levels. Haemolysis results in the release of free haemoglobin. Haptoglobin is produced in the liver, and its primary function is to bind to free haemoglobin. Therefore

low haptoglobins

is a key feature of haemolysis. It is important to remember that liver dysfunction can also result in low haptoglobins since they are produced by the liver.

Haemolysis is associated with a raised LDH (due to increased cell turnover), rather than a low

LDH

.

A positive DAT (rather than a

) is associated with autoimmune haemolytic anaemia. However, it is important to remember that there are a wide variety of causes of haemolysis including both immune and non-immune mediated mechanisms.

Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) can cause haemolysis as part of the microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia process, however, this condition would be associated with thrombocytopenia. A

A 66-year-old man is reviewed on the Medical Admissions Unit after noticing a new rash and joint pains. He also reveals that his fingers become painful in cold weather. He has a past medical history of Waldenstrom's macroglobulinaemia, for which he is not currently on any treatment.

On examination, there is a purpuric rash across both his calves. His wrists and knees are slightly tender on movement, but there is no objective joint swelling.

His blood test results are as follows:


Hb	138 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	180 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	4.8 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Na+	137 mmol/L	(135 - 145)
K+	4.4 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Urea	9.9 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	160 µmol/L	(55 - 120)


C4	low
Antinuclear antibodies (ANA)	negative

What is the most likely unifying diagnosis?
options_json: ["Systemic lupus erythematosus", "Type I cryoglobulinaemia", "Type II cryoglobulinaemia", "Type III cryoglobulinaemia", "Polyarteritis nodosa"]
explanation_text:
Raynaud's - Type I cryoglobulinaemia

This patient has cryoglobulinaemia - a condition characterised by reversibly precipitating immunoglobulins, which, in the case of type I cryoglobulinaemia, are secreted due to an underlying plasma cell dyscrasia or lymphoproliferative disorder. Features in this patient in keeping with a diagnosis of cryoglobulinaemia are his purpuric rash, arthralgia, a low C4 level, and renal impairment (Waldenstrom's macroglobulinaemia in isolation is much less likely to cause renal impairment than multiple myeloma). Features which clinch the diagnosis of type I cryoglobulinaemia include his history of Waldenstrom's, and the presence of Raynaud's phenomenon.

Many features of this patient's presentation can be seen in the context of SLE, including Raynaud's phenomenon, arthralgia, renal impairment, low complement levels and a vasculitic rash. However, as over 95% of patients with SLE test positive for ANA, SLE is much less likely in this patient. Additionally, new diagnoses of lupus in males in their sixties are epidemiologically rare.

Type II cryoglobulinaemia tends to be associated with hepatitis C, rheumatoid arthritis and other lymphomas, rather than Waldenstrom's, and is not associated with Raynaud's phenomenon.

Likewise, type III cryoglobulinaemia is less likely due to the presence of Raynaud's phenomenon and the underlying Waldenstrom's.

Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) can present with a vasculitic rash, renal impairment and arthralgia. For exam purposes, patients with PAN often present with testicular pain, a fever and a history of hepatitis B. PAN is less likely than type I cryoglobulinaemia in this patient due to the history of Raynaud's phenomenon and Waldenstrom's.

question_text: Which of the following is a cause of intravascular haemolysis?
options_json: ["Hereditary spherocytosis", "Sickle cell anaemia", "Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria", "Haemolytic disease of the newborn", "Warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia"]
explanation_text:
Intravascular haemolysis - paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria

The correct answer is

Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria

. This is a rare acquired clonal disorder caused by a somatic mutation in the PIGA gene in haematopoietic stem cells. The mutation leads to a deficiency of glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor proteins, including CD55 and CD59, which normally protect red blood cells from complement-mediated lysis. Without these protective proteins, red blood cells are susceptible to complement attack, resulting in intravascular haemolysis. This intravascular haemolysis is characterised by haemoglobinuria (especially noticeable in the morning urine due to increased complement activation during sleep), haemoglobinaemia, and elevated lactate dehydrogenase (LDH). Patients typically present with fatigue, thrombosis (particularly in unusual sites like hepatic or portal veins), and a high risk of developing aplastic anaemia or acute myeloid leukaemia.

Hereditary spherocytosis

is incorrect because it causes extravascular haemolysis, not intravascular haemolysis. This inherited disorder is characterised by defects in red cell membrane proteins (commonly spectrin, ankyrin, or band 3), resulting in spherical-shaped red cells with reduced deformability. These abnormal cells are trapped and destroyed in the spleen, leading to extravascular haemolysis. Laboratory findings include spherocytes on blood film, negative direct antiglobulin test, and increased osmotic fragility. The absence of haemoglobinuria and haemoglobinaemia distinguishes it from intravascular haemolysis.

Sickle cell anaemia

is incorrect as it primarily causes extravascular haemolysis. This inherited haemoglobinopathy results from a point mutation in the beta-globin gene, leading to the production of haemoglobin S. Under deoxygenated conditions, haemoglobin S polymerises, causing red cells to become sickle-shaped. These sickled cells are predominantly removed by the reticuloendothelial system in the liver and spleen, resulting in extravascular haemolysis. While some intravascular haemolysis can occur during severe crises, the primary mechanism is extravascular.

Haemolytic disease of the newborn

is incorrect because it causes extravascular haemolysis. This condition occurs when maternal IgG antibodies cross the placenta and bind to foetal red blood cell antigens, most commonly Rhesus D. The antibody-coated red cells are then removed by the foetal reticuloendothelial system, particularly in the spleen, causing extravascular haemolysis. This results in anaemia and hyperbilirubinaemia in the newborn, but not the features of intravascular haemolysis such as haemoglobinuria.

Warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia

is incorrect as it causes extravascular haemolysis. In this condition, IgG autoantibodies bind to red cell antigens at body temperature (37°C). These antibody-coated red cells are then recognised by macrophages in the spleen and liver via their Fc receptors, leading to phagocytosis and extravascular haemolysis. Laboratory findings include a positive direct antiglobulin test (Coombs test), spherocytes on blood film, and elevated indirect bilirubin, but not the hallmarks of intravascular haemolysis such as haemoglobinaemia or haemoglobinuria.

question_text:
A 33-year-old man with a known diagnosis of hereditary spherocytosis presents to the emergency department with weakness and lethargy. He recalls having a viral respiratory illness a week or so prior.

His disease is usually mild and he does not experience frequent crises.

On examination, he appears jaundiced.

His blood tests are shown below:


Hb	59 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	175 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	10.6 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Reticulocytes	10%	0.2-2.5
Bilirubin	46 µmol/L	(3 - 17)
ALP	44 u/L	(30 - 100)

Given the likely diagnosis, what is the most appropriate management?
options_json: ["Broad spectrum IV antibiotics", "IV methylprednisolone", "Oral prednisolone", "Supportive management", "Surgical referral for consideration of splenectomy"]
explanation_text:
Generally supportive treatment is given in the management of a patient in haemolytic crisis secondary to hereditary spherocytosis. I.e. folic acid, transfusion if symptomatic from anaemia. Steroids are not indicated

Supportive management

is correct. This is a patient with mild hereditary spherocytosis, but he is experiencing a haemolytic crisis likely triggered by a recent viral illness. The management of these crises is generally supportive, with blood transfusions if severely anaemic (there is no specific cut-off for transfusion in this patient group, but consideration must be given to the change in haemoglobin from baseline and the symptoms of anaemia).

Broad spectrum IV antibiotics

is incorrect. Antibiotics have no role in a haemolytic crisis of hereditary spherocytosis, which this patient is likely suffering from. The mainstay of treatment is supportive, with blood transfusions if the haemoglobin shows a significant drop from baseline.

IV methylprednisolone

is incorrect. This patient is suffering from a haemolytic crisis of his hereditary spherocytosis. Steroids are not indicated in the management of these crises; the treatment is supportive.

Oral prednisolone

is incorrect. This patient is suffering from a haemolytic crisis of his hereditary spherocytosis. Steroids are not indicated in the management of these crises; the treatment is supportive.

Surgical referral for consideration of splenectomy

is incorrect. This patient has mild hereditary spherocytosis and is suffering from a haemolytic crisis. The management of these crises is generally supportive. Splenectomy may form part of the long-term management of a patient with hereditary spherocytosis. Patients who may be considered for splenectomy include those with symptomatic anaemia, those who experience frequent haemolytic crises, and those requiring multiple transfusions.

question_text:
A 22-year-old woman presents in early pregnancy for booking bloods. She is normally fit and well. Her full blood count demonstrates the following:


Hb	100 g/L	Female: (110 - 160)
Mean cell volume (MCV)	60 fL	(80-100)
Platelets	170 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	6.0 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)

A subsequent blood film is otherwise unremarkable.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
options_json: ["Beta thalassemia trait", "Haemodilution in pregnancy", "Hereditary spherocytosis", "Iron deficiency anaemia", "Sideroblastic anaemia"]
explanation_text:
Disproportionate microcytic anaemia - think beta-thalassaemia trait

The correct answer is beta thalassemia trait. This causes marked microcytosis with mild anaemia due to reduced haemoglobin A synthesis.

Haemodilution in pregnancy can lead to a typically normocytic anaemia.

Patients with hereditary spherocytosis may have a normal or low MCV but it does not typically cause a significantly low MCV.

Iron deficiency anaemia causes a microcytic anaemia but the microcytosis in this case is more significant than expected for the degree of anaemia. Also, the blood film is unremarkable - in iron deficiency, one would often expect anisopoikilocytosis (variation in size and shape), hypochromia, and target cells.

In sideroblastic anaemia, there may be red cells of unequal size and abnormal shape. There is commonly basophilic stippling and target cells. The MCV may be decreased.

question_text:
A 76-year-old woman has presented to the emergency department due to persistent polydipsia and back pain of two months duration. She says she feels dehydrated, breathless and her hands hurt in the cold winter air.

She has a past medical history of monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS). Furthermore, the dermatologist presumed she had vascular purpura on her lower limbs.

On examination her hands are initially blue, they then become pale and finally red and painful.

Her blood results:


Hb	85 g/L	Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	390 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	9.8 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Na+	138 mmol/L	(135 - 145)
K+	5.1 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Calcium	3.1 mmol/L	(2.1-2.6)
Urea	9.6 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	180 µmol/L	(55 - 120)
CRP	28 mg/L	(< 5)

What is the most likely diagnosis?
options_json: ["Primary Raynaud's", "Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)", "Type I cryoglobulinaemia", "Type II cryoglobulinaemia", "Type III cryoglobulinaemia"]
explanation_text:
Raynaud's - Type I cryoglobulinaemia

Type I cryoglobulinaemia is the correct answer. This is because the patient has presented with the classical symptoms associated with multiple myeloma (Old CRAB mnemonic: >65 years old, hypercalcaemia with abdominal pain and dehydration, renal failure, anaemia and bone pain in her back) coupled with the secondary Raynaud's phenomenon evidenced by the hand symptoms/signs being indicative of the cryoglobulins which precipitate at cold temperatures. Type I is the only cryoglobulinaemia that presents with Raynaud's and is also most strongly associated with multiple myeloma out of the three types.

Type II cryoglobulinaemia is incorrect as this presents with the vascular purpura, arthralgia and renal impairment, but not the Raynaud's seen here. Moreover, these types are not typically associated with multiple myeloma.

Type III cryoglobulinaemia is incorrect as this presents with the above symptoms described in type II, but not Raynaud's and is not associated with myeloma.

Primary Raynaud's is an incorrect option because there is underlying pathophysiology (multiple myeloma), precipitating surplus immunoglobulins at low temperatures and causing the occlusion of small capillaries in the hands and leading to the Raynaud's.

SLE is incorrect as the symptoms fit best with a diagnosis of multiple myeloma. Even though SLE can present with Raynaud's and renal impairment, it does not typically cause hypercalcaemia.

question_text:
An 80-year-old woman is seen in GP due to weight loss, night sweats and fatigue over the preceding weeks. On examination, she is pale and palpation of her abdomen reveals hepatosplenomegaly. She has a past medical history of polycythaemia vera. A full blood count reveals pancytopaenia. Blood film shows a characteristic finding associated with the new condition.

What characteristic finding on blood film is most associated with this patient's new condition?
options_json: ["Heinz bodies", "Pencil poikilocytes", "Schistocytes", "Spherocytes", "Tear drop poikilocytes"]
explanation_text:
Myelofibrosis is associated with 'tear drop' poikilocytes on blood film

The condition being described is myelofibrosis. This patient is at particular risk of developing myelofibrosis: approximately 6-10% of patients with polycythaemia vera develop myelofibrosis due to marrow exhaustion.

Myelofibrosis is a myeloproliferative disorder thought to be caused by hyperplasia of abnormal megakaryocytes. Bone marrow does not produce the normal range of mature cells, leading to anaemia and eventually pancytopaenia (note early in the disease high WBC and platelet counts are often seen). Haematopoiesis develops in the liver and spleen resulting in organomegaly.

The characteristic blood film finding in myelofibrosis is

tear drop poikilocytes

. This is a result of extramedullary haematopoiesis (mainly splenic), producing aberrantly shaped red blood cells.

Pencil poikilocytes

are associated with iron-deficiency anaemia. While the patient in this scenario has anaemia, this is a result of marrow failure rather than iron deficiency so they are unlikely have have pencil poikilocytes.

Schistocytes

are associated with haemolytic anaemias. They are fragmented red blood cells, formed through mechanical damage in the circulation; the most common causes are mechanical heart valves, haemolytic anaemias and microangiopathic diseases such as DIC. There is no mention that this patient has a mechanical heart valve. While the patient has hepatosplenomegaly, it is unlikely she has haemolytic anaemia given she is not jaundiced.

Spherocytes

are associated with hereditary spherocytosis and immune-mediated haemolytic anaemias. Spherocytes are broken down by the spleen, leading to splenomegaly and anaemia. While this patient has splenomegaly, this is secondary to extramedullary haematopoiesis rather than excessive splenic consumption.

Heinz bodies

are associated with G6PD deficiency. Heinz bodies are formed through oxidative damage to haemoglobin molecules, usually through inherited mutations or drug administration. Heinz body anaemia can occur as these damaged cells are removed from the circulation by the spleen. In this scenario, the patient has anaemia but this is due to marrow failure; there is no mention of any conditions in the stem that suggest the presence of Heinz bodies. The most common genetic mutation in myelofibrosis is JAK2, but this is not associated with Heinz body formation.

question_text:
A 26-year-old medical student presents in May with nasal congestion and swelling of lips and tongue. Upon further questioning, he has consumed some uncooked pears 10 minutes ago. He often gets nasal congestion in the spring months in England, but has never noticed any swelling in his lips and tongue before.

When asked about family history he recalls his father suffers from a condition where he gets sporadic peri-orbital swelling and abdominal pains.

On examination: mild erythema and swelling of his tongue and lips, no erythema or hives noted elsewhere and no wheezing upon auscultation of his chest. All his routine observations are within normal range.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
options_json: ["Allergic contact dermatitis", "Food allergy", "Idiopathic urticaria", "Oral allergy syndrome", "C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency"]
explanation_text:
Oral allergy syndrome is strongly linked with pollen allergies and presents with seasonal variation

Oral allergy syndrome is the correct option, because the case above describes the typical history of pollen-food allergy, with the raw pears being coated with the allergen in May. This is most commonly associated with birch pollen allergy as described above with the 'springtime hayfever'.

Allergic contact dermatitis is incorrect as the history above is an allergy 10 minutes after exposure, whereas in contact dermatitis it is a type IV hypersensitivity reaction, thus arises 24-48 hours after exposure.

Food allergy is incorrect as the symptoms are localised in OAS, whereas with specific food allergy you would expect systemic symptoms such as vomiting and diarrhoea. Moreover, anaphylaxis is a more common complication of food allergy compared to OAS.

Idiopathic urticaria is incorrect as idiopathic urticaria describes the spontaneous and unrelated to known triggers (unlike in this case with pears) skin manifestation of hives and swelling.

C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency is incorrect as the swelling in this condition has an obvious trigger and there is a seasonal variation which would not be present in the deficiency syndrome. Even though there is a positive family history here, the presentation is also different, with angioedema and abdominal pain most commonly.

question_text: A 34-year-old man who is known to have glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency presents with symptoms of a urinary tract infection. He is prescribed an antibiotic. A few days later he becomes unwell and is noticed by his partner to be pale and jaundiced. What drug is mostly likely to have been prescribed?
options_json: ["Co-amoxiclav", "Trimethoprim", "Ciprofloxacin", "Cefalexin", "Erythromycin"]
explanation_text:
The sulfamethoxazole in co-trimoxazole causes haemolysis in G6PD, not the trimethoprim

Ciprofloxacin

is the correct answer as it is known to potentially cause haemolysis in patients with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency. G6PD is an enzyme that helps protect red blood cells from oxidative damage. When patients with G6PD deficiency are exposed to certain oxidative drugs like ciprofloxacin, their red blood cells can undergo rapid destruction leading to acute haemolytic anaemia, characterised by pallor, jaundice and fatigue.

Co-amoxiclav

is generally considered safe in G6PD deficiency. While penicillins can occasionally cause haemolysis, this is usually through an immune-mediated mechanism rather than oxidative stress, and co-amoxiclav is not typically contraindicated in G6PD deficiency.

Trimethoprim

is also considered safe in G6PD deficiency. While it should be used with caution in patients with folate deficiency, it does not typically cause oxidative stress to red blood cells and can be safely prescribed to G6PD deficient patients.

Cefalexin

, like other cephalosporins, is safe to use in G6PD deficiency. These antibiotics do not cause significant oxidative stress to red blood cells and are often a good choice when treating infections in G6PD deficient patients.

Erythromycin

and other macrolide antibiotics are also generally safe in G6PD deficiency. While they can have various side effects, causing haemolysis through oxidative stress is not one of their recognised complications.
